Dialogue is collaborative: two or more sides work together toward common understanding.
Debate is oppositional: two sides try to prove each other wrong.

Dialogue enlarges and possibly changes a participant's point of view.
Debate defends a participant's own point of view.
Dialogue reveals assumptions for re-evaluation.
Debate defends assumptions as truth.
Dialogue causes introspection on one's own position.
Debate causes critique of the other position.
Dialogue opens the possibility of reaching a new understanding.
Debate defends one's own conclusions as the right ones.
In dialogue, one submits one's best thinking, knowing that other peoples' reflections will help improve it.
In debate, one submits one's own conclusion as the best and right answer.
Dialogue calls for temporarily suspending one's beliefs.
Debate calls for investing wholeheartedly in one's beliefs.
In dialogue, one searches for strengths in the other position.
In debate, one searches for flaws and weaknesses in the other position.
Dialogue involves a real concern for the other person and seeks to not alienate or offend.
Debate rebuts the other position and tries to prove it wrong.
Dialogue assumes that many people have pieces of the answer and that together they can craft a more
complete solution.
Debate assumes that there is a right answer and that someone has it.

1. THE FUTURE OF LIVING WAGE

From the start, the Opportunity is to influence a high-growth community. The family-sustaining jobs and affordable housing our community wants require strategic campaigning. If we see this challenge as an opportunity, we can focus on our community's values and build a powerful message for living wage.

FRAMING THE VOICE
Values in Mind

Mission
We exist to engage people in constructing a vibrant community. We believe that a living wage helps families thrive, strengthens communities, and enhances the economic fabric of our city. We act on this belief by building a campaign for a living wage policy.

Vision
Our campaign will build power through an inclusive, multi-issue coalition that spans race, gender, age, class, and sector. We will link living wage to other community priorities like affordable housing, public transit, quality education, and community development. Together, we will advance a policy agenda that improves the lives of all working families.

Objectives
- Establish a coalition of diverse partners who can sustain a campaign over time.
- Shape public discourse and mobilize community support for a living wage policy.
- Advance a living wage policy at the local level that lifts incomes and improves job quality.
- Empower workers to exercise their rights and improve their economic security.

Strategies
Organize: Engage a broad base of community stakeholders, build strategic partnerships, and cultivate grassroots leadership.
Research & Policy: Analyze local economic and workforce data, identify policy best practices, and develop a comprehensive policy proposal.
Communications: Craft a compelling narrative, generate media attention, and activate supporters through digital and traditional channels.
Mobilization: Mobilize workers, community members, and elected leaders to demonstrate broad support and apply public pressure.

Respects
- Recognize the humanity in each person and treat everyone with dignity.
- Honor the diverse experiences and perspectives of our coalition members.
- Commit to transparency, accountability, and shared decision-making.
- Demonstrate patience, flexibility, and a spirit of collaboration.
- Celebrate small wins and maintain a hopeful, resilient outlook.

"GETTING COVERAGE BETWEEN JOBS

The future of living wage

RESOURCES

CONTACTS

by GEORGE G. BRENKERT
You are guaranteed the opportunity to maintain health insurance coverage between jobs, according to the Consolidated Omnibus Budget Reconciliation Act (COBRA). This provides that you can temporarily continue group health insurance coverage when you lose your job. Your former employer must offer this coverage.

There are some requirements and limitations:

- You must have been covered by a group health plan on the day before the qualifying event, like losing your job.
- The group health plan must continue to be in effect for active employees.
- You must elect COBRA continuation coverage within 60 days of receiving the COBRA election notice.
- COBRA coverage can last up to 18 months for job loss or reduction in hours.
- Your COBRA premiums (the amount you pay for coverage) may be higher than what you paid as an employee, since your former employer no longer contributes to the cost.
- You may have to pay the entire premium yourself, plus a small administrative fee.
- COBRA does not apply to employers with fewer than 20 employees.

For companies with 20 or more employees, COBRA requires that employers offer continuation of coverage for certain events like:
- Termination of employment for reasons other than gross misconduct.
- Reduction in the number of hours of employment.

resources.ocr_text:
The disciples are chosen, not, they are called and nothing more is said. They are chiefly men of humble life and untrained minds. The twelve, with one exception, appear to be ordinary people who have not achieved any great distinction. "The disciples were men of no social or intellectual distinction, yet Christ saw in them the possibilities of great service. In making the choice of his disciples, Jesus passed by the self-righteous and the worldly wise." And as to the disciples, their early life was not marked by any special attainments. Most of them were fishermen from the shores of the Lake of Galilee. To their calling, our Lord joined the simple fishermen at a time when the spirit of the people seemed to be much more ardent than its actual achievement. 

Their calling, the facts of which we know, indicates that they were men of pure intention and honest heart. There is no hint that they were moved by political or social ambitions. Most of them came from the humbler walks of life. So far as the records show, there was no element of self-interest in their relationship with Christ. Jesus' choice of these untrained and unknown men was not a blunder, but a revelation of the divine purpose. The lessons of instruction and training given to the disciples were the preparation for their future work. The disciples were chosen, not as finished products, but as material to be fashioned into servants of the kingdom.

The program includes full text of the process.

5 TAKING THE FIGHT
• Working with the data and insights.
• Framing the challenge as we see it, being strategic and solution-oriented.
• Identifying and harnessing the wider/global changes/trends that impact on the challenge.
• Focusing on the bigger picture and longer-term implications, not just short-term fixes.
• Suggesting/aiming for transformational rather than incremental change.

1. MAKING THE FIGHT
• Start where the humans/the members are.
• Frame the challenge as they see it, in their own terms.
• Refer to people's own experiences and understandings.
• Reflect stories that resonate for them, connect emotionally.
• Focus on the things that the members can do/control, rather than the larger systemic issues.
• What do people already know, think and feel about the challenge?
• Build on shared understandings and interests, don't just push an agenda.
• Speak in a language and style that feels familiar and accessible.

2. RETHINKING THE FIGHT
• Identify and tap into bigger, external drivers and trends.
• Explore macro-level dynamics, not just local, micro-level issues.
• Use data, evidence and wider industry/research to build the case.
• Educate, inform and inspire a new perspective on the challenge.
• Suggest new, innovative solutions that go beyond the familiar.
• Demonstrate a vision for transformational change, not just tweaks.

3. GETTING THERE
• Often, getting there will not come easily from the members - you have to inspire them, help them see a bigger pay-off at the end.
• You have to convince the "unconverted" as well as the already-engaged.
• Bring a campaigning spirit and a belief in the power of collective action.
• Help to build a sense of momentum and progress, show how change is possible.

4. NEXT STEPS
• Thank the members - "we're in this together"
• We can all do our part, we have the power to make the difference we want to see.
• A post-kit - a way for them to continue or rededicate to the cause.
• Contacts for more information and next steps.
• Calls to action: sign up, share, show your support, get involved.
• List of additional resources.

ADDENDA & NOTES

THE FUTURE OF LIVING WAGE
RESOURCES
CONTACTS
ADDENDA & NOTES
Martin Porchia por el diario
A major un salario justo
La diferencia de 400 libras esterlinas al año entre la ganancia de un trabajador típico y la de los directores ejecutivos es tal vez la mejor ilustración de la creciente desigualdad de ingresos que agobia a la sociedad británica. Mientras que el trabajador medio tuvo que hacer frente a una reducción del 10% en su salario real en los últimos 10 años, los directivos de las principales compañías vieron incrementar sus ganancias un 12% por encima de la inflación.
Ahora, un nuevo informe del TUC (Congreso de Sindicatos) ha puesto de manifiesto que las diferencias salariales se han disparado hasta alcanzar niveles sin precedentes. En 1999, los directivos ganaban 47 veces más que un trabajador normal. Hoy esa relación es de 129 a 1.
Estos datos ilustran la creciente brecha entre una minoría de gente muy rica y una mayoría de trabajadores que apenas logra llegar a fin de mes. Según el informe, en el 2000 el 10% más rico de la población británica poseía casi el 54% de la riqueza total del país, mientras que el 50% más pobre apenas controlaba el 7%. 
Estos son sólo algunos datos que confirman la evolución hacia una sociedad más desigual, con una clase media cada vez más empobrecida y una elite cada vez más lejana de la realidad de la mayoría.

Court Appointed Special Advocates (CASA) of Contra Costa County
CASA of Contra Costa County trains volunteers to be the voice and support for children in the foster care system. Volunteers are appointed by the Juvenile Court to advocate for a child's best interests in the courtroom and community. CASA volunteers work one-on-one with a child, get to know their needs, and make recommendations to the court to help the child find a safe, permanent home.

MISSION
The mission of CASA of Contra Costa County is to advocate for the best interests of children who have been abused, neglected or abandoned and are under the protection of the Juvenile Dependency Court.

VISION
We envision a community in which every child who has experienced abuse or neglect has a CASA volunteer to advocate for their best interests.

Domestic violence is a serious threat to women and an urgent public health issue.

The San Francisco Police Department receives more than 500 domestic violence calls for help each month

Since 2000, at least 25 Bay Area women have been brutally murdered by their current or ex-partners.

La Casa de las Madres is here to help.
- Two 24-hour, multilingual crisis phone lines
- On-site with the San Francisco Police Department's Domestic Violence Response Unit
- Skilled legal service coordination ensures victims' civil legal needs, like restraining orders, receive immediate attention.
- 8 week emergency shelter program supports 35 women and children per night
- Drop-in Counseling Center staff provides counseling and support groups for women who have left the shelter but wish to continue their counseling sessions and women who wish to address the impact of domestic violence on their lives.
- Our Teen Advocates are available at our Drop-In Counseling Center and also hold counseling hours at 9 San Francisco high schools to facilitate support for adolescents. Trained counselors assist each teen client with individual counseling, support groups, court and social service accompaniment, advocacy regarding legal, housing, financial and medical needs, and referrals for job training and placement.

In most communities, the reality of low-wage workers who are barely able to sustain a living after the basic needs of food, housing, child care and transportation are met is staggering. This reality is a direct result of the low-wage structure in the United States.

Our experiment is showing how living wage earned by those in the low-wage sectors can lift a household out of poverty and into self-sufficiency. Living wages can provide the dignity of being able to meet one's basic needs with the ability to save for the future.

By increasing the wage floor, more people will have access to a living wage. This promotes economic activity, greater stability for families, and increased municipal tax revenue.

This is more than just an economic experiment - it's a human rights issue. No one should have to live in poverty while working full-time. A living wage is not just a number, but the key to a dignified life.

Empowering Workers of Color:
Looking back, we can see that we've empowered more workers, many of them women, immigrants and people of color, to build the collective power needed to improve their lives. This speaks to the transformative power of organizing for living wages.

A MATTER OF BASIC BUSINESS:
WAGES, LIVING WAGE, AND THE ROLE OF PROFITS

The Maths: The problem with "The Living Wage"

• According to the national living wage figures, an employer would need to pay a living wage of £12.55 per hour.
• At this rate, a full-time employee working 37.5 hours per week would earn £24,372.50 per year.
• However, the average UK business profit margin is just 8-10% of revenue. A typical UK SME with £1 million in revenue would only make around £80,000 - £100,000 in profit.
• Paying a £24,372.50 living wage to just 4 full-time employees would wipe out all the profit for a business of this size.

The implications:
• Raising the minimum wage to a "living wage" level would force many businesses, especially smaller ones, to either:
1. Cut jobs and employee hours to offset the higher costs
2. Raise prices, potentially making their products and services unaffordable
3. Go out of business entirely

The reality is that the government cannot simply legislate higher wages without major consequences for employment, business viability, and consumer affordability. There are no easy solutions, and simplistic "living wage" proposals fail to grapple with the economic realities.

A MODEL FOR YOUR LIVING WAGE MESSAGE:

Living wage is a complex issue involving economic issues, worker justice, and moral concerns. A living wage should provide enough to meet a worker's basic needs - the budget and lifestyle for a single adult, childless household. This can vary by location, but generally includes rent, food, transportation, health care, and other necessities. It is distinct from the legal minimum wage, which is often too low to meet basic needs.

MESSAGE REMINDERS:
• Speak to the realities of low-wage workers in your community. 
• Give specific, local cost-of-living examples.
• Use words like "hard-working" and "struggling" to describe low-wage workers.
• Focus on how a living wage benefits workers, businesses, and communities.
• Avoid divisive language that pits groups against each other.
• Share personal stories to make the message relatable.
• Refer to reputable sources and studies to back up your claims.
• Connect the issue to your organization's mission and values.

Goals and Messaging
The goals is to change attitudes and spur action to increase living wages. Here are some elements of effective messaging:
• Keep it simple, clear, and compelling. 
• Focus on the "why" - the moral, economic, and community benefits.
• Avoid jargon and make it relatable.
• Emphasize the local impact and business support.
• Provide concrete solutions, not just the problem.
• Tell a story of real people and their struggles.
• Call people to a specific action they can take.

Bonus: Make it a visual message - create graphics, videos, etc. to amplify the impact.

The closer message-people can be, the more powerful it will be.

resources.ocr_text:
Side-conversations are at best a distraction - an indication that you've lost attentiveness.

They become a problem when they significantly hand off the facilitating and require an undo diversion of energy towards maintaining control.

On the other hand, a periodic waking up - what is being said and who in the facilitating session.

Occasionally the point of these side-conversations is to interject as a question to the speaker, with a bona fide intent to understand better, not to derail the meeting.

A person who makes a habit of side-conversations will likely fall for the concision that they are not making noise, but are cleverly problem-solving, when in fact they are often effectively hijacking the meeting.

Sometimes peer pressure toward being quiet during a presentation, or expectations to diligently take notes and avoid eye contact, cause a person to retreat to the safety of side-chats, rather than risk the vulnerability of asking a clarifying question.

If on the other hand, the person is new to the meeting, the impulse to whisper may come from an uncertainty about whether a question is appropriate to raise with the whole group. A welcoming tone and a culture of discourse can go a long way toward making a new attendee feel comfortable speaking up.

At a certain point, if the side-conversations are materially distracting the leader or preventing the group from clearly understanding what is being discussed, it becomes important to address the issue sensitively but directly. Calling it out explicitly rests on the leader's judgment about the situation, timing, and tone.

Experience has taught me that some amount of parallel processing - side discussions that provide a more personal connection and space for individuals to process in the moment - is natural and even valuable. The key is to keep it within bounds, so it doesn't detract from the shared focus of the group.

If the side-chatter distracts others or prevents the meeting from progressing, the leader may need to make an intervention - either reminding the group of meeting etiquette, or in some cases, confront the issue more directly with the individuals involved. But this requires discernment and care to avoid escalating tensions unnecessarily.

The underlying goal is to create an environment where people feel heard, trust each other, and can navigate differences productively. Side-conversations can play a role, but they need to be carefully balanced to be genuinely helpful, not disruptive.

Top Five Tips for Our A.L.L. (Women's Advocacy and Leadership Learning) Group:

1. Give New Challenges a Try: Believe in yourself and be open to opportunities to learn. The more you stretch your skills, the more you'll grow.

2. Do not a stranger compare yourself to always and never. Discover the courage to try new things - you may surprise yourself.

3. Progress are progressive. Each step, even a small one, counts. Celebrate the progress you've made.

4. Build up your allies. Surround yourself with people who believe in you, challenge you to reach higher, and have your back.

5. Relax and play when you can. Take care of your emotional and physical needs. It will help you stay strong and focused.

Media Organizing and Messaging
It is a crucial step in our work as advocates to effectively organize and spread our messages. To mobilize supportive constituencies, build public pressure, and shift the debate, we need strategic communication. Our language, messengers, and framing can determine whether people hear, understand, and are moved to act.

Targeting and Developing Message
To mobilize specific constituencies, analyze who your key audiences are, what messages will resonate with them, and the best ways to reach them. Think strategically about how to use different communication channels and messengers for maximum impact.

Messaging and Discourse-Shaping
To shift the broader public discourse, it's important to proactively inject our perspective, reframe the debate on our terms, and challenge the dominant narratives. Weigh how your message and framing will play out in the media and public sphere.

Campaign Strategy and Tactics
Develop an integrated communications strategy that includes earned media (press outreach), social media, advertising, grassroots mobilization, and other tactics tailored to your campaign goals and target audiences. Coordinate your messaging and activities across these different channels.

Media Relations
Building strong relationships with key media outlets and journalists can help ensure your perspective and stories get covered. Provide press with compelling narratives, data, visuals, and spokespeople. Pitch stories, respond to media inquiries, and monitor coverage.

Digital and Social Media
Leverage digital and social media to reach your target audiences directly, share your message and stories, and build an engaged online community. Develop a content strategy, use paid ads, and activate your network to amplify your reach.

Spokesperson Development
Identify, prepare, and support strong spokespeople who can articulately and persuasively represent your organization and cause. Offer media training and message guidance to help them effectively deliver your key points.

Evaluation and Iteration
Continuously assess the impact and effectiveness of your communications work. Track metrics, solicit feedback, and be willing to adjust your strategy, messages, or tactics as needed to maximize your influence.

About This Infographic
This infographic highlights some of the ways sexual violence specifically impacts transgender and non-binary people. While the information in this infographic comes from research, it is important to keep in mind that trans and non-binary people both contributed to the creation of this infographic and are part of our collective movement to end sexual violence.

Now What?
Because we know that sexual violence happens at higher rates for some communities than others based on factors such as race, sexual orientation, gender identity, economic status, disability status, and immigration status, it is vital that we make our services inclusive. To increase access for trans and non-binary survivors, organizations can work with their local LGBT center and can complete organizational self-assessments to identify opportunities to increase access (see Resources). For more information, including resources on understanding sexual violence in various communities, go to www.nsvrc.org/publications.

Definitions
Transgender: This term, sometimes shortened to trans, is often used to describe people whose gender identity or expression differs from what is associated with the gender they were assigned at birth.
Non-Binary: This term is used by some to describe people whose gender is not exclusively male or female, including those who identify as having no gender, as a gender other than male or female, or as more than one gender.
Cisgender: This term, sometimes shortened to cis, is used by some to describe people whose gender identity and expression matches the gender they were assigned at birth.

References
1. James, S. E., Herman, J. L., Rankin, S., Keisling, M., Mottet, L., & Anafi, M. (2016). The report of the 2015 U.S. Transgender Survey. Retrieved from the National Center for Transgender Equality: https://www.transequality.org/sites/default/files/docs/USTS-Full-Report-FINAL.PDF
2. Grant, J. M., Mottet, L. A., Tanis, J., Harrison, J., Herman, J. L., & Keisling, M. (2011). Injustice at every turn: A report of the National Gender Discrimination Survey. Retrieved from The National Center for Transgender Equality: https://transequality.org/sites/default/files/docs/resources/NTDS_Report.pdf
3. Seelman, K. L. (2015). Unequal treatment of transgender individuals in domestic violence and rape crisis programs. Journal of Social Service Research, 41, 307-325. doi:10.1080/01488376.2014.987943

ACTIVE LISTENING SKILLS

What is active listening?
Active listening is a skill that allows you to better understand, remember, and respond appropriately to the communication you receive. It involves more than just hearing the words that are said. It requires the listener to fully concentrate, understand, respond and then remember what is said.

The characteristics of active listening include:
- Focusing your attention on the speaker 
- Avoiding distractions while the person is speaking
- Showing that you are listening through body language and verbal cues
- Paraphrasing the speaker's message to ensure understanding
- Asking questions for clarification
- Avoiding distractions and interruptions 

Some obstacles to active listening:
- Internal distractions (thinking about other things, focusing on your own response)
- External distractions (noise, movement, etc.)
- Jumping to conclusions about the speaker's meaning
- Preparing a response while the person is still speaking

ACTIVE LISTENING

Allow you to gain insight into the person who is speaking, to listen and being willing to learn.
Allow you to get the maximum understanding of what has been said or not said.
Allow you to respond in a way that shows the person that you have heard and understood them.

ATTITUDE: EFFECTIVE LISTENING

Allows you to gather information to better understand the situation. 
Allows you to connect with the person speaking on a more personal level.
Allows you to demonstrate respect and concern for the speaker.

AFFIRMATIVE ACTION

Vision:
The vision is formed as a bold one. It was formed as an educational and human rights organization to promote equality, to break through the barriers of discrimination, and to assist in changing attitudes, policies and standards which have in the past operated to the disadvantage of persons with disabilities, minorities and women and the poor.

"We operate on the basis of consumer consciousness because we recognize the dangers of paternalistic condescension and the danger that the privileged will wish to ameliorate the condition of the unprivileged much more the form of condescension rather than by radical and structural change."

We plan to mount a campaign in order to defend the California Affirmative Action program. This campaign will draw attention to the potential discriminatory effects of Proposition 209. We will draw and display the link between the goal of Proposition 209 and the resegregation of society. We will mobilize a massive public opposition to this dismantling of hard-won civil rights.

On a community level, we plan to emntrain and strengthon affirmative action and diversity programs in our community. We will train our members and allies to become advocates and organizers for affirmative action.

In our efforts to stem the erosion of affirmative action, we will of necessity be coalition building. We will be working with other groups whose liberation is bound to the success of affirmative action, e.g. women's groups, minority groups, disability groups and labor unions.

The long-term goal of our vision is to eliminate the disparities in employment, education, health care and more broadly in the standard of living between the privileged and the marginalized in our society. We recognize that this is a radical and morally imperative goal.

Ultimately, we view the rationale for affirmative action and diversity as being inextricably linked to the struggle for the full social, economic and political equality of all members of our society. 

As a coalition, we share these common goals:
- Defend affirmative action.
- Eliminate institutional discrimination.
- Develop Civil Rights initiative.
Eventually, we hope leadership among people of color, the disabled, and women (in unity)
can replace the hierarchical and top-down leadership that has characterized the current civil rights establishment.

When housing is subsidized it means it is at least partially paid for either by a non-profit service organization or the state, city, or federal government—therefore, subsidized housing is much cheaper. There are often low income-eligibility requirements for subsidized housing, and rental of subsidized housing is often provided on a more short-term basis.

SECTION 8 HOUSING
PROGRAM DESCRIPTION: Section 8 is a federally-funded Housing and Urban Development (HUD) program designed to increase affordable housing opportunities for low-income populations. Each county has Section 8 or Public Housing. Public housing comes in all sizes and types, from scattered single family houses to high rise apartments. Each county has their own application process and wait list. In most counties, Section 8 housing facilities are managed either by the Housing Authority or the Department of Housing. It is easier to obtain Section 8 housing outside of San Francisco and Alameda Counties in the Bay Area. Section 8 Housing in San Francisco is currently completely occupied. The waiting list for new residents is 15,000 names long. There will not be an opportunity to apply for Section 8 housing in San Francisco for the next 5-10 years. When space on the waiting list becomes available, posters will be posted in San Francisco neighborhoods alerting potential applicants that they should apply.

San Francisco Housing Authority:
440 Turk Street, San Francisco, CA 94102
PHONE: (415) 554-1200
HOURS: Monday-Friday, 8AM-5PM

COMMUNITY HOUSING PARTNERSHIP
PROGRAM DESCRIPTION: Community Housing Partnership (CHP) develops and operates permanent housing for formerly homeless people with on-site support services, job training, leadership development and employment opportunities. Residents include formerly homeless singles and families. Housing facilities run by CHP include single-occupancy hotels and multiple-bedroom studios and apartments in the Tenderloin, and single to multiple family homes on Treasure Island.  
COST: Call the intake coordinator to learn more.
ELIGIBILITY: Extremely low-income homeless adults and families that are residents of San Francisco. Applications for housing can be filled out and submitted online.
HOURS: Office hours: Monday-Friday, 9AM-5PM
LANGUAGES: English and Spanish, some staff members speak Cantonese.
LOCATION: Main Administrative Office Address: 280 Turk Street, San Francisco, CA 94102; There are multiple housing locations.

Alzheimer's Day Care Resource Centers
Alzheimer's disease and other forms of dementia affect not just individuals but entire families. At our Alzheimer's Day Care Resource Centers, we offer programs for individuals with dementia as well as support for their families.

Who Is Eligible?
Residents of San Francisco aged 18 and older with Alzheimer's disease, or other dementia-related disorders, particularly in the moderate to severe stages, whose care needs and behavioral problems may make it difficult to participate in existing care programs.

Services Provided
- daytime activity programs specifically designed for individuals with moderate to severe stages of Alzheimer's Disease
- family support groups
- respite for the participant's primary caregivers
- trainings for professionals and others caring for these individuals
- referrals for caregivers to services such as counseling
- some locations may also offer transportation to daytime activity programs

Sample Questions for the ARITHMETIC TEST

Please review the sample questions to help you decide which math placement test to begin with.

If you answer 7 or fewer questions correctly, begin with the ARITHMETIC TEST.

If you answer 8 or more questions correctly, begin with the ELEMENTARY ALGEBRA TEST.

1. A student wants to schedule his time to study for his English, math, and chemistry exams. He plans to spend 1/3 of his time studying English and 1/6 of his time studying math. What portion of his time remains for him to study his chemistry exam?

A. 1/2
B. 1/4
C. 1/6
D. 1/9

2. John drove his new car to Los Angeles, which is 320 miles from his house. He used 12 gallons of gas. He wants to know how many miles he traveled per gallon of gas. Which one of the following expressions must he use?

A. 12 + 320
B. 320 + 12
C. 12
D. 12 × 320

3. Mr. Jones sold his house for $1,000,000 this year. The sale price is 40% more than the original purchase price. Which price is closest to the original purchase price?

B. $600,000
C. $625,000
D. $715,000

4. 4 5/9 - 2 1/6 =

A. 2 4/9
B. 2 17/18
C. 3 1/18

In the problem above, the quotient is closest to which of the following?

A. 6
B. 60
C. 600
D. 6000

1121 Mission Street, San Francisco, CA 94103

www.apilegaloutreach.org
For thirty years, Asian Pacific Islander Legal Outreach (API Legal Outreach) has worked to tear down long-standing barriers that have denied Asians and Pacific Islanders equal justice and equal access to our legal system. They provide legal and holistic services for victims of domestic violence and elder abuse, immigration legal services, and advocacy on social issues, including human trafficking and youth violence. They also provide offer full legal representation for unlawful detainer actions and Ellis Act eviction defense. This includes pre-eviction counseling. API Legal Outreach also provides referrals to other organizations for housing counseling and case management. Services are available in Vietnamese, Korean, Tagalog, Spanish, Russian and Cantonese.

Asian Americans Advancing Justice - Asian Law Caucus
55 Columbus Avenue, San Francisco, CA 94111
415-896-1701
http://www.advancingjustice-alc.org
Founded in 1972, Asian Americans Advancing Justice - Asian Law Caucus is the nation's first legal and civil rights organization serving low-income Asian Pacific American communities. Advancing Justice - ALC focuses on housing rights, immigration and immigrants' rights, labor and employment issues, student advocacy (ASPIRE), civil rights and hate violence, national security, and criminal justice reform. As a founding affiliate of Asian Americans Advancing Justice, the organization also helps to set national policies in affirmative action, voting rights, Census and language rights. The Housing Rights program advocates on behalf of low-income residents in the areas of housing and community development. They provide legal services including eviction counseling and negotiation through representation in unlawful detainer actions. They focus primarily on gateway communities for new immigrants, such as San Francisco Chinatown, where large numbers of tenants and seniors are in danger of displacement due to gentrification and other economic pressures. Their free legal clinics cover such topics as Supplemental Security Income, limited English-proficient tenants and seniors with knowledge of their rights and resources so that they can better preserve their homes and communities. Assistance is offered in Cantonese, Mandarin, Tagalog, and English. Please call to make an appointment.

Hours: Monday-Friday, 9AM-5PM by appointment

resources.ocr_text:
Ask the Doctor

I once had shingles and now my nerves are damaged to the point where I have a difficult time walking without any help. It's been about 4 years. What can you do to relieve the long-term pain of shingles once the rashes have healed?

I have been suffering with sciatic nerve pain running from my left hip down to my ankles. Nothing seems to help. I was told this condition can last 3 weeks to 3 months. I'm doing stretch exercises, but the pain is constant and I'm starting to walk like an old woman. I am a senior citizen (68) and have never, ever experienced this kind of pain. What can I do to prevent this?

Severe back pain should be discussed with your doctor. An MRI or x-ray may be necessary to determine the cause, especially if over-the-counter pain medicines do not help. Visiting a certified massage therapist and a chiropractor may also provide relief.

A healthy lifestyle is the key to preventing back pain:
- Maintain a healthy weight.
- Exercise your abdominal and back muscles regularly.
- Avoid smoking, which can age your spine.
- Practice good posture.
- Lift objects carefully and appropriately. — Squat with your legs and keep your back straight. Let your legs do the work.
- Yoga and tai chi can help your posture and improve strength, balance, and flexibility.

The virus that causes chicken pox stays in your body for life. In older adults, this virus causes a rash and severe nerve pain known as "shingles." Most of the time, the symptoms last a few days. In some cases the pain can last for months or years.

There is no cure for the shingles, but there are some treatment options for managing long-term pain.

Some over-the-counter and home treatment options you can try include:
- Creams made with capsaicin (cap-say-sin), which is extracted from cayenne peppers
- Ice baths or ice packs
- Sunburn lotions that contain lidocaine (ly-do-cane)

Your doctor may prescribe an anti-viral medication that can help control the outbreak. Steroid shots may be needed to quiet painful nerves.

There is a vaccine available to prevent shingles.

You can submit your questions via email to healthmatters@hpsm.org. Some questions will be published in future issues. Your name will not be listed.

1) Reflective listening:
- Paraphrase - repeat back in your own words what you heard
- Summarize - pull together the key points you've heard
- Clarify - ask questions to be sure you understand correctly

2) Reflective questioning:
- "I notice you mentioned ____. Can you tell me more about that?" 
- "That sounds difficult. What has helped you get through similar situations?"
- "I'm wondering if you could explain that a bit further so I can better understand."

Five Basic Communication Skills

1. Listening
2. Empathy: showing concern, interest, and accepting feelings without judgement
3. Disclosing: describing your own reactions, thoughts, and feelings
4. Checking perceptions: verifying your understanding of the situation

How to increase communication skills
1) Make a personal statement: "I feel..."
2) Check your body language: Face your partner, make eye contact, and avoid crossed arms.
3) Speak up about matters "you" find important.
4) Ask for feedback and respond to input. "Are you hearing me correctly?"

Here is the complete text extracted from the image:

Baby Bits

Speak Up
A recent study shows preemies may benefit from hearing their mother's voice just three hours a day. Published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, researchers discovered preemies who were exposed to recordings of their mothers singing, reading or chatting while in the NICU developed larger auditory cortices (which helps in hearing and processing sounds) than those who heard only standard hospital sounds.

5-Second Rule Works!
That long-held belief that if you retrieve food dropped on the floor within five seconds, you're in the clear for eating it was tested recently and found to be true. Researchers at Aston University in Birmingham, England reported in the Journal of Applied Microbiology that time is of the essence to prevent a transfer of bacteria. The "safest" flooring from which to retrieve food is carpeting.

Acetaminophen Use in Pregnancy 
Denmark researchers tested out their premise that acetaminophen may act as a hormone disruptor and alter brain development. They discovered a correlation between pregnant mothers' acetaminophen use and attention deficit hyperactivity disorder in kids.

Introducing Solid Foods Too Early
The American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP) has long recommended that breast milk or formula be a baby's primary source of nutrition during the first six months of life, and to avoid giving infants any solid food earlier than 4 to 6 months of age. The reasoning for this is that young babies need the nourishment that comes from breast milk or formula. In addition, their bodies may not yet be prepared for chewing and swallowing solid food.
A study conducted by the national Centers for Disease Control and Prevention found that many parents are disregarding the recommendations and introducing solids early anyway. Common reasons included: "My baby was old enough," "My baby seemed hungry," and "It would help my baby sleep longer at night."
Ideally, pediatricians say, when solids are introduced, the child should be supporting his or her head well, weighing about 13 pounds and, when you feed him, should not be pushing food back out of his mouth with his tongue.

Five Steps to Choosing a Car Seat
Motor vehicle crashes are the number one cause of death among children. Here's how to pick the best car seat:
1. Make sure the seat is appropriate for their age, height, weight and developmental level. For used seats, find out the history: Has the seat been recalled? Is it expired (average car seat life span is 4 to 6 years)?
2. Car seats can be installed rear-facing or forward-facing in the back of vehicles only. Infants must be secured in rear-facing seats until they are 2 years old or reach the maximum height and weight limit recommended by the manufacturer. Toddlers can move into the forward-facing position after age 2 or after reaching the maximum rear-facing height and weight limits.
3. The safest place to install your seat is in the back row's middle center. The side seats aren't unsafe, just install in a location that is comfortable for you to get the child in and out.
4. More than 70 percent of car seats are not installed correctly! Install using the LATCH (lower anchors and tethers for children) system or vehicle seat belt. Contact local police or fire departments for help.
5. When securing your child to the car seat, click the harness into place and tighten where you can no longer pinch the fabric of the strap. The chest clip should be raised to armpit level for maximum protection.
- Misael Abreu, CPST Injury Prevention Specialist, Boston Children's Hospital Child Protection Program

Living wage on trial
BAIL BOSTON LAW CLINIC

The campaign to establish a higher minimum wage campaign and the case for organizing low-wage workers to demand a living wage is on trial in Massachusetts. The Boston Living Wage Coalition, a group of labor, community, and religious organizations, has been at the forefront of this campaign. 

Since 1997, union organizers and grass-roots activists in this campaign have held public hearings, filed lawsuits, and waged a sophisticated campaign to require the city of Boston and various other institutions, such as Harvard, to pay employees and contractors a living wage - currently estimated at about $8.23 an hour with health benefits, or $9.64 without.

Their opponents, led by business groups like the Associated Industries of Massachusetts, have fought the Living Wage movement with an aggressive legal and political strategy to defeat this reform. The legal battle has reached the state's highest court, which is expected to rule this fall on the legality of the Boston Living Wage Ordinance.

A favorable ruling would provide a major boost to the living wage movement, not just in Boston but across the country. An unfavorable ruling would be a serious setback, requiring a redoubling of grassroots organizing and political efforts.

Justice with the Chapel and Trebles Voices
Once the most glamorous sights on the Boston scene, the Chapel at Boston College and its famous Trebles Voices Choir may again become a center of controversy and confrontation on living wage issues.

Over the past few months, graduate students who comprise much of the choir and whose hours and pay are set by the university have met with university officials to demand a living wage. The demands have met with little sympathy so far, however, and tensions are building.

The controversy pits the university's Jesuit identity and its much-vaunted commitment to social justice against its determination to hold down labor costs. Many in the college community are watching closely to see whether the university's Jesuit values or its bottom line will prevail.

A just man"t-shirt story
Harvard students angered that the university has yet to adopt a living wage policy for its employees and contractors have found a dramatic way to protest - wearing T-shirts bearing the simple slogan "A just man."

The T-shirts, which were designed by a Harvard Divinity School student, have become ubiquitous on the Harvard campus. Worn by faculty, students, and even some administrators, they have sparked widespread discussion and debate about the living wage issue.

The T-shirt campaign is part of a broader effort by Harvard students and faculty to pressure the university to pay a living wage. Their efforts have included public forums, teach-ins, and civil disobedience, with dozens of protesters arrested for staging sit-ins at the office of the university president.

The university, while acknowledging the moral force of the living wage movement, has so far resisted calls to adopt a comprehensive living wage policy, arguing that it would be too costly and difficult to implement. But the T-shirt campaign and other forms of protest have kept the issue alive and prominent on campus.

According to 1991 figures, men are the victims in 7% of spousal abuse cases and women the victims in 93%. This may be skewed by underreporting, but battered men do exist.

Be Earthquake Ready
As you know, earthquakes are very common 
in our area. Your family needs to know what
to do before the next one happens.

1. Look around your home for items that
could fall and cause injuries. Bookshelves,
mirrors, and water heaters should be
fastened to the wall. 

2. Pick a safe spot outside and away from
buildings for your family to meet after the
shaking ends. Practice quickly getting out of
your house or apartment.

3. Arrange to have a friend or family member
who lives outside of the area to be your point
of contact. Phone lines may go down in an
emergency and make it hard for people to reach
you.

4. Collect supplies and build earthquake kits to
keep in your home and car. (See next page.)

Drop, Cover, and Hold On
When you feel an earthquake:
• DROP down onto your hands and knees so
that you don't get knocked down.
• COVER your head and neck with your arms to
protect yourself from falling items. If you can,
safely crawl under a desk or table.
• HOLD ON to the desk or table to keep it over
your head.

After the Quake
Before you move, look around for any items that
may still fall on you. Watch for broken glass or other
harmful items on the ground and make your way to
your family's meeting spot.

If you are trapped, do not try to move. Use your cell
phone to call or text for help. You can also use a
whistle or tap on pipes and walls to signal for help.

As soon as possible, turn on a radio or TV to get
emergency instructions, such as shelter-in-place or
tsunami warnings if you are near the ocean.

Send a message to your out of area point of contact
by text, Facebook, or Twitter to let them know you
are safe.

Call 9-1-1 if you:
• are hurt
• smell a gas leak 
• find downed power lines

It is normal to feel nervous or depressed
after a crisis. If you feel that you need
help coping, call the Behavioral Health
and Recovery Services toll-free line at
1-800-686-0101.

BRANTNING

What is Brantning?
"Phantasomnia" is a way to stimulate creative thinking. Brantning is free expression of ideas on a given subject without the criticism of logical consistency or convention, Patriotism, Fantasy, and Free experimentation. 

The date of fundamentals of Brantning was in 1933 by Alex Oston. Though Brantning had not been used previous to 1933, the idea and method already existed as a recognized psychological means of stimulating new and useful ideas. 

The expression of ideas on a given subject without the criticism of logical consistency or convention. Patriotism, Fantasy, and Free experimentation. 

How Does it Work?
Listed below are the essential elements of a brantning session:

1. The group leader writes the problem on the whiteboard. The 
purpose is to have an immediate focus on the challenge or task. 

2. The reason for the session is explained. The participants are told to attempt to make clear to the group what information or solution is needed.

3. The Count. Rules for brantning should be clearly explained. 

A. Everyone if possible, even if they have nothing to contribute right away, should give an idea or thought. 

B. No evaluation, criticism, or discussion allowed during the brantning.

C. The quantity of ideas is more important than the quality at this stage. Ideas, no matter how "silly" or impractical they may seem, are welcomed.

D. Building on the ideas of others is encouraged.

A time limit for the brantning is set, usually 10 to 15 minutes.

BUREAU OF JUSTICE ASSISTANCE

FACT SHEET

EDWARD BYRNE MEMORIAL JUSTICE ASSISTANCE GRANT PROGRAM

Program Overview
Named after Edward "Eddie" R. Byrne, an officer in the New York City Police Department who was murdered while protecting a witness in a drug case, the Edward Byrne Memorial Justice Assistance Grant (JAG) Program is the leading federal source of criminal justice funding to state and local jurisdictions. Administered by the Bureau of Justice Assistance (BJA), the JAG Program provides states, territories, tribes, and local governments with critical funding necessary to support a range of program areas including:

- law enforcement;
- prosecution and court;
- prevention and education;
- corrections and community corrections, including reentry;
- drug treatment and enforcement;
- planning, evaluation, and technology improvement;
- crime victim and witness initiatives;
- mental health programs and related law enforcement and corrections programs, including behavioral health programs and crisis intervention teams; and
- implementation of state crisis intervention court proceedings and related programs or initiatives (including, but not limited to mental health courts, drug courts, veterans courts, and extreme risk protection order programs.

Also see Purposes for Which Funds Awarded Under the JAG Program May Be Used for more information.

Legislation
The JAG Program is authorized by Title I of Public Law 90-351 (generally codified at 34 U.S.C. 10151-10726), including subpart 1 of part E (codified at 34 U.S.C. 10151-10158); see also 28 U.S.C. 530C(a).

Funding and Awards
Since fiscal year (FY) 2005, BJA has funded over 24,000 direct JAG awards, totalling over $7.6 billion. Award information can be found at Opportunities & Awards | OJP Award Data | Office of Justice Programs.

Formula
For each state and territory, the Bureau of Justice Statistics calculates a minimum base allocation which, can be enhanced by (1) the state's share of the national population and (2) the state's share of the country's Part I violent crime statistics as reported by the Federal Bureau of Investigation's (FBI's) Uniform Crime Reporting (UCR) Program. Once the state funding is calculated, 60 percent of the allocation is awarded to the state and 40 percent to eligible units of local government. For additional details regarding the JAG formula and award calculation process, with examples, please review the JAG Technical Report.

Eligibility and Program Guidance
All 56 states and territories are eligible as well as units of local government and tribes identified annually in the JAG allocation charts. BJA posts the annual JAG Program allocation charts.1

1 States must designate a single State Administering Agency (SAA) that has authority to apply on their behalf. Contact information for each SAA can be found at www.ojp.gov/saa.

BUREAU OF JUSTICE ASSISTANCE
Leadership and Service to Achieve Safer Communities

WHO WE ARE
The Bureau of Justice Assistance (BJA) helps make our Nation's communities safer by strengthening our criminal justice system. BJA's grants, training and technical assistance (TTA), and criminal justice policy development services provide state, local, territorial, and tribal governments, as well as public and private entities, with the funding, support, resources, and best practices they need to reduce crime, support law enforcement, and combat victimization. BJA works with stakeholders to reduce crime, recidivism, and unnecessary confinement and promote a safe and fair criminal justice system.

OUR FOCUS
BJA has a proven track record of facilitating dialogue among researchers; practitioners; and federal, state, local, and tribal criminal justice executives and policymakers. As a result, BJA's investments in programs and TTA are both field-driven and evidence-based.
BJA offers support across the criminal justice spectrum via investments, education, development of tools, and stakeholder outreach and engagement. BJA resources innovate and create sustainable change in our nation's criminal justice system.
BJA also recognizes and honors the extraordinary service of public safety officers through nongrant programs. See the Recognizing Bravery & Sacrifice page at bja.ojp.gov/program/recognizing-bravery-sacrifice for further information.

Learn about BJA's many initiatives at: bja.ojp.gov/programs.

FREE TOOLKITS, TRAINING, AND TECHNICAL ASSISTANCE
BJA offers program-specific toolkits that support the field. See a listing of toolkits at bja.ojp.gov/toolkits.
BJA's National Training and Technical Assistance Center (NTTAC) is a free resource that connects agencies seeking assistance with specialized national experts who can help address their needs. Learn more about BJA NTTAC at bja.ojp.gov.

HOW WE SUPPORT THE FIELD
FUND
Invest in diverse funding streams to accomplish goals.
EDUCATE
Research, develop, and deliver information on programs that work.
EQUIP
Deliver tools and products to build capacity and improve outcomes.
PARTNER
Consult, connect, and convene.

STAY IN TOUCH
Subscribe to receive news and information from BJA at bja.ojp.gov/subscribe-enewsroom or text OJPBJA to 468-311 (message and data rates may apply).

Like BJA on Facebook at: www.facebook.com/DOJBJA.
Follow BJA on Twitter at: twitter.com/DOJBJA.
Subscribe to BJA's YouTube channel at: www.youtube.com/dojbja.

Contact us at: bja.ojp.gov/contact-us.

WHO ARE THE BEST MESSENGERS? 
TARGETING YOUR AUDIENCE & MESSAGING ALIVING PAGE

Support for living change is very popular in the United States. Yet this support often comes with passing interest, rather than a fundamental change in habit.
The most effective drivers of change are those factors that go beyond simple slogans or emotional messages. The most effective tips relate to one's everyday personal, social, and professional lives.
The message is most often effective when it is seen as a reasonable, step-by-step, achievable change - rather than a radical conversion. First, a wide range of background information needs to be clearly communicated to the target audience.
Key factors that can enable permanent lifestyle changes:
Support for a specific behavior change, along with strong social reinforcement networks
Access to appropriate, user-friendly tools and resources
Knowledge of personal benefits and practical steps for implementation
Overcoming specific barriers or challenges to adoption
Consistent positive messaging from credible, trustworthy sources
Maintaining a long-term focus and not expecting immediate results
Socially connecting the change to group identity and values
Leverage existing habits and routines, rather than creating new ones from scratch
Messages should allow for self-discovery of benefits, rather than directive commands
Enable small, incremental steps that lead to bigger lifestyle shifts over time

DIFFERENT SPOKESPEOPLE ARE BEST
Different spokespeople will be effective with different target audiences. Some effective messengers include:
Celebrities, influencers, or experts that the audience already trusts and respects
Community leaders and role models that represent the target audience
Relatable "real people" with similar backgrounds and experiences
Well-respected authorities in relevant fields or industries
Messaging should be tailored to the specific needs, motivations, and communication styles of the target audience.
Neither one-size-fits-all nor overly technical/academic approaches tend to be effective.

CASE STUDY 1. THE FUTURE OF LIVING WAGE

The present-day situation of graduate employees, as reflected in the growth of postgraduate occupations, appears to be that a significant proportion of those completing postgraduate qualifications find themselves under-employed or in temporary or casual jobs.
We need to be aware of the economic and social consequences of this situation, as it may be storing up problems for the future. 
The growth of postgraduate occupations is striking, and the increasing difficulty young people face in obtaining appropriate careers is causing concern.
By their nature, many postgraduate qualifications have been associated with professional and managerial occupations. The current situation where large numbers of graduates are unable to obtain such jobs must be affecting the return on investment in postgraduate education, both for the individuals concerned and for society.
There are a number of issues here. Firstly, there are the problems of underemployment and career uncertainty facing young people after completing postgraduate qualifications. Secondly, there are the broader economic and social consequences of this trend. And thirdly, there are the challenges this poses for the future funding and provision of postgraduate education.
We need to find effective ways of ensuring that the skills and talents of our postgraduate population are fully utilised, and that the public investment in postgraduate education delivers a good return.

Cal fresh
The is a lot of confusion about CalFresh, what it is about CalFresh?

What is CalFresh?
CalFresh, formerly known as Food Stamps, is for people with limited income to buy nutritious food. Sponsored by the USDA, the program provides a monthly amount of money, on a debit card, that can be used to purchase eligible food items at participating grocery stores.

You can get CalFresh if you meet certain income guidelines. Sponsored immigrants can also get CalFresh, even if they are not eligible for other public benefits.

Geuing CalFresh will not hurt your citizenship or immigration status. You or your family members will not become a "public charge" if you get CalFresh.

You will not have to pay it back and it will not take away from other social services you receive.

Even if you have already been accepted for Cal Fresh, be sure to renew it every year to keep receiving benefits.

For more information on CalFresh, Call 1-800-984-3663.

What else should you know about CalFresh?
- To qualify, at least one household member must be a U.S. citizen or legal immigrant.
- Sponsored immigrants can get CalFresh even if not eligible for other public benefits.
- Getting CalFresh won't hurt your citizenship or immigration status. You won't become a "public charge."
- CalFresh benefits are provided on a debit card to purchase eligible food items.
- You have to renew your CalFresh benefits every year to keep receiving them.

Financial coaching is available.
Find more information on getting CalFresh at 1-800-984-3663.

Address: 1441 L Street, NW, Suite 250, Washington, DC 20005

Hours: Monday - Friday: 9am - 5pm

The Communications & Structures of the Human Condition

In analyses of human behaviors, the dialectic of individuation and collectivization has been a central focus. The individual's need for autonomy and self-definition is balanced against the imperatives of social integration and communal belonging. This tension is played out in the ways people negotiate their relationships to others and to the larger social order.

The Communitarian Perspective

The communitarian view emphasizes the essential social nature of the human being. It holds that individuals are fundamentally shaped by their embeddedness in webs of social relationships and cultural traditions. From this perspective, the self is not an autonomous, free-floating entity, but is constituted through participation in communal practices and identification with shared narratives and values.

The Individualist Perspective

In contrast, the individualist perspective accentuates the rights, freedoms, and inherent worth of the individual. It views the self as a sovereign, self-determining agent whose identity and choices should not be overly constrained by social obligations or collective imperatives. The individualist paradigm prizes personal autonomy, self-expression, and the pursuit of one's own goals and desires.

The Communitarian-Individualist Dialectic

The tension between communitarian and individualist orientations is played out in the ways people construct their identities, manage their relationships, and participate in social institutions. Individuals may emphasize their uniqueness and right to self-determination, even as they also seek affiliation, recognition, and a sense of belonging within communities.

The Caminando Juntas Approach

Caminando Juntas recognizes this dialectic and seeks to empower women to navigate the complex interplay between individual needs and communal responsibilities. Our programs and services are designed to:

- Cultivate a strong sense of personal agency and self-worth
- Foster supportive peer networks and a collective identity
- Provide guidance in balancing independence and interdependence
- Promote civic engagement and community-building
- Develop strategies for navigating institutional and cultural barriers

Caminando Juntas envisions a world where women are able to fully actualize their potential, while also contributing meaningfully to the well-being of their families and communities. We believe that by helping women find their voices, build connections, and engage as active citizens, we can foster more vibrant, equitable, and just societies.

Human Services Agency of San Francisco
Department of Aging & Adult Services * Department of Human Services

Case Management Services
Case management helps older persons, adults with disabilities or their caregivers coordinate all the services that they may need in order live in their homes or care facilities. The case manager may assess the client's needs, develop a care plan, authorize and arrange for services, coordinate the provision of services among providers, monitor care, and help with discharge from care facilities.

Who Is Eligible?
San Francisco residents who are 60 years of age or older, or individuals between 18 and 59 years of age who are living with disabilities, who are at risk of premature institutionalization and who meet at least one of the following conditions:
- impairment in one or more areas of activities of daily living, such as eating, dressing, transfer, bathing, toileting and grooming
- impairment in two or more Instrumental Activities of Daily Living, such as taking medications, stair climbing, mobility indoor, mobility outdoor, housework, laundry, shopping and errands, meal preparation and cleanup, transportation, telephone and money management
- unable to manage his/her own affairs due to emotional and/or cognitive impairment
- impaired by virtue of a significant event or circumstance that has occurred within the past 12 months

How could this movement of former life members and supporters be nurtured? How does one go about sustaining and expanding such a grassroots campaign like this?

"This Bite Rally is a business group"*
We are a city of small entrepreneurs, independent contractors, and families who have come together to take a stand against these devastating tax increases and to demand a better future for our children.

CONTEXT: Ruis Bite is a city. How to nurture and sustain this grassroots campaign movement of former life members and supporters?

1. RUIS BITE - RISING UP
"The Bite" refers to the amount you feel when your taxes are raised.
The city of Ruis Bite is facing several tough issues:
- Budget deficit of the city is $25 million
- Property taxes have increased 25% over the last 3 years
- Citizens are frustrated with city government and lack of accountability

2. WHAT BITE RALLY IS TRYING TO ACHIEVE
Raise awareness of the financial struggles of the city
Demand fiscal responsibility and accountability from city government 
Oppose further tax increases on small businesses and families

3. STRATEGY
Build a broad coalition of supporters - small business owners, independent contractors, families
Use social media, town halls, rallies to spread the message and gain momentum
Propose alternative solutions to the budget deficit, such as cutting wasteful spending

4. CHALLENGES
Overcoming apathy and cynicism from citizens
Competing with other local issues and priorities
Lack of organizational structure and funding

5. NUTS & BOLTS OF GETTING THE MESSAGE OUT
Contacts - Reach out to local media, community organizations, elected officials
Campaign strategies - Social media, public events, door-to-door outreach
The future of living wage - Advocate for policies that support small businesses and families
Resources - Information on city budget, tax rates, financial impact on citizens

180 Howard Street, Suite 100, San Francisco, CA 94105
415-972-1200
www.community.ccyo.org
Catholic Charities CYO assists thousands of low and moderate income clients each year from all walks of life through their many housing, counseling, senior and family programs. Young or old, hungry, homeless or friendless, Catholic Charities CYO is there to address the problems facing those in need throughout the Bay Area. They offer a hand up, not a hand out, assisting people through difficult times. With 34 programs, Catholic Charities CYO is a recognized leader in providing quality, comprehensive and compassionate care for the poor, the sick, the distressed, children and youth, families, seniors and immigrants -- helping them move toward empowerment and self-sufficiency. Their programs serve people of all faiths; everyone is welcome. Catholic Charities CYO also provides financial assistance with move-in costs for low-income individuals.

San Francisco Housing Authority
1815 Egbert Avenue, San Francisco, CA 94124
415-715-3280
www.sfha.org
The San Francisco Board of Supervisors established the San Francisco Housing Authority in 1938. In 1974, the Housing Choice Voucher Program (formerly "Section 8") was introduced to the San Francisco Housing Authority. Over 10,000 individuals and families have been served through the Housing Choice Voucher Program. Today, the San Francisco Housing Authority serves over 20,000 individuals residing in San Francisco through Public Housing and the Housing Choice Voucher Program.
The waitlists for both Public Housing and the Housing Choice Voucher Program are currently closed, meaning no new applications are being accepted at this time.
If you are currently on the waitlist for Public Housing or the Housing Choice Voucher Program in San Francisco, you may qualify for a preference.
Recognized preferences for the Public Housing waitlist: Veterans, individuals who have been involuntarily displaced from a San Francisco residence, homeless individuals in San Francisco and San Francisco residents paying more than 70% of household income in rent.
Recognized preferences for the Housing Choice Voucher Program (formerly "Section 8"): Veterans, San Francisco District Attorney referrals, Public Housing residents who have been approved for an emergency transfer, individuals who have been involuntarily displaced from a San Francisco residence, homeless individuals in San Francisco, non-homeless individuals who are living in substandard housing in San Francisco, and San Francisco residents paying more than 70% of household income in rent.
You can check your waitlist status, update your waitlist preferences and update your address and phone number online on the Housing Authority website or in person at the Housing Authority.

Causa Justa :: Just Cause
2301 Mission Street Suite 201, San Francisco, CA 94110

www.cjjc.org
Causa Justa :: Just Cause (CJJC) provides free tenant counseling and case management for low-income residents of Oakland and San Francisco through their Housing Committee/Tenants' Rights Clinic. They do not have attorneys on staff, but they can give advice regarding general rights as a tenant in Oakland or San Francisco. If you are having problems with repairs, rent increases, evictions, harassment or other problems with your tenancy, or if you need advice regarding fair housing and discrimination, please call to make an appointment. Services are available in Spanish. The San Francisco clinic is the only Spanish-speaking counselors.
Office Hours: Monday and Wednesday: 1PM-5PM, Tuesday, Thursday & Friday: 9AM – 12PM and 1PM-5PM. Closed for lunch from 12PM – 1PM.

La Raza Centro Legal
474 Valencia Street #295, San Francisco, CA 94103
Phone: 415-575-3500
Fax: 415-255-7593
The Housing Law Program is dedicated to defending monolingual Spanish speaking low income tenants against eviction. Their goal is to protect clients from homelessness. La Raza Centro Legal offers full scope legal representation to their clients. They will fight for a tenant's right to stay or will help obtain a reasonable settlement. If clients are facing an eviction without just cause, Ellis Act eviction, or an owner move-in/demolition/substantial rehabilitation eviction, they will ensure that they receive adequate relocation payments. The Housing Law Program is partnered with Asian Pacific Islander Legal Outreach and Asian Law Caucus and all are committed to protecting their clients and ensuring they are well informed about their rights. They also work closely with the Eviction Defense Collaborative, Causa Justa-Just Cause, and the Justice Diversity Center among other community organizations. The Housing Law Program currently offers consultations by appointment. Please call 415-575-3500 to make an appointment.

Chinatown Community Development Center
1525 Grant Avenue, San Francisco, CA 94133
415-984-1450

resources.ocr_text:
CHEMISTRY PLACEMENT TEST

Students who wish to enroll in CHEM 101A or 103A may need to take the Chemistry placement test. See the CCSF Catalog for a description of CHEM course prerequisites. The Chemistry Placement test schedule is available at the Testing Office, Conlan Hall Rm 203, or online.

CAN I TAKE THE PLACEMENT TESTS BY COMPUTER?

You can take the English, ESL and Math Placement Tests in either a computerized or paper-pencil format.

Computerized version: Computerized tests are administered in the CCSF Computerized Assessment Center in the basement of Conlan Hall Rm E5. Seating is limited. Reservations can be made in person at the Testing Office in Conlan Hall Rm 203, or by phone (415) 239-3124.

Paper-pencil version: Students may attend the paper-pencil version of the tests on a drop-in basis. No reservation is required. For dates and times of both computerized and paper-pencil testing, consult the CCSF Placement Testing Schedule.

HOW MANY TIMES MAY I TAKE THE CCSF PLACEMENT TESTS?

1. If you have never enrolled in an English or ESL or Math class:
You may retake the placement tests after three months.

2. If you are currently enrolled in an English or ESL or Math class:
You may NOT retake the placement tests.

3. If you have completed or withdrawn from an English or ESL class:
You may retake the test(s) six months after completion or withdrawal from the class(es).

The CCSF placement tests are for initial placement only and may not be used to jump to higher courses in the program. If you wish to jump courses in ESL or English, contact the ESL or English coordinator.

DO I NEED TO BRING ANYTHING TO THE TEST?

Yes, you must bring your photo ID (e.g. driver's license, passport, etc.). All testing materials will be provided.

HOW CAN I GET A COPY OF MY TEST RESULTS?

1. You can pick up a copy of your test results in person thirty minutes prior to your scheduled orientation at the Testing Office in Conlan Hall Rm 203.
OR
2. You can print a copy of your test results by accessing them online (only if your admissions Application has been processed) at http://www.ccsf.edu/w4.

WHAT IS ORIENTATION?

Orientation is a workshop conducted by a CCSF counselor that acquaints you with the registration process, college facilities, academic and vocational programs, student services, and college procedures, as well as academic expectations and opportunities. See the Placement Testing Schedule for in-person orientation dates or complete orientation online at http://www.ccsf.edu/New_Students/Orientation.

ARE THERE SPECIAL ACCOMODATIONS FOR DISABLED STUDENTS?

Special testing and orientation for students with disabilities are available. To make arrangements and for further information, contact Disabled Student Programs and Services, Rosenberg Library, Rm 323 or call 452-5481 (Voice/TDD).

WHAT WILL I DISCUSS WITH A COUNSELOR?

Mayor's Office of Housing and Community Development
Displaced Tenant Housing Preference (DTHP) Program
1 South Van Ness, 5th Floor, San Francisco, CA 94103
(415) 701-5500
www.sfmohcd.org
In 2013, the Ellis Act Displacement Emergency Assistance Ordinance created a new preference
in all City funded affordable housing programs for tenants who are displaced by Ellis Act
evictions. In 2015, the Board of Supervisors expanded the program to include tenants displaced 
by Owner Move In (OMI) evictions. In 2016, the program expanded further to include tenants
displaced by fire.
Certain tenants who have been or may be displaced by Ellis Act or OMI evictions or been
displaced by fire may apply for a DTHP Certificate. The program offers priority to displaced
tenants for 20% of available affordable units in most new City funded affordable housing
developments. DTHP certificate holders must still meet the eligibility rules for any particular
housing unit, including income limits. To find out more about the DTHP Program, including
eligibility requirements and application information, please visit the MOHCD website at
www.sfmohcd.org. For specific questions regarding this program, please email
dthpcertificate@sfgov.org (preferred) or call (415) 701-5613 and leave a message.

Citedata for Assessing: (In order of importance)

Suicide de Plan: Are a specific described plan in mind? the plan in mind? the pills, the razor blades, or the pistol, the man in the mirror? Does the person have a desperate desire to die, or is the person dealing with life itself? does the person feel hopeless and helpless, or has the person given up completely?

How does the person describe the feelings and thoughts, all reversible and changeable are in mind: are the issues and problems seen as overwhelming and unbearable at the moment, but there may be another way? "I can't go on living like this anymore. Nothing seems to help. It's just too much for me to handle."

What are the options and resources the person has available that could help, or has the person tried? For example, "I've called a crisis line before, but it didn't really help." or "I've thought about talking to a counselor, but I'm not sure how to find one."

History of previous attempts: Does the person have a history of previous suicide attempts or self-harm behaviors? This information can help assess the level of risk and guide appropriate intervention.

Lethal means: Does the person have access to lethal means, such as guns, medications, or other methods? Restricting access to lethal means can significantly reduce suicide risk.

Protective factors: Does the person have strong social support, reasons for living, or a sense of purpose? These can serve as protective factors against suicide.

Immediate action: If the person is in immediate danger, call 911 or a suicide prevention hotline to get the person emergency assistance and support.

Remember, the goal is to provide compassionate support and connect the person with appropriate resources to keep them safe and help them through this crisis.

CITY COLLEGE OF SAN FRANCISCO
FREQUENTLY ASKED QUESTIONS ABOUT PLACEMENT TESTING

Welcome to City College of San Francisco! Now that you have submitted your application, you are ready for the next few steps—placement testing, orientation and counseling.

WHAT IS THE PURPOSE OF THESE PLACEMENT TESTS?
These tests are one way of measuring your skills in Math and English (or ESL). You and your counselor will use these results (together with other information about you) to decide on a program of courses that best suits your needs and interests. Your test results are used for placement purposes only and cannot prevent you from attending CCSF.

CAN I BE EXCUSED FROM ANY OR ALL OF THE PLACEMENT TESTS? 
You can be excused from taking any or all of the placement tests if:
1. You are waiving the English and/or Math placement test on the basis of completing specific college courses or standardized tests. *See Placement Test Waiver Form.
2. You are exempting from the assessment component on the basis of an AA degree or higher, or enrolling in no more than 9 units of courses with no prerequisites. *See the Matriculation Exemption Form.

Forms are available online or at the Office of Matriculation in Conlan Hall, Room 204. For more information, please call 239-3751.

WHICH TESTS DO I TAKE?
All students must take either the ENGLISH or ESL test:
- ENGLISH ~(1-1/2 hours) For native English speakers (or those whose primary language is English)
- ESL (English as a Second Language)~(1-1/2 hours) For those whose primary language is not English

- MATHEMATICS
City College administers three levels of mathematics placement testing:
• ARITHMETIC (45 min) - For students who need to strengthen their basic arithmetic skills or who may be ready to study Elementary Algebra.
• ELEMENTARY ALGEBRA (45 min) - For students who have studied beginning algebra and may be ready to study Intermediate or Advanced Algebra. 
• COLLEGE LEVEL MATH (45 min) - For students who wish to enroll in Trigonometry, Calculus, or higher.

Students may take one or more of the tests; however, all students must begin with either the Arithmetic Test or Elementary Algebra Test. To help you decide which test to begin with, please review the sample questions included in this packet before you arrive at the testing session. The following questions should also help you to decide which test to begin with:

SHOULD I BEGIN WITH THE ARITHMETIC OR ELEMENTARY ALGEBRA TEST?
1. Do you need a review of basic arithmetic (including operations with fractions and decimals)? Yes No
2. Do you need a review of basic algebra? Yes No

If you answered YES to Question 1 or 2, begin with the Arithmetic Test.
If you answered NO to both Questions 1 and 2, begin with the Elementary Algebra Test.

SHOULD I TAKE THE ENGLISH OR ESL (ENGLISH AS A SECOND LANGUAGE) TEST?
1. Is English the first language you learned as a child? Yes No 
2. Did you complete most of your education in the English language? Yes No
3. Do you usually speak English with your friends and/or co-workers? Yes No

If you answered NO to more than one of these questions, you should take the CCSF ESL Placement Test. Even if you have been in this country for several years, you will benefit from CCSF ESL courses, which are offered at many levels. If your results on the ESL Placement Test indicate that you would benefit from general English courses, you will be advised to take the English Placement Test.
