Why do women stay?

The following reasons have been cited as to why battered women, abused women, or women in a violent situation, remain in their abusive situation:

1. Emotional and psychological dependence on their partner. They still love them, even though they are abusive.

2. Lack of social support and isolation. They have little or no contact with family or friends, and no one to turn to for help.

3. Economic dependence. They have no money, job, skills, or housing of their own.

4. Concern for children. They may feel staying is better for the children than leaving.

5. Lack of information about resources and lack of knowledge about their rights.

6. Belief that she is in some way responsible for the abuse and can stop it.

7. Fear of retaliation or harm from the batterer if she leaves.

5. Lack of information about resources and lack of knowledge about their rights.

6. Belief that she is in some way responsible for the abuse and can stop it.

7. Fear of retaliation or harm from the batterer if she leaves.

8. Belief that the abuse will stop or get better, especially after the batterer promises to change.

9. Of course, when victims have been conditioned, over time, to believe that the violence and abuse is their fault, they often blame themselves and stay, believing they deserve it.

Meals for Seniors (http://www.sfhsa.org/136.htm)
If you are a low-income senior, you can visit a community center for tasty meals or have them delivered to you at home.

Community Dining Program
San Francisco's Office on the Aging funds numerous community dining programs, collectively called the Congregate Meals Program.

CHAMPSS Program
This new program for adults 60 or older and their spouse/partners regardless of age, provides healthy and nutritious meals at a designated restaurant. Click here for more information.

Home-Delivered Meals
If you are unable to shop for or prepare your own meals due to a physical or mental condition, and are homebound, you may be eligible to have meals delivered to your home. A small suggested donation is requested for the meal. Eligible participants will be given an opportunity to donate. No eligible participant will be denied a meal because of inability to contribute. For more information call (415) 355-6700.

Emergency Meal Program
Emergency meals are available for seniors and adults with disabilities who have no meal support and are unable to provide meals for themselves. People who are receiving inadequate or limited nutrition, which may cause imminent medical distress, are also eligible. Emergency meals are reserved for people whose income is up to 300% of the federal poverty level (currently $31,200). For more information call (415) 355-6700.

Referrals for Home-Delivered Meals may be submitted:
By Phone
A client can be referred to Home-Delivered Meals over the phone by calling (415) 355-6700.

Online
ONLY Community Providers and Discharge Planners may submit online referrals at this time. Please note, a username and password must be established at first log-in to the online referral system.
1. Go to https://ir2.sfgetcare.com to access the online referral system.
2. Read the instructions for online referrals.
Community Provider Instructions for Referring Online
Discharge Planner Instructions for Referring Online

Single Room Occupancy Food Outreach Program
This program provides weekly supplemental groceries to homebound residents of five single room occupancy (SRO) hotels in the Chinatown area.

Food Pantry Programs
These food pantry programs provide weekly or bi-monthly supplemental grocery to low income seniors and disabled adults. The sites are located throughout San Francisco. Contact 211 for eligibility and more information.

The oppression you face is real and valid.

Defining the Agreement:
Making a Case:
The community of self-identified oppressed and marginalized individuals are to be empowered and supported, not invalidated or dismissed.
The experience and testimony of oppressed and marginalized individuals are to be centered and affirmed.
They should be granted autonomy over their own narratives and conditions.
Efforts to disregard, discount, or silence their perspectives and needs are unacceptable.

Empowerment and Actions:
- Validate and center the experiences of oppressed and marginalized individuals
- Actively listen and be receptive to their perspectives
- Use inclusive and affirming language
- Provide resources and support to address their needs
- Challenge systems and behaviors that perpetuate oppression
- Advocate for equitable policies and practices
- Continuously educate oneself on issues of social justice

HEALTH SERVICES & BENEFITS
for Victims of Trafficking (VOTs) at SFGH's Refugee Medical Clinic

Health care services available for VOTs residing in SF, San Mateo, and Marin counties:
 Certified VOTs: those with Office of Refugee Resettlement certification may receive comprehensive refugee health assessment* at Refugee Medical Clinic
 Pre-Certified VOTs: those in process of certification are eligible for all standard Refugee Medical Clinic services
 Individuals suspected of being trafficked who live in San Francisco may come to the Refugee Medical Clinic for health care services for medical issues and receive services through Healthy San Francisco or other coverage options
 All VOTs: receive culturally competent services with medical interpretation by experienced practitioners

VOTs certified by the Office of Refugee Resettlement or in certification process may be eligible for 8 months of Refugee Medical Assistance/Medi-Cal benefits

*Comprehensive health assessment services for Certified VOTs include:
 Comprehensive health assessment with physical examination
 General health services for identified medical conditions
 Preventive health care, including dental screenings, Pap smears, mammograms, blood tests and immunizations
 Specialty referrals for identified health conditions and social support services
 Mental health assessments including referral linkages
 Assistance with Medi-Cal application as needed
 Discounted civil surgeon services for adjustment of immigration status/Green Card

Please note:
 Use of Medi-Cal will not affect adjustment of status/Green Card process
 Services are provided at San Francisco General Hospital's Refugee Medical Clinic:
995 Potrero Blvd, Bldg 80, 5th Floor, Room #518.
 Please bring the following to your initial appointment: any medical and immunization records, proof of residency in San Francisco (a bill in your name, identification card), and a certification letter if available.

resources.ocr_text:
CONCLUSION
When children are given in relation to the tangibles - toys and games, and books - they are sometimes drawn into concepts that do not seem to lay the groundwork for the pattern of living that the parents themselves are carrying forward. Small things, it is true, produce great results: a child learning to make a boat, to sew, or to knit - even though the result may not be a work of art - is building toward manhood or womanhood. Parents often forget this in the hurry of giving the child pleasant playthings and games. They must be reminded that the part of the upbringing which is most difficult and most delicate is the training of character and the preparation of the spiritual nature. This is the essence of education. Knowledge comes in its own time, when needed. But what is really important is the inner shaping, the inward growth, which determines the child's whole attitude toward life and his relations with his fellow-men. This is something that cannot be rushed: it must go on quietly, steadily, day by day. A child's character is built, not by precept, but by living example, by influences silently at work in the environment. It is the parents' own spiritual quality, their own attitude toward life, that in the end will decide the child's development. That is why any method of child-training must be secondary to the inner life of the home.

people who live, work, or attend school in San Francisco by maximizing existing housing stock. 
They provide a platform, tools, and support to connect homeowners and home seekers. This is
a free service that provides interviews, applications, background screening, and assists with the
housing agreement for all parties involved; mediation and referral services are available as
needed. Parties are matched based on compatible living styles and have an opportunity to

Continuing Student Counseling Department
Letter of Recommendation Policy

A letter of recommendation requires that you make a half-hour appointment with your counselor at least two weeks in advance of when it is needed. This service is never provided on a drop-in basis.

Most counselors write letters of recommendation only for students they know well. For a letter of recommendation to be effective, the counselor must be able to comment on a student's personal qualities as well as his or her academic achievements. If a counselor does not know you, he or she may decline your request for a letter.

Who is best qualified to write you a letter of recommendation?
A person who has been in close contact with you and knows you well is best suited to write a letter. This may include such persons as instructors, counselors, or administrators. The instruction sheet in a scholarship application or University Admissions application often indicates if the letter needs to come from a specific person.

What should you bring to your appointment with a counselor?
To best assist the counselor in writing your letter, please bring the following information:
- Your personal statement (if applicable)
- Your resume
- If you don't have a personal statement, write a two paragraph statement about your qualifications including your academic performance, interests, skills, and any personal qualities which you feel are significant.

When do you pick up your letter of recommendation?
The counselor will indicate to you when your letter will be ready. Do not expect your letter to be written instantly. Your counselor needs time to reflect in order to write you the best letter possible.

resources.ocr_text:
Consilience
Carolines Esays
Darwin's argument is that we have all along been unconsciously perceiving truths, which we have never been able to conscious grasp. The most we can see of the truth will be seen for a time from some other, and then be obscured by the rise and fall of this or that philosophic system...
In 1969, a paper in the Proceedings of the Hoyal Society Speech by the late Dr. C.H. Waddington showed the analogy between the process of natural selection to the steps or decisions made by a scientific commission dealing with proposed scientific projects. Momentum is building in the direction of consilience, unification of knowledge. "The hypothesis by Waddington" showed how the various disciplines of science can be welded into a seamless whole- the sciences ranging from physics through biology to the social sciences....
The basis
is that we can pursue an understanding of the world and our place in it by bringing together different disciplines using rigorous reasoning and empirical evidence, rather than treating them in isolation. This leads to consilience, or the "jumping together" of knowledge across disciplines to create a unified framework for understanding.
The key is to avoid overly narrow specialization and to seek the connections and integrations between different fields of study. Consilience allows us to identify the common threads and underlying principles that tie together diverse phenomena, rather than simply compartmentalizing knowledge.
The goal is a grand synthesis that can provide a comprehensive explanation of the natural and social world. This is a lofty ambition, but one that many thinkers throughout history have strived for, from Aristotle to E.O. Wilson. The potential benefits of consilience include more effective problem-solving, the generation of new scientific hypotheses, and a deeper, more holistic understanding of the human condition.
Of course, consilience is not without its challenges. Disciplinary boundaries can be fiercely guarded, and integrating disparate fields requires a rare breadth of expertise. There are also concerns about oversimplifying complex realities or losing the nuances of specific contexts. But the promise of consilience is that it can help us make sense of an increasingly interconnected world, revealing the fundamental relationships that underlie its rich diversity.
Ultimately, consilience represents an ambitious vision for unifying knowledge in service of a better understanding of ourselves and our place in the natural world. It is a worthy goal that continues to inspire thinkers across disciplines to seek the common threads that bind us all together.

resources.ocr_text:
CRIME HURTS EVERYONE
WE CAN HELP

HOW CAN CalVCB HELP ME?
The California Victim Compensation Board is a state program dedicated to providing financial compensation for many crime-related expenses. Victims who suffer physical injury, threat of physical injury or emotional injury as a direct result of a violent crime may qualify for assistance.

CalVCB understands that financial assistance alone does not eliminate the trauma or emotional suffering of victimization, but hopes that it can relieve some of the added pressures that arise as a result of the crime.

HOW DO I APPLY FOR COMPENSATION?
CalVCB Online allows crime survivors and those assisting them to apply for compensation online from a smartphone, tablet or computer. CalVCB Online is available in English and Spanish: online.victims.ca.gov.

WHAT IS A VICTIM REPRESENTATIVE?
A victim representative is selected by a crime victim to advocate on their behalf. A victim representative may:
• Complete the application (must be signed by the victim)
• Submit necessary documents for verification
• Receive, review and respond to all correspondence (with the exception of local Victim Witness Assistance Center advocates)
• Obtain status updates on the claim
Local Victim Witness Assistance Center advocates will obtain and submit the crime report and all other crime-related documentation needed to complete the application.

HOW CAN I LEARN MORE ABOUT CalVCB?
Call us at: 1-800-777-9229
Email us at: info@victims.ca.gov
Visit our website for details and forms at: victims.ca.gov

victims.ca.gov | 1-800-777-9229 | info@victims.ca.gov | P.O. Box 3036 Sacramento, CA 95812
*Deaf and hard of hearing: Please call the California Relay Service at 711

COVERED CRIMES INCLUDE
BUT ARE NOT LIMITED TO:
• Assault
• Child Abuse
• Domestic Violence
• Drunk Driving
• Elder Abuse
• Hate Crimes
• Homicide
• Human Trafficking
• Online Harassment
• Robbery
• Sexual Assault
• Stalking
• Vehicular Manslaughter

CalVCB CAN HELP PAY FOR:
• Crime scene cleanup
• Funeral and burial expenses
• Home or vehicle modifications for victims who became disabled
• Income loss
• Medical and dental treatment
• Mental health services
• Relocation
• Residential security
• Medical equipment if lost or stolen
There are limits on how much can be provided for each loss.
In certain situations, CalVCB can provide emergency financial assistance within 30 days.

Rev. 5/2022

Crisis Intervention Model for Suicide Crisis:

Make contact at a feeling level. Establish briefly, meet the woman where she is at, emotionally. Let her tell her story - let the woman tell her own personal ponder. history if she wants to. Active listening, picking up on feelings and thoughts.
Suicide risk assessment: Establish a collaborative, empathic relationship. Assess risk factors and protective factors. Determine level of lethality and suicidal intent.
Explore the problem: What is the problem now? Explore with her. What happened? How does she see the situation? What has she tried to solve it? What are her resources?
Stabilize the crisis: Provide support, listen. Did a resolution of the immediate crisis occur? Refer to appropriate treatment or community resource. Check out safety - is there an immediate danger? Develop a safety plan.
Summerize: Agree with the woman about what has been accomplished. If appropriate, schedule a follow-up appointment.

Resources:
- The caller's strengths and weaknesses relative to dealing with the crisis situation.
- Material that maintains or increases the woman's self-esteem and perception that she has the ability to get through the crisis.

Explore Resources:
- What are the caller's existing support systems?
- How can they be mobilized or improved?
- Discuss referral to counseling, join self-help groups, consult physician about medication, etc.

resources.ocr_text:
Chaos Simulations
In a simulated universe, natural laws are represented by mathematical rules. Patterns emerge, but we cannot always predict or explain them.

The evolution of this simulation is like that of a living organism. Over its 3.95 billion year existence, it has grown and diversified, taking on a complexity that may call into question the nature of our own creation.

Scientific method is a construct, a set of rules for understanding the world. It is not a perfect tool, but rather an attempt to make sense of nature. Even at its best, scientific knowledge is provisional and subject to revision.

Story
Imagine a vast grid of virtual blocks, each one representing a portion of a simulated universe. Imagine then, that within each block, complex mathematical rules dictate how it interacts with its neighbors - how energy, matter, and information flow between them.

These blocks, together, create a whole universe, obeying physical laws we recognize as natural. Yet this universe is not real in the way our own is. It is a computer simulation, a virtual world created by humans to study the fundamental workings of nature.

We placed the scientific method to use it, to try and understand the inner workings of our virtual universe. We expected to discover its secrets, to be able to predict and control it. But the more we study it, the more complex and unpredictable it becomes.

Safety
We would grow so focused on trying to master our creation, that we might lose sight of its true nature. It has become a world unto itself, with emergent properties we never imagined. The simulated beings within it may develop in ways we cannot foresee or control.

If we are not careful, our fascination with this virtual world could blind us to the fragility of our own. We cannot forget that it is, ultimately, a simulation - a pale reflection of the rich, messy reality we inhabit. Our universe, with all its mysteries, is the only one we have. We must be its caretakers, not its engineers.

With an interviewer who then prepares the paperwork necessary to file for a restraining order, Interpreters are available at the clinic for clients who do not speak English or Spanish. Child care is also available. Clinic appointments are scheduled on Saturdays or on Thursday evenings.

After the initial interview, CROC files the client's restraining order request at the Court and obtains a Temporary Restraining Order that lasts 2-3 weeks until a hearing. The Temporary Restraining Order must be personally served on the abuser, and CROC can assist with this service. CROC attorneys accompany clients to their restraining order hearings and arrange for interpreters if necessary. At the hearing, the Court can make a Restraining Order that lasts for up to five years.

Call 415-255-0165 to schedule an appointment for an upcoming CROC clinic.

RESOURCES FOR INDIVIDUALS WITH DISABILITIES

Independent Living Resource Center of San Francisco
825 Howard Street, San Francisco, CA 94103
415-543-6222
www.ilrcsf.org
The ILRC of SF is a group of professionals and volunteers, almost all of whom have disabilities themselves. They are passionate about supporting and empowering other people with disabilities to lead meaningful, independent lives and to actively participate in their communities. They work collaboratively with individuals to help them determine what services and programs are right for them. ILRC of SF provides information and referrals related to assistive technology, housing, employment, and eligibility for benefits, as well as free peer counseling. Above all, they are a disability rights advocacy organization, and actively encourage consumers to join their efforts to advocate for the rights of all people with disabilities. The ILRC of SF offers Housing Workshops covering laws that are applicable to tenants with disabilities, types of low-income housing and their eligibility criteria, and resources for conducting a housing search. All Housing Workshops are on Mondays at 1:30PM to 3:30PM. Pre-registration is required.

PRC
785 Market Street, 10th Floor, San Francisco, CA 94103
415-777-0333
www.positiveresource.org
PRC's diverse, committed and experienced benefits staff, comprised of a team of attorneys, advocates and legal assistants, provides direct legal benefits representation to San Francisco residents living with HIV/AIDS or individuals with mental health issues referred by specific Department of Public Health sites. They represent clients throughout the entire administrative process, including initial Social Security related disability claims, reconsideration of initial denials, hearings before federal Administrative Law Judges, and requests for review of unfavorable hearing decisions by the Appeals Council. PRC's Employment Services Program provides vocational rehabilitation and job search services to people with HIV/AIDS or with Mental Health Disabilities. The Employment Services Program assists clients who are receiving services from the Department of Rehabilitation or other mental health providers.

resources.ocr_text:
Cycle of Violence Role Play (All and C1)

C1 (Role Play): I friend to a battered woman and a peer educator on domestic violence. I am what's called an "active bystander". I've seen my friend's partner be very controlling and verbally abusive. I have observed bruises and bumps, but my friend won't talk about it. I want to help, but I don't know the right things to say or do.

C2 (Response): It will be helpful if I a) express my concern for your friend and let her know I'm there to listen without judgment. I could say something like "I've noticed your partner has been very controlling and verbally abusive towards you. I'm worried about your safety and I want you to know I'm here if you need someone to talk to." 
b) validate her experience by acknowledging that the abuse is not her fault. I could say "the abuse is not your fault. No one deserves to be treated this way."
c) avoid giving advice about leaving the relationship, as that decision is very personal and she may not be ready. Instead, I could provide information about local resources that offer support, like a domestic violence hotline or shelter, and let her know those services are available if she wants them.
d) respect her decisions, even if I don't agree with them. My role is to listen, validate, and provide support, not to tell her what to do.

Ultimately, supporting a friend in an abusive relationship requires patience, empathy and letting her know you care, without pressuring her. The most important thing is letting her know you're there for her, no matter what.

DELEGATING RESPONSIBILITY TO OTHERS

By now you've developed a pretty good reputation for the responsibility and reliability you've shown in your present job. Managers seem to appreciate your diligent work, and you've gained their trust. 

Somehow it's gotten to the point where you are expected to take on more and more tasks and decisions. In fact, sometimes you feel you've been given too much responsibility.

You want to be a team player and not let anyone down, but you're starting to feel a little overwhelmed. The workload is growing, and it's becoming harder for you to keep up with everything that's expected of you. 

Because you are so eager to please and demonstrate your capabilities, you sometimes say "yes" to requests, even when you know you're already stretched thin. Or perhaps you feel that if you don't take on the extra work, it will reflect negatively on your performance.

In other words, we are about to discuss your delegating work to others. You've got a good grasp of the task at hand, and you may even enjoy the challenge. However, the time has come to share some of the responsibility with others.

1. BENEFITS OF DELEGATION
We can start by asking "Why delegate work to others?" After all, the work will get done quicker and better if you just do it yourself, right? Not necessarily. Here are some potential benefits:

- It develops the skills and abilities of your team members. Giving others a chance to take on more responsibility is a great way to help them grow and improve their own skills.
- It frees up your own time so you can focus on higher-level tasks, planning, and strategy. You won't be as bogged down in the day-to-day details.
- It helps ensure that work gets done even when you're not around. Your team becomes more self-sufficient.
- It demonstrates trust in your team members and can boost their morale and job satisfaction.
- It can provide learning opportunities that prepare team members for future promotions or advancement.

A. Benefits to the manager
- You gain more time to focus on higher-level priorities.
- You develop a more well-rounded, capable team.
- Your workload is more manageable, reducing stress and burnout.

B. Benefits to Subordinates
- They gain new skills, knowledge, and experience.
- They feel more empowered and valued.
- They have the opportunity to take on challenges that can lead to growth and advancement.

How will your subordination think it's about time you start delegating work?

DEPARTMENT OF AGING
AND ADULT SERVICES
CRISIS ON THE AGING
The rapid growth of the population of older adults, coupled with high rates of chronic health conditions, social isolation, and poverty, has created a crisis for older adults and the systems and services that support them. Older adults are at increased risk of experiencing abuse, neglect, and exploitation as they become more frail and dependent.

PUBLIC CONSERVATOR
The Public Conservator's Office protects and serves vulnerable adults who cannot care for themselves or their finances and have no one else to do so. This includes the elderly, the developmentally disabled, and those with mental illness. The Public Conservator can be appointed by the Superior Court to manage the financial and personal affairs of individuals who are found to be gravely disabled or unable to properly care for themselves.

IN-HOME SUPPORTIVE SERVICES
In-Home Supportive Services (IHSS) is a Medi-Cal program that provides personal care services to low-income adults who are blind, disabled, or 65 years of age or older to help them remain safely in their own homes and avoid institutionalization. Services include housecleaning, meal preparation, laundry, grocery shopping, personal care services (such as bathing, grooming and paramedical services), and accompaniment to medical appointments.

ADULT PROTECTIVE SERVICES
Adult Protective Services (APS) investigates reports of elder or dependent adult abuse and neglect, including physical, sexual, financial, and emotional abuse, as well as neglect and self-neglect. APS social workers work with victims, their families, law enforcement, and other community agencies to address the situation and connect individuals to the help they need.

Here is the complete text extracted from the image:

DEVELOPING RELATIONSHIPS WITH REPORTERS

Cultivate personal relationships with reporters. This is one of the most important steps. You'll be more successful if you take time to get to know individual reporters, their interests, and concerns. Many of Actjrfs' campaigns depend on media coverage.

Identify media. Make a list: jocal, state, national. Identify both general and specialized publications, radio, TV, etc. What does each cover? Who are the key reporters?

Make ongoing contact. Once you have a list, devise ways to be in regular touch. Share story ideas, background information, newsworthy events. Be creative - events, tours, story tips.

Get to know them. Find out what their interests and concerns are. How can you help them do their job? What are their deadlines, preferred formats? Become a source they can rely on.

Develop relationships. The more they get to know you and your organization, the more likely they'll be to cover your issues. Cultivate personal rapport. Stay in touch. Offer information, respond promptly.

Here are some tips for developing relationships with individual reporters:

• Research their previous work. Read or watch their recent coverage to learn their style and interests.
• Personalize your approach. Address them by name, reference their previous work, etc.
• Get to know their schedule and deadlines. When is the best time to reach them?
• Respect their time. Don't monopolize it. Be brief and to the point.
• Offer story ideas and background information, not just press releases.
• Follow up promptly on requests for information or interviews.
• Treat them well. Provide good sources, accurate facts, and reliable comments.
• Remember their names and other personal details. This helps build rapport.
• Be accessible. Make it easy for them to reach you when they need you.
• Say "thank you" when they cover your story, even if it's not exactly how you wished.

Develop an accessible style. The more your reporters see you as a knowledgeable, responsive, and helpful source, the more likely they'll be to turn to you in the future.

THE FUTURE OF LIVING WAGE

Here are some tips on thinking strategically about the future of the living wage and how to plan your campaign:

Recognize trends. Monitoring economic and social trends is essential. What's happening with wages, cost of living, and working conditions? How are families faring? Anticipate needs and changes.

Know the landscape. Who else is working on living wage issues - labor, community groups, faith organizations, etc.? Coordinate efforts, share resources, and avoid duplication.

Look at lessons from the past. Research successes and failures of previous living wage campaigns. What worked, what didn't, and why? This can inform your strategy.

Engage the public. Build broad public support. Educate the community about living wage issues and how they affect families and the local economy.

Develop a vision. Where do you want to be in 5 or 10 years? Set ambitious but achievable goals. Map out the steps to get there.

Focus on systemic change. Beyond individual wage increases, consider policy changes that address the root causes of low wages and inadequate benefits.

CONTACTS

DO YOU QUALIFY?
You may qualify for Healthy San Francisco if you are all of the following:
- A San Francisco resident
- Uninsured for the last 90 days
- Not eligible for public insurance programs such as Medi-Cal or Healthy Families
- Between the ages of 18 and 64
- Living program income guidelines

Healthy San Francisco is available to San Francisco residents regardless of immigration status, employment status, or pre-existing medical conditions.

IF YOU HAVE HEALTH INSURANCE, KEEP IT!
Healthy San Francisco is not health insurance, and has limited services and places you can visit for medical care. If you have health insurance, do not drop it.

HOW TO APPLY
To apply for Healthy San Francisco, you will need to meet with a program Application Assistant. You will be asked to provide documents such as personal identification, proof that you live in San Francisco, and proof of your family income and assets.
During the application process, the assistant will let you know whether or not you qualify.

Make an appointment
To find an enrollment site near you, make an appointment to apply, or for more information, please visit www.healthysanfrancisco.org or call 3-1-1, the City's information line.

Don't wait until you're sick to seek medical care.
Healthy San Francisco participants receive access to regular check-ups and enjoy established, trusting relationships with doctors who are familiar with their medical histories and special medical needs.

PROGRAM FEES
There are two types of fees that may be required after you join Healthy San Francisco: A Participant Fee and a Point-of-Service Fee.

Participant Fees
Your Participant Fee is based on your family size and household income. If your income is below a certain amount, you may not be required to pay a Participant Fee at all.

Point-of-Service Fees
A Point-of-Service Fee is a small fee paid when you visit your doctor, pick up a prescription, or go to the emergency room. The amount of this fee depends on which Medical Home you belong to, and your household income. If your income is below a certain amount, you may not be required to pay a Point-of-Service Fee at all.

To figure out what your Participant Fee might be, use the chart below.

SAN FRANCISCO EMPLOYERS & THEIR EMPLOYEES
Employers with 20 or more employees may choose to make a payment to the City on behalf of their employees to comply with the Health Care Security Ordinance (HCSO).
Employees who meet program eligibility requirements will be invited to apply for Healthy San Francisco. Employees who are not eligible to apply will be assigned Medical Reimbursement Accounts to pay for out-of-pocket medical expenses.

While Healthy San Francisco provides basic and ongoing medical care, the program is not health insurance. If you currently offer health insurance, do not drop it.

For more information about participating in Healthy San Francisco either as an employer or as an uninsured person working in San Francisco, please visit www.healthysanfrancisco.org or call 3-1-1, the City's information line.

DYVNT
Interest: Content  
Description: What are your own-experiences
Relationships
Connections: "What are the 'details' that draw your attention - the story within the one you've been told..."

It's all about discovery - uncovering questions.
Over-telling a problem guarantees its repetition.
Understanding the feature of the speaker.
Listening to their point of view. 
Languages, geography, culture, back to ourselves.
And so on the spiral goes...
As, "Why do I tell myself this story" becomes the question.

Returning:

Over-telling a problem guarantees its repetition. 
Over-telling - convincing - suggesting that once a problem is identified, the way to address it is to repeat the problem over and over. 
Long-term, this approach leaves one mired in the problem rather than free to find resolution.

Life learning suggests that, in fact, the real understanding has a reality level, and real under-standing. 
Over-focusing on one's problem points of view. 
This how the problem is communicated - is important to notice.
What is important is listening for where movement, aliveness and creative life-force might lie.

Challenges of Active Listening:
• By being some open to hearing what is for others, we remember we know not all of it.
• By communicating more about our want than our past, we create an invitation.
• By installing your computer with the most recent and reliable versions, you create an opportunity for new information to live.

By not-judging the present,
you expand the field of vision.
By supporting what is working, even a little, 
you cultivate the possible.
By receiving the story for its gifts - even in distress - 
you make a non-judgmental space possible.

By responding in a spirit of exploration, in a non-judged, non-judgmental way, you make a path for something new.

Call for free, confidential community service information and referrals, including food, housing, immigration, employment assistance, substance abuse treatment, senior services and more.

Available 24 hours a day in more than 150 languages.

AFFORDABLE HEALTH COVERAGE
Get assistance finding low-cost health insurance for you and your children. Learn how to apply for Medi-Cal, Healthy Families, and Healthy Kids & Young Adults.
• San Francisco Health Plan: (415) 777-9992 or (888) 558-5858
Hours: Mon-Fri 8:30am-5:30pm, www.sfhp.org.
Available in English, Spanish, & Chinese.

FOOD ASSISTANCE & NUTRITIONAL SUPPORT
Food Assistance
Many working families are eligible to receive a card (like an ATM card) to help buy groceries. Get up to several hundred dollars a month in food assistance.
• SF Food Assistance Program: (415) 558-1001 or www.benefitsf.org
Hours: Mon-Fri 8am-5pm. Available in English, Spanish, Chinese, Russian, Vietnamese, & Tagalog.

Emergency Meals & Food Boxes
• Food pantries, meal programs & emergency food boxes: Call 2-1-1, www.211bayarea.org.

Nutritional Support
• Women, Infants, & Children Program (WIC): (415) 575-5788, www.sfdph.org/dph/comupg/oprograms/PHP/WIC/ 
WIC.asp. Available in English, Spanish, & Chinese.

HELP WITH YOUR FINANCES
Open a Bank Account
Open a checking or savings account at one of several participating banks and credit unions, even if you have had trouble with an account in the past or have never had an account before.
• Bank on San Francisco: Call 2-1-1, www.bankonsforg.

Free Financial Management Classes
Learn how to budget, save, build credit and manage a bank account at a free financial management class.
Find out where and when there are classes near your home or work.
• Bank on San Francisco: Call 2-1-1, www.bankonsforg.

Free Financial Guidance on the Web
Find info on credit repair, budgeting and finances at The Beehive.
• www.thebeehive.org
Available in English and Spanish.

Help with Money Troubles
If you are experiencing money troubles, need to pay off debt or avoid bankruptcy, Consumer Credit Counseling Service of San Francisco can help put you in control of your financial future.
• Consumer Credit Counseling Service of San Francisco: 1(800) 777-7526, www.cccssf.org

HELP WITH UTILITY BILLS
Lower Your PG&E Bill
Most families who receive the Working Families Credit are also eligible for a 20% discount on their monthly gas & electric bill.
• PG&E: 1(866) 743-2273, http://www.pge.com/myhome/customerservice/financialassistance
Available in English, Spanish, Chinese, & Vietnamese.

Lower Your Home Phone Bill
If you currently receive Medi-Cal, SSI, Food Stamps, Health Families or WIC, you may qualify for help with up to half the cost of your basic residential phone bill through the California Lifeline Telephone Program. 
• California Lifeline Call Center: 1(866) 272-0349
English: 1(866) 272-0350 Spanish; 1(866) 272-0356 Cantonese/Mandarin; 1(866) 272-0355 Vietnamese; 1(866) 272-0353 Tagalog

You have a range of coverage options.
Covered California offers plans with four levels of coverage: Bronze, Silver, Gold and Platinum. At each level, the health insurance company pays for a percentage of your annual health care costs. The benefits offered within each level are the same - no matter which health insurance company you choose. To pick the plan that's right for you, you can compare costs and look at the network of hospitals and doctors in your area.

Coverage   Annual    Paid by health
            deductible insurance company  Paid by you
Bronze     $5,000    60%                40%  
Silver      $2,000*   70%                30%
Gold        *0        80%                20%
Platinum   *0        90%                10%

* Silver is the only level where your deductible and other costs may be lower based on your household income. 
* If you choose Platinum or Gold you will pay a higher monthly premium, so that when you need medical services you can pay less.
* If you choose Silver or Bronze you can choose to pay a lower monthly premium, but when you need medical services, you pay more.
* A minimum coverage plan, which covers worst-case scenarios, is also available for those under 30 or who can prove financial hardship.

Episcopal Community Services
165 Eighth Street, 3rd Floor
San Francisco, CA 94103
(415)487-3300
www.ecs-sf.org

Episcopal Community Services is San Francisco's largest nonprofit provider of homeless services. Their mission is helping homeless and very low-income people to obtain the housing, shelter, jobs, and essential services needed to prevent and end homelessness, and they serve more than 8,000 people annually. Their services include supportive housing, emergency shelter and meals, a shelter behavioral health team, employment counseling, job training, adult education, and services for aging and disabled adults. 

ECS's three shelters provide homeless individuals with a clean, safe place to sleep and daily meals. ECS shelter staff collaborates with many volunteers and outside agencies to sponsor 12-step programs as well as on-site clinics such as podiatry, chronic disease management, flu shot and medical referrals. Shelter staff maintain a shelter library and organize support groups and therapeutic activities (gardening, art, music, etc.).

Their behavioral health team is piloting San Francisco's Coordinated Housing Assessment Program, conducting outreach to homeless San Franciscans and coordinating with housing providers to house those assessed to be the most vulnerable when units become available. ECS is also piloting a two-year effort to enroll homeless people in Medi-Cal and Medicare through the Affordable Care Act.

ECS provides permanent supportive housing for almost 1,200 formerly homeless people across ten properties in the Tenderloin and SOMA. The following services are available to residents: food pantries, job counseling, case management, mental and medical health services, support groups, and afterschool programs with academic tutoring and recreational activities.

ECS's Senior Center provides nutritious lunches and daytime programming, Monday-Friday. This includes educational and socialization programming as well as case management and other support services.

Their six-month culinary training program prepares homeless adults for jobs in food services.

ECS's Adult Education Center helps students with basic literacy, adult education, GED preparation, and job counseling.

GLIDE
330 Ellis Street, San Francisco, CA 94102
415-674-6000
www.glide.org

GLIDE features multiple programs and services for those in need, including a daily meal service, health services, a domestic violence program, and a walk-in center where beds in San Francisco's shelter system can be reserved. GLIDE, in collaboration with the Seasons of Sharing Fund and Catholic Charities, provides access to financial help for individuals and families with back rent, rental and security deposits, and some other major expenses. They also can provide emergency vouchers for clothing, food boxes and household items. The GLIDE Family, Youth and Child Center provides case management, workshops, parenting classes, activities and more. 

There is a licensed early childcare education center and after school programming on-site.

We can also be reached by:
Email: http://evictiondefense.org/
Phone: (415) 947-0797
Fax: (415) 947-0331

**Please use phone and email for administrative matters only. Unfortunately we have no resources to return phone messages and emails about client services.**

Rental Assistance
If you are behind in your rent, you may be able to avoid having an eviction filed against you. 
Our Rental Assistance Disbursement Component (RADCo) provides interest-free loans and grants to tenants residing in the City and County of San Francisco who have fallen behind in their rent due to a temporary financial setback.

To qualify for rental assistance EDC staff must approve your application and you must meet the following criteria:
• You live in San Francisco and are not a Housing Authority tenant.
• Your household has sufficient income to pay your future rent and expenses.
• You plan to stay in your home for at least six months.

Note: You do not have to have a three-day notice to qualify for help. Likewise, you may still be able to get help even if you have already been sued for eviction.

If you drop-in at our office, please be sure to bring the following documentation with you. This will speed up the application process, although we may request additional information depending on your situation:
• Proof of the amount of rent owed through the end of the current month.
• Proof of the regular amount of your monthly/weekly rent.
• Proof of how long you have lived in your home.
• Proof of total household income.
• Photo ID.
• Landlord's name, address, and telephone number.
• Other items may be required on a case-by-case basis.

Fact Sheet Tips
Fact sheets are simply "fact sheets" - they provide information, data, and resources on a given topic. They are often simpler and shorter than brochures, designed to be quickly read and distributed.

Fact Sheet Tips
- This and that sheet are simple, just the facts. They are formatted in an easy-to-read manner.
- For ease of reading, have your information, formatting, and layout consistent. Keep it clean and simple.
- Print fact sheets on colored paper to make them stand out.
- Don't use jargon or make the facts too complex. The goal is to inform, not lecture.
- Include only what people need to know. No filler!
- Use bullets, lists, and short paragraphs to organize information.
- Include key contact information, resources, and how-to's.
- Just the facts, ma'am. Focus on who, what, when, where, why, and how.
- Include graphics, logos, or photos to break up text and make it more visually appealing.
- Keep it to one page if possible. Two pages max.
- Make sure to review, edit, and proofread before printing.

WHAT TO INCLUDE IN
A LIVING WAGE FACT SHEET:
- Introduction
- What is a living wage?
- Why is it important?
- How is a living wage calculated?
- What are the benefits of a living wage?
- What are the impacts of not having a living wage?
- Conclusion

resources.ocr_text:
Here is the complete text extracted from the image:

Facts You Should Know

What is sexual assault?
Sexual assault is any unwanted sexual activity. It includes acts such as unwanted touching, fondling, oral or anal sex, or vaginal intercourse. Sexual assault is never the survivor's fault, no matter what the circumstances.

Who is typically affected by sexual assault?
Sexual assault can happen to anyone, regardless of gender, age, race, ethnicity, social status, or sexual orientation. The vast majority of sexual assault victims are women, but men and children are also affected.

What is the impact of sexual assault?
Survivors of sexual assault can experience a wide range of emotions and reactions, both immediately after the assault and for a long time afterwards. These can include fear, anxiety, depression, post-traumatic stress, difficulty with relationships and intimacy, and physical health problems. Survivors may also develop unhealthy coping mechanisms like substance abuse. The impact is often profound and long-lasting.

Who can be a perpetrator of sexual assault?
Perpetrators of sexual assault can be strangers, acquaintances, friends, family members, or intimate partners. They can be of any gender, age, race, or social status. Most perpetrators are known to the victim.

What is the right to sexual assent?
The right to sexual assent means that every person has the right to decide what happens to their own body. It is a fundamental human right. Sexual activity without consent is a violation of that right and is considered sexual assault.

What is the RCMP "No" to SM, "no" TO rape, "no" to sexual assault?
This is a policy or guidance from the RCMP that clearly states sexual assault, including assault through use of SM or BDSM activities, is never acceptable. Consent is required for all sexual activity.

Who can I contact for support after a sexual assault?
There are several organizations and resources available to provide support, counseling, and information to survivors of sexual assault. These include crisis lines, victim services, counseling centers, and sexual assault centers.

What is sexual harassment?
Sexual harassment is any unwanted sexual behavior that makes a person feel uncomfortable, embarrassed, or unsafe. It can include comments, jokes, gestures, displays, or physical contact of a sexual nature. Sexual harassment is a form of discrimination.

What is the Sexual Assault Support Line?
This is a confidential, 24-hour support line for survivors of sexual assault. They offer crisis intervention, emotional support, information, and referrals to local services. The number varies by location.

What is the Sexual Assault Centre?
Sexual Assault Centres provide counseling, support groups, legal/medical information, and referrals for survivors of sexual assault and their loved ones. Services are free and confidential.

Mission Statement of Family Resource Center: The Family Resource Center is a growing community of connected and supported Vermonters. Ourresources are centered on connecting people and families to the information and services they need. Our mission is to be a catalyst and advocate for the well-being of all individuals and families in Vermont.

Vision Statement: We believe that all people have inherent dignity, worth, and the ability to grow and develop. Our mission is to advocate for and support all Vermonters, particularly those who are vulnerable, marginalized, or under-served in our communities. We walk alongside individuals, couples, and families as they navigate life experiences and challenges, offering tools, resources, and guidance to foster their well-being and help them reach their full potential.

Our programs are designed to provide holistic, wrap-around support to individuals and families. This includes offering education, counseling, and advocacy on a variety of topics to address the complex needs individuals and families may face. We also work to build a stronger community by connecting people to local resources, creating peer support networks, and advocating for systemic change.

Our Service Categories Include:
1. Specialized Children's Services: Activities for children, and the well-being of families with children, including early childhood education, parenting support, mentoring, and summer learning.
2. Family and Community Wellness: Programs designed to support the overall health and well-being of individuals, couples, and families, including counseling, life skills coaching, and community-building activities.
3. Mental Health and Recovery: Services to support those facing mental health challenges or in recovery, such as support groups, therapy, and connection to resources.
4. Mentoring, Employment, and Educational Programs: Initiatives to help individuals achieve their educational and career goals, develop job skills, and access resources.
5. Services to Support Immigrant and Refugee Families: Programs tailored to the unique needs of immigrant and refugee families, including language classes, cultural workshops, and support navigating systems.
6. Senior Services: Activities and resources to support the aging population, including transportation, social opportunities, and caregiver support.

By providing these services, our organization aims to support the family and community resilience of the Vermonters we serve. We are committed to empowering individuals and families, advocating for their needs, and fostering a more connected and equitable Vermont.

FAMILY VIOLENCE CLINIC

VIOLENCE AGAINST WOMEN:
The Family Violence Prevention Fund assists over 1,500 women each year. Based on an analysis of 270 federal and state funded domestic violence and sexual assault programs, we found that in a single day, almost 60,000 women and children were served, and nearly an additional 12,000 could not be served due to a lack of resources.

VICTIMS:
• Victims are primarily women
• 63% required medical treatment for the injuries
• 10% had been strangled the last assault
• 66% of the women had been assaulted during pregnancy
• the violence often escalates over time, escalating from slapping and pushing to beating and choking
• for 50% of the victims, the abuse started after pregnancy

APPENDIX: 
• 67% had a history of alcohol abuse
• 58% had been sexually assaulted as children, in addition to the current battering they were experiencing
• 6.8% had been threatened with a knife or gun
• 60% had sustained minor physical injuries and some had major injuries such as broken bones, black eyes or loss of consciousness
• 67% had self-esteem issues due to the constant criticism and diminishment of the abuser
• 63% had a psychiatric disorder, most often PTSD, but also depression and anxiety disorders
• In most cases, the battering continued after separation or divorce

Farmers Market Shopping Tips

• Have a general list in mind ---Shop with a generic list of what you need for the week and let the farmer's selection, what's in season, fill in for you. For instance, you might know that you want three kinds of snacking produce, and four vegtable dinner sides. In the height of summer, you might come home with three fruits, a cabbage, lettuce, green beans, and sweet corn. If you are shopping for a recipe that calls for a specific vegtable and you don't see it, ask a farmer what would be a good substitute. It is possible to come home with too much stuff and end up wasting it. So make sure you know what you need and get those things, maybe a few yummy extras, but be careful not to over-buy.

• Do a lap ----Take a few minutes and walk around. Look at the prices of the items on your list at different stands. It stinks to pay $2 for a container of strawberries at one stand and then pass another one where they're $1.

• Bring Cash ---- All farmers accept cash. Some might accept other payment methods (including food stamps EBT) and some markets provide a credit-card-for-token service. These are nice options when you need them but cash is fastest and is the easiest way to budget. You can't spend more than you have, right?!

• Carry your own bags -----Many farmers are interested in sustainability and their budget so they don't invest in grocery sacks. Bring your own cloth bag or basket to carry your goodies home. If you plan on buying dairy or meat items, an insulated bag or soft cooler is a good idea.

• Shop early --- The best selection will be available at the very beginning of the market. This tends to be when the farmer's are most chipper and the crowds are lowest too. The stuff that comes off the top of the vendors' boxes is fresher and less smashed than the stuff that spends the day on the bottom of the box. If you can, get to the farmer's market at the start time.

• Shop late --- The previous tip still stands, but if you can't get to the market first thing do not despair. A lot of vendors will just want to unload what they've got left and you can get super cheap, and tasty, goodies at the end of the day.

• Shop for the 'rare' items first -- Farmers play a game every week where they try to bring exactly the right amount of produce so that they sell out during the day. Some have a very limited supply of certain items. If you know you want something in limited supply, make a beeline for the booth and buy it first.

First i. Introduction

Cosmic's attitudes to science and technology (such as to attitudes that science and technology will save the world) have always been ambivalent. It is not science itself that causes problems but the way science and technology are used by those with power. Many people see technology as the solution to the world's problems - the "technological fix". But this is a dangerously simplistic view. Science and technology can be used either for good or ill.

2. Rational consideration:

This evaluation is based on the assumption that technology has no basic values of its own but can be turned to good or bad ends, depending on the values of those who control its use. This means that "this evaluation has no basis", because the solution to the problems technology causes must be sought, not in technology itself, but in the social, political and economic framework within which it operates.

3. Anger -

May be a sign that the scientific/technological system is a manifestation of deeper social and economic factors that are seen as beyond the control of the individual.

4. Fear -

This is rational in the sense that the sheer scale, complexity and power of many modern technological systems can seem to threaten individual control or choice. People who feel powerless in the face of these impersonal forces may resort to fear and anxiety as a response.

5. Harms occurring: 

We might see harms occurring from the misuse of technology (environment, health hazards, etc.) but feel powerless as individuals to do anything about it. Feelings of frustration, helplessness and anger may then arise.

6. Personal action: 

If an individual feels powerless to influence the direction of technological change, then a sense of personal ineffectiveness may lead to an attitude of indifference or cynicism rather than active engagement.

FIVE STEPS TO SUCCESS

1. Establish Your Goals
- Decide exactly what you want to accomplish. 
- The goals should be specific, measurable, attainable, relevant, and time-specific.
- Explain your goals in detail and put them in writing.

2. Identify Your Needs
- Have a clear idea of your current situation, skills, and resources.
- Assess the gap between your current situation and your goals. 
- Examine the problems and obstacles that are preventing you from achieving your goals.
- Determine what additional knowledge, skills, or resources you need.

3. Frame the Issue for Maximum Impact
Do you know how the issue you are facing concerns others? How will addressing it affect them? 
- Write a short, compelling description that explains the issue, who it affects, and why it matters.
- It should convince people that your issue deserves attention, support, and action.

4. Create a Media Plan
Consider how to communicate your issue effectively through various media channels.
- Print - Making media contacts, developing press releases, and securing media coverage.
- Radio/TV - Coordinating interviews, developing talking points, and managing your message.
- Online - Creating a website, using social media, and leveraging digital tools.

5. Create a Media Impact 
- Develop an action plan to generate media interest and coverage.
- Identify key messages, spokespeople, and opportunities for media exposure.
- Measure the results of your media outreach and make adjustments as needed.

Winning Strategies for Media Impact

FRAMING THE NEWS
For from being an objective, "view from nowhere," news is inevitably shaped by the subjective views of those who produce it. Newspapers, television broadcasts, and online publications all make interpretive choices in determining what is news. Newspeople inevitably bring their own biases, perspectives, and angles to their reporting, consciously or not. Newsmakes are engaged in what is called "framing"—the process of selecting certain aspects of a perceived reality and making them more salient in a communicating text, in such a way as to promote a particular problem definition, causal interpretation, moral evaluation, and/or treatment recommendation for the item described.

How Framing Works
Frameworks function to highlight selected aspects of a situation, making them more noticeable and meaningful, while simultaneously obscuring and diverting attention from other aspects. Frames shape not only what audiences think about an issue, but how they think about it. Frames highlight some features while ignoring or downplaying others, and as a result, shape the issues in the public discourse.

The Power of Framing
When news is framed a particular way, it can have a significant impact on public opinion, political decision-making, and even long-term social change. Framing a social problem as an issue of personal responsibility or as a product of social injustice can completely change the "solution" that seems appropriate. Similarly, how a political candidate is framed as either an honest reformer or a greedy flip-flopper can influence how voters perceive the candidate.

6 Campaign Strategies
• Stay on message: Repeat your key points over and over
• Dramatize the issue: Use vivid examples and emotional appeals
• Control the debate: Set the terms of what is discussed
• Appeal to values: Frame issues in terms of cherished beliefs
• Simplify the argument: Reduce complex issues to simple choices
• Change the subject: Shift attention to a different issue

THE FUTURE OF LIVING WAGE

SAN FRANCISCO MUSEUMS FREE ADMISSION DAYS
Many of San Francisco's museums have at least one day each month where people can visit for free or at a reduced price. Call 3-1-1 for the most up to date information about when each museum is open to the public for free.

THE SAN FRANCISCO SHAKESPEARE FESTIVAL'S FREE SHAKESPEARE IN THE PARK
Free Shakespeare in the Park provides an opportunity for everyone to see high quality, professional theater free of charge. Performances are held each summer at the Presidio's Main Post Parade Ground Lawn (between Graham St & Keyes Ave, near the Officer's Club & Visitor's Center) and seating is general admission. Bring a picnic or purchase snacks at the festival. For more information and a schedule, go to www.sfshakes.org/park/index.html.

SAN FRANCISCO YOUTH SPEAKS - WRITE2PASSAGE: AN UNDER 21 OPEN MICK SERIES
Two youth open mics events each month that serve as excellent entry-level opportunities for new writers. These open mics are hosted by Spokes members and are always free. More information is available at www.youthspeaks.org.

STERN GROVE MUSIC FESTIVAL
Stern Grove Festival is an admission-free performing arts series in Sigmund Stern Grove, an outdoor amphitheater located at 19th Avenue and Sloat Boulevard in San Francisco. 

The series features a variety of performances each year from June through August. Seating is general admission. Bring your own picnic or purchase food at the Grove Café. The festival schedule is available at www.sterngrove.org.

STREET FAIRS/NEIGHBORHOOD FESTIVALS
Haight Ashbury Street Fair (the second weekend in June), The North Beach Festival (June), Castro Street Fair (first Sunday in October)

THE YERBA BUENA GARDENS FESTIVAL
The festival presents a diverse program of free music, theater, dance, cultural events, and children's programs between May and October in Yerba Buena Gardens (Mission between 3rd and 4th Streets). Seating is general admission and picnics are welcome. More information and a schedule are available at www.ybgf.org.

Begun in Fall 2014, the Concerts with Conversation series highlights local, emerging, and seasoned artists in an intimate setting. We invite the audience to stay after each performance to engage in lively discussion with the artists.

Artists are encouraged to share their music and talk about their creative process, inspirations, and how they see their work engaging with issues of our times. These conversations provide unique opportunities to connect with the artists in a more personal way.

All concerts are free and open to the public. Seating is limited, so be sure to arrive early. For more information, please contact the Women's Resource Center at 415-647-3015 or info@sfwrc.org.

Community Music Center: 544 Capp St, San Francisco, CA 94110 / 415.647.6015 / www.sfcmc.org

Health Care Coverage Options
• Medi-Cal
Medi-cal helps pay for a wide variety of medical services for children, seniors and disabled individuals with low incomes. This program is expanding to cover more Californians, including single adults between the ages of 19-64 without dependent children.

In Person

Online

resources.ocr_text:
Getting Help at Home

Many disabled and older people need help with daily tasks. They often count on family members to aid them with bathing, getting dressed, cooking, cleaning, and driving. These family members often have to quit their jobs, or reduce their hours to help.

The In-Home Support Services (IHSS) program, managed by Health Plan of San Mateo, can provide pay for caregivers and other home helpers.

Eligibility
To join the program you must:
- Be a California Resident. 
- Be eligible for Medi-Cal or Supplemental Security Income (SSI).
- Live at home, outside of a hospital or care facility.
- Complete a Health Care Certification with your doctor.

Health Care Certification
You can start the process by talking about the help that you need with your doctor or case worker if you have one. Your doctor will fill out a form that describes the types of tasks that you need help with.

Case File: Anita
Anita has been in terrible pain for the past several months. She has a chronic illness that has made it hard for her to get around. She can't remember when she last saw her doctor.

Anita's neighbor helped her cook meals, shop for groceries, and get to appointments. When her neighbor decided to move away, a care coordinator from Health Plan of San Mateo made a referral to the In-Home Support Services (IHSS) program.

She has since hired an in-home caregiver and sees her doctor often. With IHSS, Anita has been able to continue living in her own apartment.

The state will review this form and decide how many hours of help per month you need. The most serious cases can have up to 283 hours of help each month. Each person has different needs, so this number is decided on a case-by-case basis.

Once you have been approved, you can start paying your caregiver with the funds given to you. This program pays an hourly rate slightly more than minimum wage.

Under state law, you are allowed to appeal a denial.

Gillespie Center

This systematic discrimination and collective dullness it produces, together with the general effects of poverty, ignorance, and degradation, have the effect of developing in the slave-race a type of character very unlike that which is naturally developed in the negro, so far as he preserves his natural integrity and strength. Predisposed to disease, the negro, through his attachment to the climate, his adaptation to the soil, and his local attachments, finds himself in a position where the combined influence of natural and social causes tends to degrade his physical powers and deteriorate the species. An hour's discussion of colonization would suffice to show a group of slaves that their only chance for elevation, or even escape from ultimate extinction, lies in removal from the country. The philanthropist will tell you that this degradation is accidental and temporary, and may be overcome by extending education and religious privileges to the slaves. Without denying the importance of moral influences, it must be admitted that the most essential and permanent causes of this deterioration are material. Under the same severe discipline which deadens his affections, the slave is taught that his true interest lies in a system of forcible resistance to the claims of the master, while his moral nature is crushed by the perpetual consciousness that his position is the result, not of crime, but of a fate over which he has no control, and which he cannot alter. The negro race is thus left to the solitary resource of mere animal propagation, and must be destined to a fate not much above that of domestic animals bred for the shambles.

Personal factors: An individual is conscious, and unconscious, emotions and institutions that shape his or her condition. The unconscious and institutional conditioning by institutions such as cultural, economic, and political forces by organizations and relationships that can persist longer that personal control. This conditioning can produce personal and social constraints that an individual may not be free to resist or change with individual will power alone.

Organizational factors: A national association and systematic changes in unconscious and institutions conditions and processes associated with race, gender, economic status, citizenship that get reproduced over generations. These factors shape personal identity, social networks, and economic opportunities beyond an individual's immediate control.

Institutional factors: national laws, cultural norms, economic systems, political organizations that impact individuals in systematic and often unconscious ways, beyond personal control or resistance. These institutions shape personal identity, social networks, and economic opportunities in ways that can persist over generations.

Our DAILY FREE MEALS PROGRAM fills your body and soul with a nourishing meal in an atmosphere of respect, acceptance and love.
GLIDE's program is the only one in San Francisco to provide 3 nutritious meals a day, 364 days a year, to the city's poor, homeless and hungry.

Daily Meals
We began serving meals in 1969 as a volunteer-run potluck for 50, and now serve on average 2,163 meals a day with the help of 30 kitchen and security staff and thousands of volunteers each year. In 2014, GLIDE served 108,511 meals to seniors, 93,481 Coffee House meals, and 2,481 meals to families with children.

Breakfast: 8am - 9am

Dinner: 4pm - 5:30pm (Monday - Friday) and bagged lunches served Noon - 1:30pm (Saturday & Sunday)

Senior Meals
The dining hall is reserved for seniors each morning from 7:30am - 8am.

Holiday Meals
GLIDE invites the community to special meal services during the Holidays, including Thanksgiving and Christmas. View our current Holiday Meals Schedule.

Women's Breakfast
We welcome participants of GLIDE's Women's Center drop-in support group, Women on the Move to breakfast between 10:30 am - 11am daily.

Serve A Meal
GLIDE relies on 60 volunteers each day to help keep the meals programming running. View opportunities and sign up to serve a meal.

Text in Image:
El Impacto del Buen Samaritano
"Yo emigré de México a los Estados Unidos y al llegar a los Estados Unidos tuve que lidiar con las dificultades de aprender un nuevo idioma y también con pobreza. En concepto de escuela me uní al programa del Buen Samaritano a través de su coordinación con la Unión de Estudiantes Latinos. Mis grados mejoraron y empecé a trabajar con mis compañeros para organizar eventos en nuestra escuela y comunidad. Ahora soy un Líder de Jóvenes en El Buen Samaritano, y rudo a jóvenes que están interesados en la oportunidad de encontrar el camino correcto, en hacer una diferencia y en convertirse en nuestros líderes del futuro."
- Luis Becerra

Nuestra visión es que familias inmigrantes se sientan fuertes e independientes, con la confianza en sí mismos de lograr sus sueños, servir como líderes a sus comunidades, y reforzar nuestra sociedad diversa.

Desde 1894

Got Questions, Comments, Complaints?
Your Go-To Guide to the CPUC
July 2015

Are you a resident and need assistance with a billing, service, or safety issue with a utility and have already contacted the company and spoke to its representative?
The California Public Utilities Commission's (CPUC) Consumer Affairs Branch is here to help! The Consumer Affairs Branch assists residents who have questions about rates or services regarding electric, natural gas, telephone, or water utilities and assists residents who are unable to resolve an issue with their utility company.

Call: 1-800-649-7570

Visit: www.cpuc.ca.gov/PUC/CEC/e_complaint/

Write: CPUC Consumer Affairs Branch, 505 Van Ness Ave., San Francisco, CA 94102

Would you like to comment on a CPUC proceeding or policy issue?
Contact the CPUC's Public Advisor's Office to provide your views, or informal comments, on CPUC proceedings and/or policy issues. Written informal comments sent through email or U.S. Postal Service is the most effective way to thoroughly and accurately provide your feedback on a CPUC proceeding and/or policy issue. The Public Advisor's Office also provides information and advice to residents and groups on how to formally participate in a CPUC proceeding as well as how to file a formal complaint and Alternate Dispute Resolutions.

Call: 1-866-849-8390 or 415-703-2074

Visit: www.cpuc.ca.gov/PUC/aboutus/Divisions/CSID/Public+Advisor/

Email: public.advisor@cpuc.ca.gov

Write: CPUC Public Advisor's Office, 505 Van Ness Ave., Room 2103, San Francisco, CA 94102

Have a complaint about an intrastate moving company, limousine, airport shuttle bus, or Transportation Network Company (TNC or ride-share company)?
Contact the CPUC's Transportation Enforcement Section to file a complaint about passenger carriers, i.e. limos, ride-share company, or intrastate household goods carriers, i.e. moving companies.

Household goods carriers (moving companies): 1-800-366-4782

HELPLESSNESS

HANDLING DIFFICULT SITUATIONS

Because many of the people who come here are dealing with difficult, stressful and challenging situations, it is important that you understand the problem and how to handle the situation. We are here to give you as much support and advice as we can.

- A Person may become pre-cautious and show to handle a crisis. Reacting by offering silence and how to handle Pacific is a.

A listless person may be emotionally disturbed. Dominate the discussion. Often, these needs a rational point of view. Frequently, they just need a person to listen and pay attention.

What is a hyperactive person? Often, they have difficulty describing what they want. They may be nervous, excited, and possibly even angry. Encourage them to breath deeply, pauses to collect their thoughts, and give them time to express themselves.

If the person is effected, with the individual during a crisis, it is effective to provide a quiet and calming environment. Often this reduces the person's anxiety about the situation.

- A Person who is aggressive or abusive will assist you often needs to be firmly asked to lower their voice or told you will not be able to continue the discussion unless they can control themselves. It may be necessary to suggest that you talk again when both of you are calmer.

This individual is easily to suggest that due to their extreme emotion, it may be better to wait and talk again when you both have had time to collect your thoughts. Helping them regain self-control is important to continue the process.

Often an argumentative person will recognize, with help, that they are not really listening but reacting with high emotion. Bringing their attention back to the issue and your willingness to have a thoughtful discussion, if they can lower the intensity, will often be helpful.

A Person who is silent and withdrawn may find it difficult to explain the problem or why they are there. Patience and gentle questions to draw them out will demonstrate your concern and the fact that you want to understand before offering advice or assistance.

UNDERLYING FACTORS WORKSHOPS
Lesson Plan: Theory x Worldview Permawork
1. Identification is how the effects of the elimination of the causes of social oppression are manifested. Worldview or the way one sees the world will significantly determine one's global sense of self, relationships, goals and expectations.
2. No one is naturally or genetically born as an oppressor or victim. There is no human being is born as an oppressor, and no one is naturally or genetically born to be oppressed.
3. Oppression is not systemic. It is the mentorship in which groups who are classified as "superior" or having power in a particular context, are taught to oppress those who are classified as "inferior" or have less power. However, this oppression must be manifested through individual attitudes and behaviors.
4. Biological differences between human beings do not, in and of themselves, cause harm or justify superiority. Differences between human beings exist in terms of variation in physical characteristics, culture, language, skills, and perspectives, but these differences do not necessitate the development of hierarchical social structures, nor do they justify the unequal distribution of rights, resources, and opportunities.
5. Differences in social and economic power in health and play vital, play critical, and deeply related sociohistorical influences on health, education, and socioeconomic opportunities. Social institutions, ideologies, and policies contribute to and perpetuate disparities in health, education, and economic opportunity and status.
6. The perception of oppression is made possible by the conditioning of view. People who are the target group of a particular form of discrimination may not always see or understand that they are being oppressed, whereas others in dominant or privileged groups may not always recognize the oppression that targets others.
7. The condition of both groups the target group and the non-target group is perpetuated through a cycle of oppression, which includes attitudes, beliefs, social institutions, and systemic factors that maintain the oppressed status of the target group. This cycle can only be broken through conscious awareness and action.
8. In addition to force and the threat of force, oppression is perpetuated through the normalization of systemic discrimination, the naturalization of social hierarchies, and the internalization of oppressed beliefs by members of the target group. Breaking this cycle requires both individual and collective transformation.

HEALTH AND WELLNESS
PUBLIC HEALTH COVERAGE PROGRAMS

The following is a brief list of free or low-cost public health coverage programs young adults may be eligible for. Since each has its own eligibility criteria and enrollment procedures, a list of common access points will follow.

MEDI-CAL
Medi-Cal provides medical, dental and vision coverage to beneficiaries; services are generally provided at no cost; however, if an individual is working and makes over a certain amount, there may be a share of cost. Services are available to low-income adults and children based on set eligibility requirements. Eligibility requirements are complex and depend on income and family size.

HEALTHY FAMILIES
Healthy Families provides medical, dental and vision coverage to children for a fee of $4 to $12 per month, per child. The maximum fee charged to one family would be $36 per month. Eligibility requirements for the Healthy Families program are less stringent than those for Medi-Cal. Parents are eligible to enroll any uninsured dependent up to the age of 19.

HEALTHY WORKERS
Healthy Workers is offered to providers of In-Home Support Services (IHSS) and a select category of temporary, exempt as-needed employees of the City and County of San Francisco. Healthy Workers members have access to medical services through the San Francisco Department of Public Health (DPH). The cost is $3 per month, which is deducted from paychecks.

HEALTHY SAN FRANCISCO
Healthy San Francisco is not insurance, but a reinvention of the San Francisco health care safety net, that has been implemented to make primary medical care more accessible to all San Franciscans. It provides a Medical Home and primary care physician to each program participant. Participants also have access to specialty care, urgent and emergency care.

¿Califica usted?
Used pueden calificar para Healthy San Francisco si cumplen con lo siguiente:
- Es residente de San Francisco
- No ha estado asegurado los últimos 90 días
- No es elegible para los programas de seguro público, tales como Medi-Cal o Health Families
- Tiene entre 18 y 64 años
