Healthy San Francisco está disponible para los residentes de San Francisco, sin importar su condición migratoria, situación de empleo o condiciones médicas preexistentes.

Si usted cuenta con seguro médico, ¡Consérvelo!
Healthy San Francisco no es un seguro médico y cuenta con servicios y lugares limitados que puede visitar para recibir atención médica. Si cuenta con seguro médico, no lo cancele.

COMO SOLICITARLO
Para solicitar Healthy San Francisco, necesitará cumplir con un programa asistente de solicitudes. Se le pedirá que proporcione documentos tales como identificación personal, constancia de que vive en San Francisco y constancia de los ingresos y acciones de su familia. Durante el proceso de solicitud, el asistente le hará saber si califica o no.

Haga una cita
Para encontrar un lugar de afiliación cerca de usted, haga una cita. Para hacer su solicitud y obtener más información, por favor visite www.healthysanfrancisco.org o llame al 3-1-1, la línea de información de la ciudad.

No espere a enfermarse para buscar atención médica
En Healthy San Francisco los participantes tienen acceso regular a exámenes, consultas y atención médica especializada con médicos familiarizados con sus historiales clínicos y necesidades.

CUOTAS DEL PROGRAMA
Hay dos tipos de cuotas que pueden ser requeridas después de que usted se une a Healthy San Francisco: la cuota de participante y la cuota de punto de servicio.

Cuotas de participante
Su cuota de participación se basa en el tamaño de su familia, su ingreso y su actividad disponible. Si su ingreso está por debajo de cierta cantidad, es posible que no tenga que pagar la cuota de participante.

Una cuota de punto de servicio es una pequeña cuota que se paga cuando visita a un médico, recoge una receta a la farmacia o la clínica de la casa de salud a la que pertenece y a su ingreso familiar. Si su ingreso está por debajo de cierta cantidad, es posible que no se le requiera el pago de ninguna cuota de punto de servicio.

Empleadores de San Francisco y sus empleados
Los empleadores de San Francisco pueden elegir participar en el programa Healthy San Francisco proporcionando a sus empleados acceso a este programa. Los empleados que trabajan en San Francisco que no son residentes de la ciudad y por lo tanto no son elegibles, pueden recibir un 75% de descuento en la Cuota de participante que pagan cuatro veces al año.

Para más información sobre cómo participar en Healthy San Francisco, ya sea como empleador o como empleado que trabaja en San Francisco, visite www.healthysanfrancisco.org o llame al 3-1-1, la línea de información de la ciudad.

The District Borce of the Bstate

Resolution No. 052-81 
to have the District Board make a finding of fact and determination that on area of the Bstate is blighted and that redevelopment of such area is necessary in the interest of the public health, safety, morals, and welfare.

The Board of Supervisors of the Bstate met in regular session on the 5th day of March, 1981, at the hour of 2:00 o'clock p.m.

Resolution and Determination: 
1) A survey of the conditions existing in the Bstate has been made, and it has been determined that an area of the Bstate described as follows is blighted:

Consisting of approximately 98 acres in the central business district of the City, and generally bounded on the north by the Burlington Northern Railroad right-of-way, on the east by 8th Street, on the south by Washington Street, and on the west by 5th Street. This area has experienced a general deterioration of improvements and is considered detrimental to the public health, safety, morals, and welfare.

2) Upon the basis of this survey, it is hereby resolved that the District Board has duly considered the matter and has determined that the described area of the Bstate is blighted and that redevelopment of the area is necessary in the interest of the public health, safety, morals, and welfare.

3) In making this determination, the District Board has considered such relevant factors as: 
- the age, condition, and use of the existing structures
- the effect of environmental influences
- the extent of incompatible land uses
- the social and economic liabilities of the area
- the predominance of defective or inadequate street layout
- faulty lot layout in relation to size, adequacy, accessibility, or usefulness
- unsanitary or unsafe conditions
- deterioration of site or other improvements
- conditions which endanger life or property by fire and other causes

4) The findings and determination made herein shall be the basis for the District Board to undertake and carry out a redevelopment project in the described area of the Bstate pursuant to the Bstate Redevelopment Law. 

This resolution shall be effective immediately.

The Homeless Advocacy Project (HAP) of the Justice & Diversity Center (JDC) may be able to help you if you are homeless, or threatened with homelessness, and you have a disability or minor children living with you.

HAP is only able to provide assistance with certain types of legal issues. These include:
- Applications for Supplemental Security Income (SSI – federal disability benefits) and issues related to SSI applications
- Eviction defense, especially if you are accused of causing a nuisance or your landlord has obtained a default judgment against you
- Immigration documentation, if you are in the country legally but have lost your immigration documents or have not taken the steps needed to get proper immigration documents
- Brief advice and referrals to other projects or agencies that can help you.

HAP also provides supportive social services. Through JDC's holistic model, social service staff work with attorneys to address clients' legal and underlying psychosocial needs. They can assist clients with a wide range of issues, including health related problems, poverty, mental illness and addiction.

St. Anthony Foundation
150 Golden Gate Avenue, San Francisco, CA 94102
415-241-2600
www.stanthonysf.org

The mission of the St. Anthony Foundation is to feed, heal, shelter, clothe, lift the spirits of those in need, and create a society in which all people flourish. They are committed to providing the poor of San Francisco with basic needs and services as a gateway to reclaiming their sense of dignity and progressing toward stability. Their services include a dining room serving nearly a million hot meals each year, the Tenderloin Technology Lab offering free computer classes and one-on-one counseling, a medical clinic, a drug and alcohol treatment program for men, a free clothing program and a social work center. The Social Work Center's social workers are skilled professionals who utilize their intimate knowledge of the social services terrain to advocate for clients trying to address one-time or ongoing needs. They can help with things as simple as getting a California ID to secure employment, obtaining a child's birth certificate to enroll them in school, or more complicated matters like applying for social benefits plans for client to gain and maintain stabilization.

SAN FRANCISCO RENT BOARD - RENT CONTROL
PROGRAM DESCRIPTION: Rent control is administered by the San Francisco Rent Board. In San Francisco, most tenants are covered by rent control. This means rents can only be raised by certain amounts per year. Tenants who do not have rent control can have their rent increased by any amount at any time with proper 30 or 60-day notice. Knowing the rent control status of an apartment is important.

LOCATION: 25 Van Ness Ave., San Francisco, CA 94102
CROSS STREET: Market
WEBSITE: www.sfgov.org/site/rentboard_index.asp

SAN FRANCISCO TENANT'S UNION
PROGRAM DESCRIPTION: The San Francisco Tenant's Union maintains an informative website at www.sftu.org, including comprehensive information on rent control and tenant's rights, as well as rent control law and rules and regulations that can be downloaded. They also maintain a tenant's rights legal clinic.

PHONE: (415) 282-6622

SEASON OF SHARING FUND
PROGRAM DESCRIPTION: The Season of Sharing Fund is a housing assistance fund for individuals that are elderly, disabled, or have low incomes. It has been set up by the San Francisco Chronicle, and each year businesses and individuals contribute to the fund. The fund is administered to Community Based Organizations throughout the Bay Area, and is given in the form of one-time grants for short-term assistance.

ELIGIBILITY: Senior citizens (60+) or disabled individuals and low-to-moderate income families with dependent children who have a critical one-time need and who reside in the counties of Alameda, Contra Costa, Marin, Napa, San Mateo, San Francisco, Santa Clara, Solano or Sonoma.

PHONE: Contact the 2-1-1 information and referral line to be referred to a local CBO that administers grants from the fund.
WEBSITE: www.seasonofsharing.org

HOUSING

Having a place to call one's own is very important. There are many different types of housing available, some are temporary, some are transitional and some are permanent.

HOUSING: INFO TO KNOW AND SHARE

QUESTIONS TO CONSIDER BEFORE RENTING AN APARTMENT
When an individual is looking for an apartment, there are certain things they should ask their prospective landlord before moving in or signing anything:
- How much is the rent?
- Is there a lease, if so, how long is it?
- Are utilities, like gas, water, or garbage, included in the rent?
- Is there a security deposit?
- What is the total amount due before moving in?
- When is the rent due?
- What is the penalty for a late rent payment?
- To whom do you give, or where do you send the rent to?
- When will the apartment become available?
- Who do you call for repairs and maintenance?
- Individuals should look carefully for anything that needs repairing before signing a rent or lease agreement.

Some San Francisco rentals are rent controlled, which means they are less expensive, because the landlord cannot charge full market value because of local controls. To learn more about rent control in San Francisco, go to www.sfgov.org/site/rentboard_index.asp. For more information about renter's rights see San Francisco's Tenants Union: www.sftu.org.

resources.ocr_text:
How You Can Support Your Friend

In addition to listening, you can help in other ways:

• Share what you've learned. Pass on any materials about domestic violence you've found.

• Explain that it happens to others too. Let your friend know she's not alone.

• Encourage your friend to get help. Explain how to call a domestic violence agency or shelter for information and support. Offer to drive her there.

Tell your friend it's not her fault. People who are battered often believe they cause the violence.

Explain that domestic violence is against the law. No one has a right to hit or hurt others.

Tell your friend how you're willing to help. Be clear about what you can and can't do.

Help Her Make a Plan

Help your friend think about what to do if the violence happens again. She can:

• Know every way she can get out of the house or apartment.
• Know where she can go and how to get there.
• Pack an emergency bag with keys to the car and house, money, and copies of important papers (birth certificates, photo ID, restraining orders). Keep it outside the house or leave it with a neighbor or friend.
• Build a support group of friends and family who would be willing to help in an emergency (transportation, shelter, money, childcare, etc.).

Help her think about how she can be safer. She can:
• Find out about agencies, programs and shelters that offer services to battered women.
• Join a support group.
• Get counseling.

EAT RIGHT BE BRIGHT
If your children are receiving free or reduced school meals, your family may be eligible for the CalFresh program. CalFresh is a food assistance program that helps low-income individuals, families and households by adding to their food budget. The program provides a means to purchase healthy and nutritious food. People who qualify for the program receive their benefits through an Electronic Benefits Transfer (EBT) card, which is a debit-like card, that can be used at most grocery stores around the county.

1. "I believe that there are organizations that through their work are doing an amazing job of creating positive change in the world. The YWCA is one such organization. I see the YWCA as a leader is advocating for women's rights and social justice. They have a long history of fighting for gender equality, reproductive rights, and racial justice. The YWCA's mission is to eliminate racism and empower women. This mission has guided the organization for over 160 years and continues to be at the heart of their work.  

Some highlights of the YWCA's work include: They are a champion for pay equity and economic advancement of women. They also provide critical services like domestic violence services, affordable childcare, and social services to communities in need. The YWCA is also leading the way in advocacy for racial justice reforms and policies that address systemic inequity. Overall, the YWCA is making a real and lasting difference in the lives of women, families, and communities."

2. "Excallent leaders at the YWCA do so much to advance the organization's mission and goals. They are great advocates who really understand the complexities of the communities they serve and how to deliver impactful programming. The YWCA's staff and volunteers are truly the heart and the core of the communities and deliverances of the YWCA's services. They are dedicated, hardworking individuals who contribute invaluable time and energy to advancing the YWCA's mission.

I think it's also important to recognize the real financial challenges that non-profit organizations like the YWCA often face. They do so much with limited resources and I think it's crucial that we as a society find ways to better fund and support the critical work of organizations like the YWCA."

3. "Communication skills. The nature of the work that YWCA staff do often requires strong communication and interpersonal skills. They need to be able to effectively engage with and support diverse communities and individuals who are dealing with a wide range of issues and challenges. Strong written and verbal communication abilities are essential.

Empathy and cultural competence. The YWCA serves a very diverse population of women, children, and families. The staff need to have a deep understanding and appreciation for the unique experiences and perspectives of the communities they work with. They need to be able to provide services in a culturally sensitive and trauma-informed way."

IDENTIFICATION CARDS OR DRIVER'S LICENSES

GETTING AN IDENTIFICATION CARD OR DRIVER'S LICENSE:
A Driver's License or a State ID Card can be obtained at the Department of Motor Vehicles (DMV). A State ID Card is the form of identification for people who do not drive. For more information on how to obtain a Driver's License, individuals may want to look at a copy of the California Driver's Handbook at their nearest DMV office. The process for obtaining a Driver's License includes a written test followed by a behind-the-wheel driving test. If possible, it is very helpful to make an on-line appointment with the DMV to save time before going in. For DMV locations outside of San Francisco or for specific information please refer to the DMV website listed below.

WALK-IN LOCATION:
San Francisco Department of Motor Vehicles
1377 Baker Street, San Francisco, CA 94117
(Cross Street is Fell)
PHONE: (800) 777-0133
HOURS: 8AM-5PM M-F, 9AM-5PM Wed

DOCUMENTATION REQUIREMENTS:
To obtain a Driver's License or State ID, the following information is needed:
- Social Security number
- Proof of one's birth date (i.e. Birth Certificate, Driver's License, etc.)
- Proof of full name (i.e. Driver's License, ID card, etc.)
- U.S. Citizenship or Immigration documents

COST: There is a $28 fee to obtain a Driver's License, a $22 fee to renew one, and additional fees to take the written and driving tests. There is a $23 fee to obtain a State Identification Card. If you meet the income-requirements for eligibility, all of your fees can be reduced to $7.

Governmental and non-profit entities assistance in getting a reduced fee: Individuals who are eligible to receive an I.D. card at the reduced fee may verify their eligibility with a form that can be obtained and filled out through a governmental or non-profit entity other than the DMV; these agencies and organizations may include a specific clinic or program run by the Department of Public Health or a community-based organization for vocational training or re-entry. A representative from the organization must fill out the document titled "Verification for Reduced Fee Identification Card" and give it to the applicant for further processing at the DMV. A correctly filled out form should verify the applicant's eligibility for the reduced fee.

INFORMATION TO KNOW AND SHARE

GETTING IDENTIFICATION

BIRTH CERTIFICATES
GETTING A BIRTH CERTIFICATE:
A Birth Certificate is an important document needed in order to obtain identification and benefits. If the individual was born in San Francisco, he/she can get a birth certificate at the offices of the Department of Public Health. If the individual was born in another city in California or elsewhere outside of the City and County of San Francisco, the most convenient way of obtaining a birth certificate will be by contacting or visiting the Recorder's Office in the county in which he/she was born.

WALK-IN:
Department of Public Health, Birth Certificates
101 Grove Street, Room 105
San Francisco, CA 94102
PHONE: (415) 554-2700: 311
HOURS: 8AM-4PM, Monday-Friday

MAIL-IN REQUEST:
If an individual is unable to obtain a copy in person, he/she may also make a mailed-in request to the State for a birth certificate. This mailed request must include a check or money order made out to the California Department of Health Services, a Birth Certificate Application, a Sworn Notarized Statement, and a formal written or typed request for a Birth Certificate.

MAIL TO:
California Department of Health Services
Office of Vital Records- M.S. 5103
P.O. Box 997410
Sacramento, CA 95899-7410

DOCUMENTATION REQUIREMENTS:
To obtain a birth certificate, the following information is required:
- Individual's full name
- Individual's date of birth
- Individual's Mother's maiden name
- Individual's Father's full name
- Individual's place of birth (including the hospital if they know it.)

COST: $14 is the fee to obtain a certified copy of a Birth Certificate
PAYMENT METHODS: Credit Cards, Bank Cards, Cash, Money Orders, and Checks are all accepted.

Alexandrina must get a living wage
Experts are warning that companies may try to avoid paying a decent "living wage" to their workers. This could increase profits but leave many families struggling to make ends meet. That's why it's vital that we make the business case for the living wage - and ensure firms that pay a living wage are rewarded.

While a living wage can increase short-term costs for businesses, the long-term benefits of increased productivity, staff retention, and a stronger local economy make it a wise investment. Studies show that workers who are paid a living wage are more motivated, work harder, and are less likely to leave their jobs. As a result, companies that pay a living wage often see better customer service and lower recruitment and training costs. 

Many of the most successful and competitive companies in the world, like Costco, Aldi, and Starbucks, are already paying living wages because they understand the business case. It's time for more companies to follow their lead.

To create a society where everyone earns enough to live with dignity, we need to do more to promote the living wage. This could include public procurement policies that give preference to living wage employers, tax incentives for businesses that pay a living wage, and public awareness campaigns to celebrate companies that do the right thing.

When businesses do the right thing, we should all support them. Offering employees a living wage isn't just good for workers - it's good for business, too.

Telephone: NEW DIRECTIONS
KEY NOTES

CAMPAIGN STRATEGIES

THE FUTURE OF LIVING WAGE

RESOURCES

CONTACTS

ADDENDA & NOTES

Experiencing justice and equality, Ending the privatization, exploitation and corporatization of human services, Building the capacity of social movements to lead the fight for economic and social justice, Supporting organizations engaged in collective bargaining and worker organizing, Organizing strong, sustained local and national campaigns to win new, higher minimum wages and social protections, Continuing to advance the living wage model across the US, Fostering the leadership and power of low-wage workers and their allies, Developing comprehensive, multi-pronged strategies to raise the floor and set a higher standard for the treatment of all workers in the US.

When you gain access to Telephone: NEW DIRECTIONS, you are usually offered standard resources and referrals to an array of other services. Instead, this handbook is our chance to go beyond the typical and to offer a deeper analysis and bolder visions for change. 

How are you connecting the dots between the various issues you work on - from wages and working conditions to housing, healthcare, childcare, transportation and more? Are you seeing the common threads and harnessing the potential for collective power? This handbook aims to provide tools, strategies, and inspiration to help you do just that.

Normative and distributive justice: How can we build a society that values all work and workers - not just the most skilled or "productive"? What policies and programs are needed to ensure a decent standard of living for all? 
Economic restructuring: How can we challenge the dominant economic model that concentrates wealth and power in the hands of a few, and instead build an economy that works for the many? How can we build worker power and challenge corporate power?
Racial justice: How can we address the deep, structural inequities that consign so many Black, Latinx, Asian, and Indigenous people to poverty-wage jobs with few protections? What strategies can advance racial equity in the economy?
Gender justice: How can we revalue the work done by women, especially women of color, and ensure their full economic security and empowerment?
Environmental justice: How can we build an economy that is sustainable and regenerative, not extractive and polluting? What policies can create green jobs and a healthy planet for all?

The handbook is divided into five sections that delve into these questions and more:

1. CAMPAIGN STRATEGIES 
Provides an overview of proven and innovative strategies for winning living wages and economic justice, drawing from case studies and insights from campaigns across the country.

2. THE FUTURE OF LIVING WAGE
Explores the key policy debates, innovations, and challenges shaping the future of the living wage movement - from the federal minimum wage to municipal policies, universal basic income, and beyond. 

3. RESOURCES
Offers tools, data, and other resources to support your living wage and economic justice work.

4. CONTACTS
Includes a directory of living wage and worker organizations, movement leaders, and other key allies you may want to connect with.

5. ADDENDA & NOTES
Provides space for you to take notes, jot down ideas, and personalize this handbook for your own work.

We hope this handbook will help you make new connections, find inspiration, and strengthen your campaigns for a more just economy. Let us know how else we can support your work.

KEY TO CONFLICT RESOLUTION

1. Isolation is a pre-requisition to conflict resolution. That is, you must isolate the problem from other related issues. People tend to get lost in a number of side issues, thus the problem itself is often lost.

2. Commitment to resolving the issue rather than using the issue as a way of maintaining or generating power is essential. Commitment must be on the part of both parties.

3. Consideration of relative dignity, or merit, form the basis to the position. In other words, people tend to bargain or negotiate in terms of each other's bargaining position rather than the merit of the case.

4. Each person must be treated and seen as possible. Each person's concerns are valid and conclusion is seen as just.

5. Each person treats the other concerns as genuine. People generally assume that the concerns of others are either exaggerated or unfounded. This prevents the communication and trust being established.

6. Each operates to feel that the agreements are just and mutually satisfying. Rarely do agreements last without this.

7. The agreement should be in writing so that it is clear and so that it is an agreed upon set of stipulations.

8. It is useful to have the natural person, follow up on the agreement, to see it is being complied with.

resources.ocr_text:
Be a Good Friend to Yourself and Others

Know...
Why youth stay in abusive relationships
    They may believe resources are not available. 
    They may not trust adults, including police or school officials.
    They may be afraid of getting in trouble if they went against their parents' wishes.
    They may fear other situations at home or school or on the streets.
    They may feel at fault for using drugs or alcohol.
    They may fear being "outed" if they are gay, lesbian, bi-sexual or transgender.
    They may feel ashamed, embarrassed, isolated, depressed, scared, etc.
    They may feel afraid their peers will blame them.

How you can help a friend get out of an abusive relationship
    Educate yourself about dating violence.
    Listen and believe your friend.
    Be supportive and non-judgmental.
    Don't put your friend down for staying.
    Point out the strengths of your friend.
    Explain to your friend that s/he is not to blame.
    Remind your friend s/he cannot change the abusive person.
    Talk about your concerns.
    Help your friend find out how to set up a safety plan.
    Help your friend talk to adults who can help.
    Offer resources, such as La Casa de las Madres, Riley Center, SFWAR, and CUAV.
    Take care of yourself and don't get directly involved in a dangerous situation.

How you can prevent violence in a dating situation
PROTECT YOURSELF
    Talk about what you both want.
    Go out on group dates with people you know and trust.
    Stay in public places.
    Always have money for bus or cab to get home on your own. 
    Use cell phone to let a friend know where you are (beware of no signal or dead battery).
    Learn self-defense (hit and split; stun and run).

PROTECT YOUR PARTNER
    If you are an abuser, admit that you have a problem.
        Make a commitment to yourself: "I will not force sex or hit."
        Find a counselor or support group or someone else to talk to.
        Get help for drug and alcohol problems. 
    Respect your partner and yourself; you CAN choose not to abuse.

resources.ocr_text:
Leadership Practices
Leaders, as we know, play a key role in energizing an organization.
Leaders set a tone and style and do much to shape the culture of the
organization. As role models, they have a significant influence on
the attitudes, behaviors, and performance of the people they lead.

Challenges for Organizations:
• Leaders are too often preoccupied with operational issues.
• Leaders need to engage the organization, to empower and
inspire people to perform.
• Leaders need to do a better job of articulating vision,
direction, and strategy.

Inspiring a Shared Vision:
Leaders need to create a compelling vision of the future based on
shared aspirations and dreams. They then need to enlist others in
this vision by appealing to their values, interests, hopes, and dreams.
Effective leaders transform the organization by energizing and
empowering people.

Enabling Others to Act:
Leaders need to foster collaboration and build spirited teams. They
empower others to take action and make a difference. They
understand that mutual respect is essential to sustaining the
extraordinary efforts of people.

Modeling the Way:
Leaders show people by their own example how to live the values
they espouse. They are recognized for their steadfast commitment
and their ability to follow through on promises and commitments.

Encouraging the Heart:
Leaders recognize individual contributions and celebrate the values
and victories by creating a spirit of community. They provide their
people with encouragement, support, and appreciation for their
efforts.

Case study
Struggle in the Mountains:

Building Strength for a Road Ahead
Living With Courage

One of the summer-long hikes that Romainia's women's clubs organize each year is the one to Moldoveanu Peak, the highest mountain in Romania. The physical and emotional challenge of climbing this 8,346-foot mountain is part of the clubs' effort to encourage women to set and achieve personal goals. The journey to the summit, they believe, can offer insights into living with courage, strength, and resilience in the face of life's difficulties.

Sarah, one of the hikers, remembers the mental and physical strain of the ascent. "The climb was brutal - the trail was steep and rocky, and the altitude made every step a struggle. There were times when I felt like I couldn't go on." At one point, Sarah fell behind the group and considered turning back. "But I kept hearing the voice of the group leader in my head, telling us that we could do it if we just took it one step at a time. So I kept going."

The Steady View: Moving Forward
Sarah's determination paid off when she finally reached the summit. "The view from the top was absolutely breathtaking - rolling green hills and valleys as far as the eye could see. In that moment, all the struggle and pain of the climb faded away. I felt a sense of accomplishment and pride that I had never experienced before."

Sarah recognizes that the lessons she learned on the mountain have carried over into other areas of her life. "When I'm faced with a challenge now, I try to remember how I felt on that climb. I know that if I take it one step at a time and push through the difficult parts, I can achieve my goals."

The Steady View: Mountaineering Can Offer Insights
The Romania women's hiking club organizes these challenging climbs as a way to help women develop the mental and physical resilience needed to navigate life's difficulties. "The mountain is a metaphor," explains the club leader. "The struggle to reach the summit mirrors the struggles we all face in our daily lives. But if we approach those struggles with courage and determination, like the women on the Moldoveanu hike, we can overcome them and emerge stronger on the other side."

Living Wage Reloaded:
A TIME FOR ECONOMIC JUSTICE: A NEXT FRONTIER
By Neal Gorenflo
The current Living Wage movement - which began with work on municipal living wage laws in Baltimore in the 1990s - has achieved significant but still limited success. We've passed living wage laws in over 140 cities and counties across the U.S. But there is much more work to do.

The key challenge now is to expand the living wage movement beyond city and county governments to impact a larger number of workers and businesses. This means moving toward a system-wide living wage policy that aligns the value of work with the cost of living.

This is the next frontier for the living wage movement. We call it "Living Wage Reloaded." It aims to create a new economic blueprint - one that recognizes the value of all work and ensures that all workers can meet their basic needs.

The communizations strategy:
The communizations strategy is a powerful new approach that can help us get there. It involves creating a network of interconnected enterprises - both for-profit and nonprofit - that are all committed to paying a living wage. The goal is to build an alternative economic system from the ground up, one community at a time.

This approach has several key elements:
- Identifying sectors and industries that are ripe for a living wage transformation
- Recruiting businesses, organizations, and community leaders to participate
- Providing training, tools, and other support to help them transition to a living wage model
- Building connections and synergies between the participating enterprises
- Documenting and sharing the lessons learned to inspire and guide others

The result will be an ever-expanding network of living wage employers that can demonstate the viability and impact of this new economic model. As this network grows, it will exert increasing pressure on the broader economy to align with living wage principles.

The communizations strategy is already underway in several communities, with promising early results. We believe it represents the most powerful path forward for the living wage movement.

We invite you to join us in this exciting next chapter. Together, we can build a more just and sustainable economy - one that values all work and ensures that everyone can meet their basic needs.

resources.ocr_text:
Looking for Housing in San Francisco?

• Walk around & look in the areas that you like. You may be surprised by how many people don't advertise in the paper or on the internet but do post notices in their windows.

• Bring your own credit report. Everyone can get one free credit report per year - go to www.annualcreditreport.com.

• Use the Internet. The public library has computers to use if you do not own one.

• Go prepared to fill out application forms & provide references. Rental resumes are useful, especially if you have a pet......

• Occasionally buildings have lotteries for prospective tenants. Look for notices at social service agencies.

Low-income housing

TENDERLOIN NEIGHBORHOOD DEVELOPMENT CORP. (TNDC) - 201 Eddy St., SF www.tndc.org 415-776-2151
Have numerous buildings primarily in the Tenderloin - permanent housing for both individuals and families. 
Direct occupancy line: 358-3938

CHINATOWN COMMUNITY DVLPMT. CENTER - 1525 Grant Ave., SF www.chinatowncdc.org 415-984-1450
Have buildings in Chinatown and other neighborhoods in SF. Hotel, studio & family housing with 1, 2 or 3 bedrooms.

MISSION HOUSING DEVELOPMENT CORP. - 474 Valencia St. #280, SF www.missionhousing.org 415-864-6432
Affordable housing primarily in the Mission district. Housing for seniors, families and persons with diverse needs.

INDOCHINESE HOUSING DVLPMT. CORP. (IHDC) - 340 Eddy St., #100, SF www.ihdc.org 415-441-2872
Have two buildings in the Tenderloin for singles, families and seniors.

MERCY SERVICES CORPORATION - 1360 Mission St. #300, SF www.mercyhousing.org 415-355-7100
Develops and operates low-income housing. Tenderloin properties are 111 & 205 Jones (415-474-2680).
Visit website for current listings.

TENDERLOIN HOUSING CLINIC - 472 Turk St., SF www.thelinc.org 415-771-2427
Has "Modified Payment Program" which provides cheaper permanent housing for individuals in residential hotels they contract with. Also have legal services, tenant organizing and supportive services.

THE CECIL WILLIAMS GLIDE COMMUNITY HOUSE - 333 Taylor St., SF www.glide.org 415-674-6100
Permanent supportive housing for low-income individuals and families in the Tenderloin.

CARITAS MANAGEMENT CORPORATION - 1358 Valencia St., SF www.caritasmanmgmt.com 415-647-7191
Manages and rents over 50 buildings in San Francisco from SRO's to family apartments.

ASIAN, INC. - 1167 Mission St, 4th floor, SF www.asianinc.org 415-928-5910
Provides income-based affordable housing listings in San Francisco. Work with properties that accept Section 8 Vouchers and other rental assistance programs. Listings include studios, and 1-4 bedrooms.

Other low-income housing resources

INDEPENDENT LIVING RESOURCE CENTER (ILRC) - 825 Howard St., SF www.ilrcsf.org 415-543-6222
Holds regular housing information workshops for physically & mentally disabled adults. Bulletin board with some current housing information. Does not actually own any buildings.

MAYORS OFFICE OF HOUSING (MOH) - 1 South Van Ness, 5th Floor., SF www.sfgov.org/moh 415-701-5500
Offers below market rate rental information, plus below market home ownership and down payment assistance.

Reports provide data and information for a range of ways to address living wage issues. Reporters provide thoughtful coverage that gives voice to different perspectives. The goal is to spark interest, have an informed discussion, and move toward solutions.

Constructing the Report

This report should be easy to read and understand. It's an overview that the general public can engage with. The language and focus are approachable, not overly technical.

The report should include:
- An introduction to living wage issues in your community. 
- Data on the cost of living, income levels, and employment trends. 
- Profiles of workers and families struggling to make ends meet.
- Recommendations for policy changes or other solutions.
- Resources for further learning or getting involved.

The goal of the report is to illustrate the real-life impacts of low wages and lack of economic security. Focus on creating a human connection - these are your neighbors, coworkers, and community members. Giving voice to their experiences is powerful.

The report should not overwhelm readers with too much data or jargon. Keep it clear, concise, and compelling. Use plain language, real-world examples, and visuals to drive the points home.

Maximizing Reach and Impact

Once you've constructed the living wage report, think creatively about how to share it widely. Some ideas:

- Post the full report online and promote it through social media, email lists, and local media outlets.
- Develop a short summary or fact sheet that can be easily shared and distributed.
- Host a press event or public forum to discuss the report's findings.
- Reach out to local leaders, policymakers, and influencers to brief them on the report.
- Partner with community organizations to amplify the report through their networks.

The goal is to get as many people as possible reading, discussing, and taking action based on your living wage research. With the right strategy, your report can be a powerful tool for change.

MANAGING CONFLICT

Dealing with conflict in a relationship or family is not always a natural or easy process. There are steps one can take to move towards resolving conflict:

• Communicate: this involves exchanging information about a situation and expressing one's concerns and views. Use active listening skills to understand the other's perspective.

• Identify feelings: consider how you feel and how the other person might be feeling. Unresolved feelings can sometimes escalate a conflict.

• Compromise: instead of focusing solely on your position, try to find a solution that takes both people's needs into account. This may involve negotiating and finding common ground.

• Apologize: if you realize you have done or said something hurtful, acknowledge it and apologize. This can help diffuse tension.

• Consider alternatives: Explore other ways of looking at the issue. Try to understand the other person's point of view. Can a solution be found that resolves the conflict?

Smoothing things out: Instead of confronting issues head on, sometimes people try to smooth over or avoid the conflict. This may provide temporary relief but the underlying issues remain unresolved. They may recur or escalate over time.

Compromise: Instead of coming to blows, it is possible to work through a conflict. Each person's concerns, needs and interests should be given attention. They may not be exactly what either person wants but a solution that accommodates both is possible.

Use of Power: Power can be used to win a conflict, but this leaves the other person feeling defeated. Over of view One's party vision or view may prevail but at what cost to the relationship?

Conflict can also be handled by using a mediator, facilitator or counselor. This allows for a setting where there is a skilled third party to assist in the resolution process. One party's power over the other is reduced, communication is facilitated, and mutually satisfactory solutions are sought.

Research indicates that conflict is best approached to consider both people's legitimate interests of needs. If persesses, the best interests of the conflict likely if persesses, the best interests or the least intrusive positions that can be engaged. It is also essential to have a balance of dealing with conflict (i.e. compromise, continuing problem-solving) versus avoiding it, which can perpetuate problems.

MEDIA BARS PART 3

The Assisted self-help is the work of Rosalie Riegle and her students in Political Science and Community Studies at the University of San Francisco. The students of three classes from Winter '92 to Spring '93 were taught to use these media bars in the service of community organizations.

Daybook
The daybook is organized to collect the unifying forces of the group--common interests, needs, and commitments. Individuals add their personal entries daily so that plans, goals, and aspirations emerge naturally. This provides a "taking stock" opportunity.

Bro-roll
The Bro-roll has a history of events for a group or community that acts as an ongoing memory of their development. It includes the names of each member who has contributed, and has a way of maintaining that feeling of continuity.

Activeality
These are the happenings on the center as a whole. It traces the various activities, discussions, trips, and events that constitute the genuine everyday life of the group.

No comment
No comment is a dangerous thing to say to someone who's telling you of a very important matter.

"Consider this: a movement is a dangerous thing. It suggests one of two things: (1) You are on the verge of something that everyone longs for and that will ultimately upend your world. Or (2) you are about to erupt into something no one really wants but which is coming at you like a freight train."

MEDIA BARS PART 4

Lead
A leader is someone who can assemble a small, cohesive team and direct their joint efforts toward a specific objective. This requires the ability to define the objective, grasp the team members' individual strengths and weaknesses, and motivate them to work together effectively.

Op-ed (Opinion Editorial)
In modern American journalism, the "op-ed" page is the section of a newspaper usually opposite the editorial page and devoted to contributing writers' opinions, sometimes critical of the paper's editorial position.

Op-ed (Opinion Editorial)
Often writers from a political, social, or economic "opposite" position to the paper's—are invited to contribute op-ed essays to provide balance and alternative viewpoints. The goal is to stimulate debate and diversity of opinion.

Photo-op (Photo Opportunity)
Organized events of media-worthy occurrences, such as politician's, sports figures' or special interest groups' controlled activities specifically designed for news coverage and press photography.

Servo-the Service
Where services are here to assist the needs of the community, not to coerce or force action.

The Service
A reminder that the true service is not to impose one's will, but to assist others in the realization of their own.

Message #2: The Solution

Campaigning: The campaigns and strategies we use are focused on solving the problem with a view to meaningful, lasting change. We use a range of strategies including: media, policy, public education, community organizing, lobbying, and legal strategies.

Messaging: Messaging is critical. We ensure the message is clear, compelling and resonates with the people we need to influence. We know that the language we use can inadvertently reinforce the problem, so we are very careful about the words we choose.

Resources: Here you will find a range of resources that provide more detail on the issues, strategies, and campaigns. We hope these will be useful as you consider how to get involved.

Contacts: The people listed here are key contacts for the organization. They can provide more information, support your involvement, and connect you with others working in this area.

5. Nuts & Bolts of Getting the Message Out

- Media: Proactive media engagement is critical to raising awareness and building public support. We use a range of tactics including press releases, media interviews, opinion pieces, social media etc.
- Digital: Our digital platforms allow us to directly engage with people, share information, and mobilize action. This includes our website, email newsletters, and social media.
- Events: Public events, forums, and workshops enable us to bring people together, share information, and facilitate discussion and action.
- Advocacy: We undertake targeted advocacy with decision-makers to influence policy and practice change.

Message #3: A Call to Action

Now that you know about the problem and our approach, what is your next step? We hope you'll join us!

There are so many ways to get involved. Contact us to learn more about:
- Volunteering your time and skills
- Making a financial contribution
- Sharing this information with your network

Your involvement and support are critical. Together, we can build the power we need to drive lasting change.

MORETTS FOR MEDIA EVENTS

Services provided if you need someone to talk on your behalf:
- My prices are discounted for nonprofit organizations.
- I create communications, crisis management plans, media outreach, messaging and advertising for nonprofit, advocacy and community organizations.
- I get the word out and mobilize the media and your message.
- I strategize public awareness campaigns.
- I connect with journalists, bloggers, podcasters, tv/radio producers to shape stories.
- I get you media interviews and help prepare.

Sheila Russell, Founder 
Moretts Public Relations 
phone: 1-234-567-0123
email: sheila@moretts.com
website: www.moretts.com

CHECKLIST FOR NEWS EVENTS

o News release 
o Media advisory  
o Messaging/talking points handout
o Logistics: time, date, location, media parking, interviews
o Signage, photo ops for media
o Location, timing and set-up of event: clear visibility, easy access, comfortable
o Speakers/presenters: brief biographies, contact info, talking points
o Collateral materials: fact sheets, FAQs, press kits
o Staffing: greeters, spokespersons, technical support
o Video: prerecorded b-roll footage for media to use
o Photos: for social media and news coverage
o Follow up: additional interviews, information, photos for media

MEDIA EVENTS
o News conference: Announce significant news, update on an ongoing issue.
o Media briefing: Provide background information, prep media for a story.
o Press availability: Informal Q&A with reporters.
o Media tour: Show reporters your facility, programs, etc.
o Special event coverage: Cover a special event like a ribbon cutting, groundbreaking.
o B-roll footage: Pre-record video for media to use in news stories.

Developing a Media Event Checklist:
o Purpose: What is the goal? Announce news, provide information, increase visibility?
o Timing: When is the best time for media to attend?
o Location: Where is it most convenient and visually appealing for media?
o Spokespersons: Who will speak and handle interviews?
o Materials: What collateral will you provide (press kits, fact sheets, etc.)?
o Visuals: How can you make the event more visually compelling?
o Follow up: How will you follow up with media after the event?

Effective Media Events:
o News driven: The event should have genuine news value.
o Well organized: A detailed checklist and timeline keep things on track.
o Interactive: Provide opportunities for Q&A, b-roll, photos.
o Newsworthy visuals: Use the event setting to create compelling visuals.
o Prepared spokespeople: Spokespersons should be media trained.
o Follow up: Provide additional materials, interviews, information after the event.

CONTACTS

Phone: (212) 285-3025 
Fax: (212) 285-3044
www.nelp.org
Our Network: Brokers
Living Our Values

ADDENDA & NOTES

Doing Our Network Booster:
Living Our Values

From the Perspective of the Campaign:
"The campaign will need to consider its goals, both for the short term and the long term. Short-term goals may be to get a living wage ordinance passed, while long-term goals may be to maintain that ordinance and to expand its coverage over time."

"We hope this workbook is a practical guide for those engaged in a living wage campaign and a useful tool for the important work ahead. No campaign is the same, but we believe the general principles and strategies outlined here can be applied to campaigns in a wide range of contexts."

It's the development of a strategic campaign, not just the passage of an ordinance, that is critical. The campaign must consider how to build a movement that can sustain itself over time.

"Meanwhile, the Chamber of Commerce and other business interests may mount a campaign against the living wage, so the campaign must prepare for that. Developing relationships with key leaders and constituencies, and implementing an effective communications strategy will be essential." 

"One area that requires special attention is the question of monitoring and enforcement. Living wage laws are meaningless if they are not enforced. Thus, the campaign should determine how the law will be enforced and by whom."

MUST SEE BEFORE 5 P.M.

PART 5

Issue featured in image: Women's Resource Center

Organization/Service: CHECKLIST FOR MONITORING SELF-CARE MEDIA

Eligibility: Here is a checklist to help you evaluate the self-care media you consume. Answering the questions can provide insight into whether the media is enhancing or diminishing your well-being.

1. Does the content make you feel inspired, empowered, and optimistic about the future, or does it leave you feeling fearful, anxious, and hopeless? 
2. Does the content make you feel connected to others, or does it make you feel isolated and alone?
3. Does the content encourage you to take care of yourself, or does it encourage harmful habits and behaviors?

Nathan Waterston: 2.19.2019 - 2.20.2868

Submitted to the Sacramento Bee: Sponsored by the California Chamber of Commerce

"Ways we can make progress on Economic Strategy"
By Nathan Waterston

We've come a long way as a society in achieving greater economic progress and ensuring a good standard of living for all. However, we still face many pressing economic challenges that we as a community must come together to address in meaningful ways. Though it may not be easy, I believe we have the power as a people to move the needle on these issues - if we work together strategically and put the needs of the whole first.

Many of the economic problems we face today have proven to be stubbornly persistent, from income inequality to the rising cost of housing and education. The grim reality is that progress has been slow, and for too many in our community, the American Dream remains elusive. We must do more.

It's clear that simply providing a "band-aid" on these deep-seated issues will not be enough. What's needed is a comprehensive, long-term economic strategy that addresses root causes and makes bold, transformative changes. This will take political will, innovative thinking, and a real commitment to equity and shared prosperity.

The good news is that we have many proven, effective policy tools at our disposal - from reforming outdated regulations to rethinking our tax system, from targeted public investments to innovative new approaches to education and workforce development. What's required is the vision and leadership to put these pieces together into a cohesive, ambitious plan.

And that, my friends, is where you come in. As engaged citizens, your voices and ideas are crucial. I encourage you to get involved, to speak up, to share your perspectives and experiences. Together, we can chart a path forward that works for everyone in our community, not just the privileged few.

This is not an easy challenge, to be sure. But I believe that if we approach it with open minds, a spirit of collaboration, and a deep commitment to the common good, we can make real and lasting progress. The stakes are high, but the potential reward - a more just, equitable, and thriving economy - is immense.

So let's get to work. The future is ours to shape.

Sincerely,
Nathan Waterston

Are You Worried About a Friend?
You may suspect something is wrong even if your friend doesn't talk about it. 
If you can answer yes to some of these questions, your friend may be in a violent relationship.

Does your friend:
- Act withdrawn, worried or depressed?
- Not want to talk as long or as much on the phone?
- Refuse invitations to do things together?
- Talk less about the relationship?
- Have bruises and/or other injuries?
- Wear clothing or make-up to cover up injuries?

Does your friend's partner:
- Put her down in front of other people?
- Seem possessive and/or jealous?
- Make decisions for her, such as what to wear, where to go or what to do?

There are ways you can help and support a friend who's being abused.

Your Friend May Not Talk
Your friend may deny the violence or make excuses for the partner's behavior. Your friend may even be angry with you for asking.

People who are being abused:
- May not even admit to themselves that they're in a violent relationship.
- Often hope or believe the violence won't happen again, even if it's happened many times.
- May be embarrassed, ashamed or afraid to talk about it.

If your friend won't talk, don't force it. Say that you're concerned, you care, and you want her to be safe. Try to stay in touch.

Your friend may come to you for help later. Be ready to help when she wants to take steps.

Learn About Domestic Violence
Before you bring up the subject, find out all you can about domestic violence.

- Call your local crisis line or the National Domestic Violence Hotline at 1-800-799-7233.
- Ask for materials about domestic violence.
- Ask what resources are available in your area. 
- Ask for advice on how best to help your friend.
- Look up the National Domestic Violence Hotline on the Internet at www.ndvh.org.

NATIONAL PARK SERVICE

KNOW YOUR ENEMY

RANKING & MISSIONING - PART 1
By the NPS, SHR Project

There are six major threats to our parks: Air Pollution, Exotic Species, Urbanization, Fragmentation, Overuse, and Global Climate Change.

MISSION-DRIVEN MANAGEMENT: A SYSTEM FOR PARKS
As the National Park Service evolves to meet new challenges, it must maintain its core mission of protecting natural and cultural resources. To do this, we must adopt a "mission-driven" management approach - one that centers on achieving specific goals and targets, rather than simply reacting to problems as they arise.

A mission-driven approach has several key components:
- A clear mission statement that articulates the park's primary purpose and goals.
- Identified measurable objectives that support the mission.
- Strategies and actions designed to achieve those objectives.
- Monitoring and evaluation to track progress and make adjustments as needed.

This systematic approach ensures that parks make decisions and take actions that are directly aligned with their core mission and intended outcomes. It provides a framework for prioritizing resources, tackling complex issues, and demonstrating accountability.

THREATS AND STRATEGIES
The six major threats to our parks are:
1. Air Pollution
2. Exotic Species 
3. Urbanization
4. Fragmentation
5. Overuse
6. Global Climate Change

For each threat, we must develop specific strategies and actions that directly address the causal factors and work toward measurable objectives that support the park's mission. The mission-driven approach provides a structure for this process.

RANKING & MISSIONING - PART 2
The second part of this process is "Ranking and Missioning" - evaluating the threats, setting priorities, and aligning strategies and actions with the park's mission.

This involves several steps:
1. Assess the severity and scope of each threat.
2. Determine which threats are most critical to the park's mission.
3. Identify the primary drivers and causal factors for the priority threats.
4. Develop strategies and actions to address those drivers.
5. Ensure the strategies and actions directly support the park's mission and objectives.
6. Allocate resources to implement the priority strategies and actions.

By following this structured approach, parks can make informed, mission-driven decisions that effectively address their most critical challenges. This helps ensure limited resources are directed toward the actions most likely to protect the park's natural and cultural treasures.

ENEMIES AT THE GATES
CLIMATE CHANGE AT THE STATE LEVEL

Navigation Strategies

Section: Navigation Strategies
This kit contains many different components and strategies to assist clients in navigating their environment. It includes information, checklists, and tools to help with.

Special Notebook Format
Organizing this information in a notebook, that they will refer to with the media, is a critical strategy. This format allows the client to maintain the key information, refer back to it as needed, and to add or change things as their situation evolves.

What This Kit Is Not:
This kit is not a canned or boilerplate program. It is a set of tools and information to be tailored to the individual needs and preferences of each client. Flexibility and customization are key.

Who Is It For?
This kit is designed for individuals who are navigating a variety of challenging life situations - everything from domestic violence, to substance abuse recovery, to poverty, to managing a disability.

What Will It Teach You?
This kit will teach techniques to:
- Identify and prioritize the challenges you are facing
- Develop a plan of action to address those challenges
- Implement that plan and track your progress
- Advocate for yourself and access the resources you need
- Manage ongoing stressors and maintain your wellbeing
- Adapt your strategies as your situation evolves

The information and activities in this kit can help build skills in areas like:
- Goal-setting and action planning
- Time management and organization
- Communication and self-advocacy
- Stress management and self-care
- Accessing community resources

Ultimately, this kit is designed to empower you to take control of your life situation and work towards your goals, despite the challenges you may be facing.

NEW'S RADIO

Explore the ways in which radio has been used to bring about change in women's lives and communities.

Importance of stories: Radio is an important tool in making the voices of women heard. It allows us to share our stories, our struggles, our victories, and our visions. Consider the power of oral storytelling, which has been an integral part of many cultures throughout history.

Campaign strategies: Radio has been used by women's rights advocates to reach wide audiences and mobilize support for their causes. Creative use of radio drama, interviews, call-in shows, and other formats can raise awareness and inspire action.

THE FUTURE OF LIVING WAGE

There are essentially three ways in which an 
advocacy group can get its message on the radio:

1. It can try to get radio stations to cover the issue through news, public affairs, and talk shows.

2. It can buy airtime and produce its own programming.

3. It can try to get the radio station to play its prerecorded public service announcements.

Whatever the approach, the key is to develop a compelling strategy that will attract and hold the listeners' attention.

CONTACTS

This mission of No More Humans is to create a safe space for marginalized individuals to share their stories of survival, growth, and healing. We honor the diversity of the human experience by providing opportunities for self-reflection, personal growth, and community connection.

Good living wage means to be able to live well, send kids to school with right school supplies, go for occasional outing, and to be able to buy some good clothes. It enables women to invest their time in caring for their family's needs rather than working long hours to make ends meet. 

It suggests mere earning may not be enough, the family must be healthy and happy. A living wage is a wage sufficient to provide not just the basic necessities of life, but the elements that give life dignity.

Income is not just for personal care, it goes for the whole family. It includes food, clothing, shelter, health, transportation, and recreation. So, a living wage must factor in the needs of the entire family, not just an individual.

Struggle for a living wage must be a continuous process that has to focus on the following:
- Indexing the minimum wage to inflation so that it keeps pace with the cost of living
- Ensuring the government set a high standard of minimum wage
- Pushing for payment of a minimum wage that allows a worker to live above the poverty line
- Ensuring that the minimum wage is not just an individual wage but a family wage
- Linking minimum wage to productivity gains
- Lobbying for policies, guidelines and regulations that promote a living wage for all

Staging Meta Events and Process
- Mapping the economic landscape
- Identifying the living wage estimate
- Determining the threshold of poverty
- Estimating the cost of living
- Calculating the productivity gains
- Advocating for a policy framework for living wage
- Negotiating with government and corporations
- Building a public campaign for living wage
- Monitoring the implementation

So, when you have mapped the issues, identified the living wage benchmark, estimated the cost of living, calculated the productivity gains, advocated for policy changes, negotiated with the government and corporations, and built a public campaign - you are ready to stage a meta event, a symbolic event that showcases your demands and mobilizes public support.

Check to see the contacts, and the other resources to see how you can further strengthen your campaign. Persistent campaign, capacity building, and networking will be key to your success.

RESOURCES:
- Reports to see trends, facts, and data
- Organizations to network with, to share best practices
- Policy insights to advocate for change
- Case studies to learn from successful experiences

CONTACTS:
- Individuals and organizations who can provide further information, data, analysis
- Experts who can guide you on the technical aspects
- Partners who can collaborate and support the campaign

resources.ocr_text:
On the record
If you habitually over-promise, you'll be unable to meet expectation. On the other hand, if you under-promise and then over-deliver, you'll be viewed as a hero. 
Concision is the key to communication. Conversely, prolixity is the bane of understanding. The best communicators are those who can convey complex information in a simple, straightforward manner.
Carefully, you must present your message. Not only what you say, but how you say it matters. Too little elaboration can leave your audience perplexed; too much can bore them to sleep.
The timing of your delivery is also critical. Delivering the wrong message at the wrong time can undermine even the most carefully crafted communication.
Punctuality, too, is a virtue. The world's time is precious; respecting it commands respect in return.
The medium of your message should match its content. A high-stakes announcement belongs in a formal setting, not a text message.
Rhetoric alone won't suffice. Your words must be backed by credible data and authentic substance.
Consistency is key. Contradictory statements undermine your authority and your cause.
Empathy and emotional intelligence are equally vital. Understanding your audience's perspective enables you to craft a message that resonates.
Over time, you'll develop a reputation. Be mindful - it's hard to shed a bad one, but easy to tarnish a good one.
Engagement from your audience is the litmus test. If they're not listening, your message has failed.

resources.ocr_text:
The Venerable Reverence Carter 
City College of San Francisco
Bulletin January 27, 2006

The Venerable Reverence Carter (YRC) provided a supportive environment in which women students were encouraged to become active participants in their own development which women may have been discouraged from in the past. He promoted an environment in which women students were empowered to voice their concerns and ideas. He challenged his students, both men and women, to widen their perspectives on vocational and career choices. Additionally, he was a champion for his female students, and he encouraged women to pursue careers and vocations that were not considered traditional women's roles at the time.

Over-Optimization 
The Venerable Carter was concerned that over-optimization, especially in areas like technology, can lead us to lose sight of the more holistic aspects of human development. He cautioned against students becoming overly focused on a narrow career path, at the expense of broader intellectual and personal growth.

Organizational Design
The Venerable Carter saw a need to evolve organizational structures and management approaches to better support the full development of all individuals, not just focus on efficient task completion. He advocated for more participatory, inclusive, and empowering organizational models.

Project SURVIVE 
The Venerable Carter launched Project SURVICE, an initiative to enable women students to actively engage with the local community. The project supported women's studies and women's voices as part of the college curriculum.

Honors of Operation
The Venerable Carter was honored by the college for his significant contributions to advancing opportunities for women students. 

Originally, A Woman's Resonance Center (later called the Bodice) was established in 1994, serving to enhance office skills and personal development for the WRC students, many of whom were returning to college.

Policies
The WRC does not discriminate on the basis of gender, identity, race, sexual orientation, age, disability, or any other legally protected status.

resources.ocr_text:
Winning Wages: A Media Kit
for Successful Living Wage and
Strategies for Activists and Organizers: What

Should I try: Get a "Wow!" from potential audiences, The best thing you can do is project an image and a personality that inspires confidence. People buy from people they like and trust. So, if you warm the audience up first with some light, friendly chatter, you can then slide into your message more smoothly.
Don't: Talk about your personal history, academic degrees, or publishing credits. The audience is there to hear your message, not your resume.
Do: Share a relevant, compelling story that illustrates the key points of your message. Stories connect with people on an emotional level and help your message stick.
Don't: Lecture or read from a script. It's boring and impersonal. Speak from the heart and connect with the audience.
Do: Use vivid, concrete language to paint a picture. Avoid abstractions and jargon.
Don't: Overwhelm the audience with too much information. Focus on your strongest, most impactful points.
Do: End with a clear call to action. What do you want the audience to do next?
Overall, your goal should be to deliver a polished, professional, and persuasive presentation that leaves the audience thinking, "Wow, I really connected with that person and their message."

THE FUTURE OF LIVING WAGE
RESOURCES
1. DEFINING THE PROBLEM
2. UNDERSTANDING THE ISSUE
3. GETTING LEADERSHIP BUY-IN
4. FRAMING & MESSAGING
5. NUTS & BOLTS OF GETTING THE MESSAGE OUT
6. CAMPAIGN STRATEGIES
Determining if it's happening - Look for signs like high turnover, difficulty retaining employees, difficulty finding qualified applicants, and complaints from employees about low pay. Gather data on compensation, benefits, and cost of living in your area.
Understand the issue - Research the history and context of living wage efforts, the ethical and business case for paying a living wage, and common objections and counter-arguments. Learn about best practices from other campaigns.
Get leadership on board - Engage with executives, managers, and board members to understand their perspectives, concerns, and needs. Find common ground and make a compelling case for change.
Frame the issue effectively - Develop clear, compelling messages that resonate with different stakeholders. Use data, stories, and visuals to illustrate the need and benefits. Anticipate and address common objections.
Nuts & bolts of the campaign - Identify and mobilize key allies, build a diverse coalition, create an action plan with timelines and accountability, and be ready to respond to opposition.
Campaign strategies - Tailor your approach to your organization's culture and decision-making processes. Consider a step-by-step, incremental approach if needed. Maintain momentum and persistence.

Demand for a Minimum/
Prevailing/Living Wage
• Demand a realistic minimum, prevailing, or living wage that provides a decent standard of living.
• Support efforts of workers and their unions to demand and negotiate higher wages.
• Advocate for an increase in the minimum wage.
• Support policy proposals that would tie the minimum wage to the cost of living.
• Promote the adoption of a "living wage" ordinance in your community that requires employers to pay a wage that allows workers to meet their basic needs.
• Engage in public awareness campaigns to highlight the challenges of living on low wages.

What Else Can You Do?:
• Tax the rich to redistribute wealth
• Pass laws that make it easier for workers to join unions
• Support public sector employment and investment in social services and infrastructure
• Ensure a strong social safety net (e.g. affordable housing, healthcare, childcare, education)
• Challenge corporate power and the concentration of wealth

Savings Goals, and How to Achieve Them:
To get insight into your finance: The first step is to know where your money is going. Start by listing all your income and expenses. Make sure to include fixed expenses like rent, car payment, and insurance as well as variable expenses like food, gas, and entertainment. This will help you understand your spending patterns and identify areas where you can cut back.

Once you have a clear picture of your financial situation, you can start setting savings goals. These could be short-term goals like building an emergency fund or long-term goals like saving for a down payment on a house. Break down your goals into smaller, more manageable steps and create a plan to achieve them.

Budgeting is a key tool for reaching your savings goals. Create a budget that allocates your income towards your expenses and savings. Be realistic and flexible - your budget should evolve as your circumstances change.

Automating your savings is another effective strategy. Set up automatic transfers from your checking account to your savings account so the money is tucked away before you have a chance to spend it.

Staying motivated is crucial. Celebrate your progress and reward yourself for hitting milestones along the way. Remember, achieving your savings goals takes time and discipline, but the payoff is worth it.

Pulling from your finances: Borrowing can be a useful tool, but it's important to understand the risks and costs involved. When taking out a loan or using credit, consider the interest rate, repayment terms, and how it fits into your overall financial plan.

Emergencies happen, and having a rainy day fund can help you avoid going into debt when unexpected expenses arise. Aim to save 3-6 months' worth of living expenses in an easily accessible savings account.

Life events like buying a home, starting a family, or retiring require careful financial planning. Work with a financial advisor to create a comprehensive plan that aligns with your goals and helps you navigate major life transitions.

Managing your credit: Your credit score is a key factor in securing loans, renting an apartment, and even getting hired. Check your credit report regularly and dispute any errors. Pay your bills on time and keep your credit card balances low to maintain a healthy credit score.

Protecting your finances: Safeguard your financial information by using strong passwords, monitoring your accounts for suspicious activity, and being cautious when sharing personal data online or over the phone.

Identity theft can have serious consequences, so take steps to protect yourself. Regularly review your credit report, be wary of phishing scams, and consider freezing your credit if you suspect fraud.

Preparing for the unexpected: Life is unpredictable, but you can take steps to protect yourself and your loved ones. Having the right insurance coverage can help you weather unexpected events, from medical emergencies to natural disasters.

Review your insurance policies regularly and make sure you have adequate coverage for your needs. Consider disability, life, and homeowner's or renter's insurance to safeguard your financial well-being.

Peninsula Ballet Theatre
1880 South Grant Street, San Mateo
(650) 342-3262 • PeninsulaBallet.org

PBT provides ballet and dance training based on the Cuban Vaganova method so prized by choreographers, artistic directors and audiences. Classes are offered to all ages, with open enrollment year round. Students learn from working artists in a nurturing, inclusive environment that inspires passion, joy and a firm dance foundation.

As Peninsula Ballet Theatre approaches its Golden Anniversary, celebrating 50 years of service to the greater Bay Area, its class offerings continue to grow. Over 250 students, ages two to 82, take classes in ballet, jazz, contemporary, hip-hop, ballroom, dance fitness, musical theater acting and singing. All teachers are professional dancers and educators who remember how their love for dance began when they were young. These teachers instill the tradition of classical technique needed to develop dancers who move joyfully and confidently with balance and beauty.

The Ballet Division offers graded classes based on ability, age and aptitude for the serious ballet student. The Dance Division is designed for students wishing to add dance to augment their other studies. Tuition includes the opportunity for all students to perform in the annual Student Showcase. After completing the introductory level, students are eligible to audition for children's roles in professional productions such as Nutcracker, Cinderella, and Sleeping Beauty.

The nurturing, welcoming environment includes four professional studios with sprung floors, a studio for ballroom classes and a Pilates studio. Wi-Fi, tables and chairs in a spacious well-lit lobby provide space for homework before or between classes.

With programs for all ages, abilities and aspirations, Peninsula Ballet inspires passion, joy and discipline in all its students.

They say a picture is worth a thousand words. In the media, a picture can often speak louder than words. Images have the power to shift mindsets, provoke emotions, and change the course of a conversation.
Images can inspire hope. They can reveal human dignity, beauty and resilience. They can help us see the world through a different lens.
Images can also perpetuate stereotypes. They can reinforce beliefs that are hurtful or even dangerous. An impactful photo can unintentionally obscure more than it illuminates.
Make sure photographs and stories positively showcase the challenges and resilience of living wage and minimum wage workers. Avoid images that feel voyeuristic, that sensationalize poverty, or that reinforce negative stereotypes.
...
Tips for Better Photo-Ops:
- First and foremost, always fill ways to visually depict the human dignity, creativity, and resilience of minimum wage and living wage workers. Their strength and determination should be the focus.
- Be mindful of camera angles, framing, and context. Avoid shots that feel intrusive or diminish the subject.
- Consider diverse settings that reflect the full breadth of low-wage work, from offices to factories to service jobs.
- Highlight personal stories that put a human face on the living wage issue. Show workers in their homes, with their families, engaging in their communities.
- Seek out and collaborate with workers themselves to shape how they are represented. Give them agency in the process.
- Remember, you shape the narrative. Use your platform to humanize the living wage movement, not exploit it.

This for"The Pitch"

Offer reporters something they need or research. Find ways to help them produce a good story--and help your organization. The most important thing here is to offer reporters ideas that fit their needs, not just to promote your organization.

Pitch timely and relevant stories. Reporters are busyand need you to do more than bring them your soapbox rhetoric. Think about stories they could use right now, and pitch ones that speak directly to their audience and their publication's mission.

Offer reporters specific, concrete story ideas. Rather than a vague "We have a great program you should cover," be specific: "Here's a short video you could use that highlights how parents are coping with the high cost of childcare." 

Respect their needs and deadlines. Reporters are under tremendous pressure. Respect their deadlines and work within their schedules. Don't pester them or make demands.

Begin with research. Take time to learn about the reporter, the beat, the publication, and the type of stories they cover. Tailor your pitch accordingly.

Keep it brief. Pitch the story in a succinct email or voicemail. Avoid verbal diarrhea or overwhelming them with details they don't need.

Be sincere, not salesy. Share your story with enthusiasm, but don't turn it into a sales pitch. Reporters can smell a sales job a mile away.

Follow up thoughtfully. If they don't respond, wait a week or two before following up briefly. Don't hound them.

Say thanks, even if they pass. Reporters appreciate a gracious response, win or lose.
