resources.ocr_text:
Powerful Non-Defensive Communication

1. As Questions... Open-and-sincere.
Through information gathering, a non-defensive, open-and-sincere tone can help diffuse a tense situation. Asking questions shows that you want to understand rather than simply be right. When you ask open-ended questions beginning with "what" or "how", it can make the other person feel heard and understood.

2. Make Positive Observations. Start here.
Purpose: To express and daily your concern, thoughtfulness, and care. Examples: "I notice that today you seem in a hurry and look a little worried." "You seem to have been here a long time now and I wonder how you're doing?" Instead of a negative evaluation, make an observation about what you've noticed. This allows you to bring up something in a less confrontational way.

3. Predict Consequences. Set your intention.
Purpose: To convey your own reaction and concerns, without being accusing. "If you don't let me know what you need, I'm afraid I won't be able to help you as much as I'd like." "I noticed you get a little defensive when I bring up this issue. If this continues, I'm worried it could damage our working relationship." State how you see the situation unfolding, to bring attention to it without blame.

Avoid Using: "You" statements like "You make me feel" or "You're always..." These can sound accusatory. Instead, use "I" statements to express your own experiences and concerns.

When you do want to deliver constructive feedback, match your positivity with concrete suggestions, and focus on future improvements, not past mistakes. This helps the other person feel empowered, not attacked.

Using a kind, patient and predictive communication style can strengthen understanding between you, even in difficult situations.

Pregnant Again
A couple of years later, shortly after my mom passed away, I became pregnant with my daughter. Fortunately, this pregnancy went smoothly. We found out early that she wasn't going to be born with cystic fibrosis and, while my blood pressure did get high at times, it was managed well with a medication that is safe to take during pregnancy. I had a fantastic doctor who knew my history and made sure the appropriate testing was performed.

The author with her husband, Steve Faraudo, and son, Giulio, just hours after he was born.

My daughter, Bella, was also born perfect at 8 pounds, 9 ounces. I thought I might be pushing my luck by having another child, but she was beautiful and I was still alive. 

Nowadays, there's even better treatment for women who are at risk of developing preeclampsia. New research shows that if you give a low-dose aspirin to an expecting mother at 12 weeks of pregnancy, it decreases her risk of developing preeclampsia by up to 40 percent by enhancing the effectiveness of placental implantation, Druzin says.

But this treatment is only for women who are at risk because they've had a history of preeclampsia, diabetes, kidney disease, lupus, obesity or high blood pressure, he says.

Every day, I look at my two kids who are now 8 and 5, and I feel like I'm witnessing a miracle. I know a lot of parents say that about their kids. But if you've had complications in your pregnancies, that sense of amazement is tenfold. Most importantly, these difficult pregnancies have given me gratitude. Whenever my kids transform into "wild animals," I remind myself just how incredible they are and how grateful I am to have them in my life. 

Teresa Mills-Faraudo is an associate editor and Bay Area Parent and mother of two.

- Preeclampsia Foundation - www.preeclampsia.org.
- March of Dimes - www.marchofdimes.org/complications/preeclampsia.aspx.

Staff at Project Homeless Every Day Connect work directly with those seeking services, as well as with case managers & staff from other agencies, to make connections to those often hard-to-access resources, services & goods that can provide additional or necessary ingredients for a successful move out of homelessness, transition into housing, or avoidance of housing loss. They connect their participant partners to comprehensive social & medical services & other supportive services. These services include: vision, hearing, dental, general medical, mental health, addiction treatment & recovery services, harm reduction programs, food, clothing, computer access & classes, transportation, employment services, Medi-Cal, SSI, SSDI, income assistance & other financial services.

24/7 Customer Service Center

www.211bayarea.org
211 is an easy to remember, toll-free phone number that connect callers with local community services, such as food, shelter, counseling, employment assistance, quality child care and more. During a disaster, 211 provides critical information about evacuation routes, food and shelter, as well as job search and permanent housing support during long-term recovery. 211 is confidential and available 24 hours a day in more than 150 languages.

311 San Francisco
24/7 Customer Service Center
Call 311 (within SF only) or 415-701-2311
www.sf311.org
The City and County of San Francisco established 311 to provide an easy-to-remember telephone number that connects residents, businesses, and visitors to Customer Service Representatives ready to help with general government information and services. The 311 Customer Service Center provides a prompt, courteous and professional customer service experience 24 hours a day to San Francisco residents, visitors, and businesses seeking general information and services. 311 also operates the Shelter Reservation Waitlist. Say things like "That's an interesting point, but let's get back to discussing strategies for staying safe." or "I'm not here to debate that issue, I'm here to provide information that can help keep you safe." Maintain a calm, neutral tone and refocus the discussion.

If a student tries to interrupt or take over the discussion, gently but firmly interrupt them and say "I need to keep us on track with the agenda. Let's move on to the next topic." If they persist, remind them of the ground rules at the beginning about allowing everyone to participate. You can also say "I want to make sure everyone has a chance to ask questions and get information, so I need to limit interruptions so we can get through the material." The goal is to redirect the energy while maintaining control of the discussion.

Caution: Words
Remains and or pain of survivors in the audience can sometimes be brought to the surface. Be mindful, don't minimize, and validate their experience. 

For men who feel the discussion is biased against them, validate their feelings and say something like "I understand you may feel this information doesn't apply to you, but violence can happen to anyone regardless of gender. The strategies I'm sharing are useful for everyone." Then refocus the discussion.

Conclusion: The final suggestion is to not lose sight of the instructional goals and to use facilitation techniques to keep the discussion on track and beneficial for all participants. Maintain an objective, educational tone and do not get drawn into unproductive debates. The goal is to provide helpful information in a safe, supportive environment.

Background: 
The Summer Retreat provides a program of training and development for residents of Summer Acres Community. Summer Acres is a community housing development serving low-income families. This program has consistently received positive feedback from participants, who have reported increased confidence, skills, and engagement in their communities after attending. The retreat takes place over four days and three nights, and provides opportunities for recreation, peer learning, and personal reflection. 

My proposal is to limit the travel time for a shorter summer retreat, reducing the retreat to two days and one overnight stay. This will allow us to provide the core programming and benefits of the retreat, while reducing costs associated with extended travel and accommodations. Reducing the overnight stay from three to one night will result in $500 in savings for lodging costs, as well as reduced mileage and meal costs. This will allow us to provide a meaningful retreat experience to residents at a lower overall cost.

Proposal: That the Associated Student government fund a two-day, one-night Summer Retreat for residents of Summer Acres Community, at a total cost of $3,000.

resources.ocr_text:
QUICK PRIMER FOR HEADING OFF THE OPPOSITON

By Saumirah McElroy, Communications Center for Feminist Studies

Brace yourself, the 'opposition' is about to come calling. They have an agenda, and they will use all the tricks in the book to try and get what they want - whether that's a piece of your funding, an endorsement of their views, or simply the validation that comes from being granted an audience. 

So here are a few tips to help you get out ahead of the 'opposition' and ensure your organization's voice and mission stay front and center.

Recognize their agenda: Savvy opponents will try to frame the conversation in a way that serves their interests, not yours. Don't let them. Be clear about your organization's priorities and values, and don't get sidetracked.

Know your allies: Identify the individuals and organizations that share your goals and views. Reach out to them and coordinate your response.

Anticipate their moves: Research your opponents, understand their tactics, and be prepared to counter them.

Stick to your guns: Don't get drawn into debates or discussions that are designed to undermine you. Stay focused on your core mission.

Enlist your community: Mobilize your supporters, volunteers, and clients to show up and lend their voices. The more visible and vocal your base, the harder it will be for the opposition to steamroll you.

Mind the media: Proactively engage with journalists and outlets that are sympathetic to your cause. Frame the narrative before your opponents get a chance to.

FRAMING IS EVERYTHING PART 4

Women's health and medical centers are often the targets of anti-choice groups that masquerade as "pregnancy resource centers" or "crisis pregnancy centers". These fake clinics engage in deception and misinformation to discourage people from accessing comprehensive reproductive healthcare.

Here are some key points to keep in mind:

- They pretend to offer comprehensive medical services, but many don't even have a licensed medical provider on staff.
- They use manipulative tactics like free ultrasounds to lure people in and then subject them to anti-choice propaganda.
- They often locate their centers near actual women's healthcare clinics in order to confuse and mislead patients.
- They may try to get you to endorse or partner with them, which would lend them credibility.

Because they rely on deception, the best way to counter them is with clear, honest information. Educate your community about what these fake clinics are and how to spot them. And be vigilant - if they try to engage with you, shut them down firmly and without apology.

Some other ideas:
- Partner with local reproductive rights groups to raise awareness.
- Post clear signage at your facility identifying it as a licensed medical provider.
- Warn patients about these deceptive centers and advise them on how to verify a clinic's credentials.

Ultimately, your goal should be to protect the integrity of your services and ensure your clients have access to the full range of reproductive healthcare options. Don't let the 'opposition' undermine that.

resources.ocr_text:
Sexual orientation, sex, gender identity or expression, physical or mental disability, status as a veteran, national origin or immigration status are not legitimate bases for employment decisions. These hiring practices would be unlawful under the Civil Rights Act of 1964, the Americans with Disabilities Act, the Age Discrimination in Employment Act, and other federal and state laws.

Applicants should be evaluated based solely on their ability to perform the essential functions of the job. Companies should ensure that their screening and selection procedures do not have a disparate impact on protected groups, and that they provide reasonable accommodations to qualified applicants or employees with disabilities.

Qualification criteria must be job-related and consistent with business necessity. Companies should review their policies and practices to ensure compliance with equal employment opportunity laws.

An analysis of the racial and gender composition of a company's workforce can help identify potential issues, but should not be the basis for preferential treatment or numerical quotas in hiring. Affirmative action programs may be permissible in certain circumstances to remedy past discrimination, but should be narrowly tailored.

Employers should provide training on unconscious bias and effective strategies for reducing bias in hiring and management decisions. They should also ensure that managers and employees understand their obligations under equal employment laws.

READING SKILLS AND SPEED READING PROGRAMS
For Children and Adults

THIS SUMMER IN DALY CITY, 
SAN FRANCISCO, AND ON CAMPUS

Program for 4-Year-Olds and Entering Kindergartners
In this fun summer program, your child will learn to read. Children in this program learn letter recognition, beginning phonics, and easy sight words. Your child will learn to read simple words and short sentences, and will develop a love of books and reading.

Program for Entering 1st Graders
In this fun summer program, your child will learn to read independently. Children in this program learn phonics and sight words, improve comprehension, and develop a love of books and reading. Your child will get excited about learning to read and get off to a great start in first grade.

Program for Entering 2nd Graders
In this fun summer program, your child will become a fluent, independent reader. Children in this program build solid phonics and word-attack skills, and develop reading fluency and comprehension. Your child will gain confidence and develop a love of books and reading.

Program for Entering 3rd Graders
In this fun summer program, your child will become a strong, fluent reader. Children in this program develop long-word decoding skills, reading fluency, and good comprehension. Your child will gain confidence and develop a love of books and reading.

Program for Entering 4th and 5th Graders
In this fun and effective summer program, your child will become a skilled, enthusiastic reader. Students in this program develop long-word decoding skills, fluency, and strong comprehension. Your child will complete homework more quickly and easily, be more successful in school, and develop a love of books and reading.

Programs for Entering 6th-8th Graders and Entering 9th-11th Graders
In these effective and enjoyable programs, your student will improve comprehension in both fiction and non-fiction, and will learn to read twice as fast. Students in these programs learn the best way to read textbooks, take notes, and study for tests. Your student will complete homework more quickly and easily, get better grades, and enjoy reading more.

Program for Adults, Entering 12th Graders, and College Students
Learn to double your reading speed in difficult material and triple your reading speed in easier material, while improving comprehension, concentration, and retention. You'll save time and get more out of everything you read!

REGISTERING TO VOTE

If an individual is a US citizen and over the age of 18, then they are eligible to vote in elections held in the county where they officially reside. In order to vote, all citizens must first register. Even a citizen who is currently incarcerated for a misdemeanor crime may still vote. If a citizen is currently incarcerated for a felony crime, however, they may not vote.

Individuals can register to vote, or re-register, online at the California Secretary of State website, at: www.sos.ca.gov/elections/elections_vr.htm. The registration form is available in both Spanish and English. Within 7-14 days after they have registered online, the individual will be sent a registration card in the mail that they must then sign and return to the Secretary of State's offices to finalize their registration. Individuals may also register at their local library branch or the DMV. The Secretary of State offices also maintain a hotline in many languages to offer assistance and information about voter registration:

English: (800) 345-VOTE
Spanish: (800) 232-VOTA
Chinese: (800) 339-2857
Vietnamese: (800) 339-8163
Japanese: (800) 339-2865
Tagalog: (800) 339-2957
Korean: (866) 575-1558

Individuals may also register to vote at the San Francisco Department of Elections at City Hall:

HOURS: Monday-Friday, 8AM-5PM
LANGUAGES: English, Cantonese, Mandarin, Russian, and Spanish
LOCATION: 1 Dr. Carlton B. Goodlett Place, Room 48 (basement)
San Francisco, CA 94102
PHONE: (415) 554-4375; TTY (for hearing-impaired individuals): (415) 554-4386
Website: Individuals can register to vote, learn about voting options, register to vote by mail (absentee ballot voting) or re-register with a new address all at this local website: www.sfgov.org/site/elections_index.asp

Citizens who have been convicted previously and have served out their felony sentence and/or probation and parole, may re-register and begin to vote again. Citizens who are currently incarcerated, and wish to vote, should contact the Sheriff's Prisoner Legal Services at (415) 558-2427 and request a voter registration form.

Remedies Consultants

"As well as being professional therapists, we have extensive experience in the field of domestic abuse and have worked in the area of domestic violence for over 15 years. Our role is to provide a safe, non-judgemental and supportive environment for individuals to explore their experiences and develop coping strategies and life skills to enable them to move forward in their lives."

Our approach is based on a mixture of techniques, including Gestalt, Person-Centred, Cognitive Behavioural Therapy, Neuro-Linguistic Programming and Mindfulness. We work with individuals to help them gain a deeper understanding of themselves, increase self-awareness and develop their own resources and strategies for change.

We offer:
- Individual Counselling
- Relationship Counselling
- Life Coaching
- PTSD and Trauma Work
- Domestic Violence Support
- Anger Management
- Mediation

Phone: 07576 955 666
Email: info@remediescs.co.uk
Website: www.remediescs.co.uk

What is the Resource Binder?

The Resource Binder is a collection of information on organizations and services available to women, with the goal of providing direct assistance and referrals to help meet their needs.

Once of the key strategies:
One of the key strategies of the key strategic
interventions has been to compile a comprehensive resource guide to connect women with the full range of services in the community. This connects directly to our mandate to facilitate the woman's journey and make this as smooth and supportive as possible.

The Resource Binder contains information on services and organizations that can provide assistance and support to women in diverse areas of their lives. This includes information on housing, counselling, legal services, financial assistance, employment, education, and more. 

The information is organized by category to make it easier to navigate. Each entry includes the organization's name, contact information, a brief description of services offered, eligibility criteria, and other relevant details.

The Resource Binder is intended to be a comprehensive and up-to-date guide that can be used by staff, volunteers, and the women we serve to quickly identify and access the supports they need.

More On the Website:
Do you have the staff capacity to maintain the website? This website is probably helpful, but we're not able to keep it as up-to-date as the Resource Binder. The binder gets regular updates when we learn of changes to services or new resources.

How & Why to Frame Living Wage News

The article focuses on how to frame the discussion around living wages in a way that resonates with the public. It provides strategies and suggestions for effectively communicating the need for living wages.

Resource Stories:
- This article focuses on how to frame the debate around living wages in a way that is more compelling and persuasive to the general public. It provides guidance on effective messaging and framing.
- The goal is to shift public opinion towards supporting policies and efforts that ensure workers are paid a living wage that allows them to meet their basic needs.
- The article discusses strategies for framing the living wage issue around themes of family, morality, and economic security rather than just focusing on wages and costs.

We Frame Stories for Two Reasons:

1. To make an issue resonate more powerfully with the public and their values.
2. To counter common misconceptions and narratives that work against the living wage cause.

Reframe Stories:
- Shift the focus from "costs" and "wages" to how living wages impact families, communities, and the economy.
- Emphasize the moral imperative of paying workers enough to live on and support their families.
- Highlight how living wages contribute to economic security and opportunity.
- Counter arguments that living wages will hurt businesses and the economy.

How to Frame a Model:
- What is the issue? Living wages and worker poverty
- Who does it impact? Working families, communities, the economy
- Why does it matter? Moral, economic, and social justice reasons
- What's the solution? Policies and efforts to ensure living wages

The article provides guidance on effectively framing and communicating the living wage issue to shift public opinion and build support for related policies and initiatives.

Their services also include a Community Office that offers drop-in services, support groups, community education and follow-up support to former residents of their residential programs.
Rosalie House is a twenty-six bed emergency shelter that houses half of all beds available in San Francisco for this purpose. The Arc of San Francisco
1500 Howard Street, San Francisco, CA 94103

The Arc San Francisco is a nonprofit service, education and career center for adults with developmental disabilities and their families living in San Francisco, San Mateo and Marin counties. Started by parents over 60 years ago, they now serve more than 640 clients, providing vital postsecondary education, life skills, career, independent living, health and wellness advocacy and recreation services that empower their clients to achieve their highest potential and live a fulfilling quality of life.
The Arc's Housing Advocates help clients find affordable housing that meets individual needs, preferences and financial realities. Through individualized assessments, The Arc works to find the right match for every prospective tenant, whether it's a senior seeking her own studio or a young adult looking for roommates to share a flat. The Arc's Housing Advocacy team helps clients navigate the difficult process of finding and qualifying for housing, including Section 8 requirements. For more information about The Arc's Residential and Housing Advocacy Services, contact Joe Femino, Residential Services Director (415) 255-7200 x135

RESOURCES FOR INDIVIDUALS WITH HIV/AIDS

AIDS Housing Alliance
350 Golden Gate Avenue, San Francisco, CA 94102
415-552-3242
www.ahasf.org
AIDS Housing Alliance has developed a comprehensive suite of housing services that are available to the LGBTQ and HIV communities in San Francisco. Their services include: housing referrals, eviction prevention, rapid rehousing, back rent grants, move-in deposit loans, rental subsidies for job training participants, clinic, tenants rights counselling, job training & supportive employment, and public policy advocacy. People seeking services must attend their Drop In Clinic on either Monday or Tuesday starting at 10AM. Same day appointments are provided on a first-come, first-served basis. Bring ID, letter of diagnosis, and proof of income - if you have them. For back rent or move in deposit bring 3-Day notice, lease, or move in offer letter.

Anger and Parenting
Dealing with feelings

All parents get angry at times. 
But it's never OK to hurt your child.

Getting angry is natural. Sometimes you feel like it's your right to act out your anger - to shout, to discipline, to give your child the punishment you think they deserve. 

Yet there are many healthier, more positive ways to deal with your anger and frustration as a parent.

If you feel angry, ask yourself: 
"Get away. Cool a little."
"What's really troubling me - and what can I do about that?"
"How can I let my child know I care, even when I'm upset?"
"Am I tired or stressed? What do I need?"
"Can I do something helpful, even a little thing, to feel better?"

If your anger feels very strong, it may be time to take a break and get support. Don't shame or criticize your child - or yourself. 

Children learn how to handle their own feelings by watching how their parents do it. So be a role model for healthy anger management.

What is a healthy relationship?

It is a mutually satisfying arrangement where two people care about each other and make an effort to meet each other's needs. They show respect and concern for one another's feelings and well-being. There is a balance of give and take, and each person feels safe, heard, and valued. In a healthy relationship:

- The people involved display care, trust, and understanding towards each other.
- There is open communication about needs, feelings, and concerns.
- There is equality in the relationship - no one person has more power or control than the other.
- Differences can be worked through respectfully.
- Boundaries and personal space are respected.
- Both people take responsibility for their own actions and behaviors.

Pharmacy @ SAFEWAY
Phone: 541-344-0622
Address: 1950 Franklin Blvd, Eugene, OR 97403
Hours: Open 24 hours

What is an unhealthy relationship?

In an unhealthy relationship, one or both people may feel controlled, intimidated, or unsafe. Warning signs include:

- Extreme jealousy or possessiveness
- Belittling, name-calling, or public humiliation
- Physical, sexual, emotional, or financial abuse
- Isolating the other person from family and friends
- Unpredictable mood swings or explosive anger
- Lack of personal boundaries or privacy
- Disrespect for the other person's feelings and needs

It's crucial to be aware of these signs and seek help if you or someone you know is in an unhealthy relationship. You deserve to feel safe, respected, and valued in your relationships.

Funded by the Bureau of Justice Assistance (BJA), the National Sexual Assault Kit Initiative (SAKI) aims to create a coordinated community response that promotes survivor healing and ensures just resolution to sexual assault cases through a comprehensive and victim-centered approach, building jurisdictional capacity to prevent accumulation of unsubmitted sexual assault kits (SAKs) in the future and supporting the investigation and prosecution of cases for which SAKs were previously unsubmitted.

As of June 2021, SAKI has accomplished the following:
(136,060) SAKs inventoried
(81,563) SAKs sent for testing
(72,447) SAKs tested to completion
(29,207) DNA profiles uploaded
(13,531) CODIS hits

(19,630) investigations
(1,778) cases charged
(1,159*) convictions
(*includes plea bargains)
(1,875) CODIS hits to serial sex offenders
(7,118) CODIS hits to serial violent offenders

Total (FY15-FY21) > $282

SAKI
SEXUAL ASSAULT
KIT INITIATIVE
Pretrial, Accountability, Justice.

Guiding and Supporting a Victim's Choice to Participate
in the Prosecution of Sexual Violence

Efforts to eliminate the accumulation of untested sexual
assault kits (SAKs) have confirmed what has long been
suspected: a significant number of sexually violent
perpetrators commit serial crimes—both sexual and
otherwise—against multiple victims. Additionally, a
high level of crossover offending1 exists. When crossover
offenders face accountability without delay for their crimes,
future victimizations may be prevented. Thus, through
investigation and skillful prosecution practices are essential
to identifying and convicting these offenders.

The decision to prosecute requires more than sufficient
evidence to demonstrate an offender violated a criminal
statute. Prosecutors consider many factors when choosing
to prosecute crimes; these factors include the crimes' impact
on the victim and the community, the extent of the harm
caused by the offense, and the victim's willingness to testify
or participate in prosecution at all.2

A victim engaging with the criminal justice system is
somewhat uncommon because, among other reasons, the
criminal justice process can expose sexual violence survivors
to unique traumatization. Multidisciplinary response
efforts that are victim-centered and trauma-informed
can greatly reduce the level of trauma associated with a
survivor's decision to report a sexual assault. However, the
reporting process may remain daunting. Victims may find
that the various criminal justice components essential to a
meticulous and fair prosecution are difficult or distressing,
even when these actions are completed with great care;
these components may include interviews, evidence
collection, public court proceedings, and cross-examination
at trial. These components may be perceived as barriers to
participation, as well as other case-specific factors (e.g., lack
of social support, witness intimidation) may result in some
victims ultimately declining to participate in the legal
process, avoiding service of process, or refusing to appear
under subpoena.

Victims may be unable to participate in the legal process as
a result of their need to prioritize their own healing, recovery,

or needs; when this happens, prosecutors may experience
an inherent tension between (1) supporting the victim and
their own responsibility to uphold the law and (2) serving
the public more broadly. Even highly skilled prosecutors may
not be able to overcome the legal challenges of a sexual
assault case without a victim's testimony.

This is where advocates and other allied professionals can
play an important role in supporting victims as they navigate
the criminal justice process. This brief will explore strategies
that can assist advocates and other allied professionals
with seeking to guide and support victims throughout the
criminal justice process. These strategies will help ensure that
victims are fully informed about their choices and that their
interests are protected throughout the process.

The Role of Advocacy
Advocacy can come from a variety of sources and each
comes with distinct benefits and limitations. Services most
legal advocates can provide include, but are not limited to,
the following:

• Explaining the various components of the criminal justice
system and describing the victim's potential role at
each step

• Helping victims make informed decisions about their
potential participation

• Advocating for the victim so that law enforcement,
the prosecutor, and/or the court prioritize the victim's
concerns and interests

• Attending meetings and/or court with the victim
• Obtaining or organizing resources that may better allow
the victim to participate (e.g., transportation, childcare, a
note for work)

• Providing general support to the victim as needed

Community-based advocates are those employed external
to the criminal legal system and often work for rape crisis
centers or other nonprofits. These advocates may support
victims navigating the legal system in the ways previously
mentioned, but they typically do not have direct access to
the victim's case or the individuals (e.g., law enforcement
personnel or prosecutors) working on the case. Allied
professionals may come from a number of professions

2 American Bar Association. (2017). Criminal Justice Standards for the Prosecution Function—Standard 3-4.3. https://www.americanbar.org/groups/criminal_justice/

Rewriting Sentences
These questions ask you to rewrite sentences in your head. You will be given a sentence,

correct or conventional usage in grammar, choice of words, sentence construction, and

"Sample Media Advisory - For media planning and outreach, we recommend including the following key elements: 
• Headline - A clear, concise title that captures the news or event
• When - Date and time of the event 
• Where - Exact location of the event, with address
• What - Brief description of the event or announcement 
• Who - Key speakers, presenters, or attendees
• Why - Significance or importance of the event or announcement
• Contact - Name, phone, email for media inquiries"

THE FUTURE OF LIVING WAGE
"What living wage is needed for a single adult to be able to afford a basic but adequate standard of living? Here is the data:
• Basic living wage (2018): $13.70 per hour
• Minimum wage (2018): $11.00 per hour
• Living wage gap: $2.70 per hour
• Trends: Living wage has increased by 2.1% per year since 2013, while minimum wage has remained flat.
• Causes of the gap: Costs of housing, child care, transportation, and health care have grown faster than inflation.
• Implications: Workers earning minimum wage have an increasingly difficult time affording basic needs.
• Policy solutions: Increase minimum wage, expand tax credits, subsidize child care and health care."

RESOURCES
"Sample resources for living wage campaigns:
• Job Gap Study: A project that calculates the living wage needed in different cities and states.
• MIT Living Wage Calculator: Provides estimates of the living wage needed in different locations.
• Living Wage for Families Campaign: Advocates for living wages and other policies to support families.
• Economic Policy Institute: Conducts research and analysis on issues related to living wages and economic security."

CONTACTS
"For additional information or to get involved:
Jane Smith, Coordinator
Living Wage Coalition
123 Main St.
Anytown, ST 12345
(123) 456-7890
jane@lwcoalition.org
www.lwcoalition.org

Hours: Mon-Fri 9am-5pm"

6. CAMPAIGN STRATEGIES
- Organize and direct public action, demonstrations, and media campaigns
- Lobby local and state government officials and policymakers

- Develop and disseminate public education materials
- Work to change public attitudes and build popular support for a living wage

THE FUTURE OF LIVING WAGE
- Community ownership of the process and outcome is key to sustainability
- Living wage policies must be embedded in local government to withstand challenges
- Low-wage workers must be engaged as leaders and spokespeople
- Linking living wage to other social and economic justice issues expands the base

Social Protection: Can Basic Income Grants Turn the Tide? 
- An overview of the rationale, implementation, impacts, and limitations of basic income grants as a tool for poverty reduction and social protection.

Green New Deal - Mobilizing for a Just Transition:

Community and Cooperative Ownership: 
- Explores how community ownership models can build economic and political power for low-income communities.

Communicating About Low-Wage Work: 
- Provides guidance on how to effectively communicate about low-wage work and living wage policies.

CONTACTS
- Coalition Coordinator: coordinator@atlantalivingwage.org

Sample Questions for the ELEMENTARY ALGEBRA TEST

Please review the sample questions to help you decide which math placement test to begin with.

If you answer 5 or fewer questions correctly, begin with the ARITHMETIC TEST.

If you answer 6 or more questions correctly, begin with the ELEMENTARY ALGEBRA TEST.

1. If x = -4, y = 3, and z = -1, find the value of 3x + 2(y - z)
A. -4 B. -5 C. -8 D. -20 E. -40

2. Solve for x : 4(x - 5) = 1 - 3x 
A. -19/7 B. 6/7 C. 10/3 D. 3 E. 21

3. Subtract: 
A. -14/15x B. -2/15x^2 C. -2/15x^3 D. 6x-20/15x^2 E. -2/5x-3x^2

4. Find the solution to the following system of equations:
3x + y = 4
5x - 3y = -5
A. (1, 1) B. (1, 5) C. (-1/2, -5/2) D. (5/2, 1) E. (1 5/2, 2)

5. Multiply and express the answer in lowest terms:
A. (x+5)/2x B. (x+5)/3x C. ((x-5)(x+2))/2x(x-2) D. ((x+5)(x+2))/2x(x-2) E. ((3x-10)(3+6x))/(-24)

6. Simplify: √48x^5
A. 4√3x^5 B. 16√3x^5 C. 4x^2/√3x D. 16x^2/√3x E. 16x^4/√3x

7. Simplify: (81x^-8y^12)^1/4
A. -3x^2y^3 B. 3y^3/x^-2 C. 3y^3/x^2 D. 81y^3/x^2 E. 81y^3/4x^2

8. Let f(x) = x^2 - 3x + 1. Evaluate f(a + 3)
A. a^2 - 3a + 1 B. a^2 + 3a + 1 C. a^2 + 3a + 2 D. a^2 - 3a + 4 E. (x^2 - 3x + 1)(a + 3)

9. Susan has 2 more than 4 times as many books as her roommate has. Together they have 42 books. Which of the following equations could be used to determine the number of books Susan has?
A. 4(x + 2) = 42
B. x + 4(x + 2) = 42 
C. 4x + 2 = 42
D. 4x + 2 + x = 42

In 1997 , over 13,000 ca l ls were made to domestic violence cri s is
l ines in San Franci sco. Domestic vio lence continues to be a
major heal th, socia l , and economic issue facing our community.

The San Franci sco Domestic Violence Consortium i s a network of 
over 35 non-profit, community-based organizati ons and government 
agencies that work to end domestic violence in San Francisco. The
Consortium provides resource and referral services to survivors
of domestic violence and their chi ldren, and works to create long-
term solutions to domestic violence through prevention, direct
services, policy, and systems advocacy.

SERVICES: Here are some of the services offered by Consortium 
members. Services vary, so please contact an 832-i 992 member to
i nquire about specific services in your area.

- Crisi s line and emergency shelter
- Legal services, including restraining orders
- Counseling and support groups
- Chi ldren's programs
- Transitional housing and economic assistance
- Communi ty education and prevention

Domestic violence is a pattern of coerci ve and controlling
behaviors that one intimate partner uses against another.
It can include physical, emotional, sexual, economic or
technological abuse. While anyone can experience domestic
violence, the majority of survivors are women and the majority
of abusers are men. Domestic violence crosses all racial, ethnic,
socioeconomic, educational, age and sexual orientation l ines.

In 1986, San Francisco created a pioneering and comprehensive
response to domestic violence that has served as a model for the
rest of the nation. The Consortium was formed to coordinate
this response and ensure that survivors have access to a full
range of services and that the community works together to end
domestic violence. 

HOURS: The Consortium is available 24 hours a day, 7 days a week.
Member programs have various hours - contact the 932-1992 number
to inquire.

ELIGIBILITY: Services are available to all survivors of domestic
violence, regardless of gender, age, sexual orientation, income,
immigration status, or disability. Some programs may have
additional eligibility requirements.

San Francisco Free Medical Chart
October-December 2014
Page 1 / Turn page for more clinics

Adults; Teens; Seniors; Children; Women; Men; Everyone
San Francisco Health Insurance
Healthy SF. 615-4588, $0-full bill. SF residents 18-64. Call M-F 8:30am-5:30pm for appts & drop-in health care access for poor people (incl. the uninsured) who can't get MediCal or other insurance. At the intake appointment, they'll ask for proof of SF residency, and proof of income, & you can choose a clinic to provide your primary care. Cantonese, English, Mandarin, & Spanish.

MediCal. 1440 HARRISON ST. (bet 10th and 11th). 863-9892. Free. (855) 355-5757 M-F 8am-5pm.
Health insurance for all documented California residents with income less than 138% of the poverty line ($16,104 a year for a single person). Apply in person or online at <www.mybenefitscalwin.org>.

SF Health. 777-9992. $0-full bill. (8:30am-5:30pm). <www.sfhp.org>. Call or go online to find out if you qualify for publicly funded health care incl. Medi-Cal, Healthy Kids & Healthy Workers.

Urgent Care
San Francisco General Hospital. 1001 POTRERO AVE (at 23rd St). 206-8000. All insurance accepted. Will help SF residents without insurance enroll in HealthySF or MediCal. No one turned away for lack of funds. Call for appt M-F 8:30am-5pm; closed holidays. Urgent care M-F 8-11:30am, 1-4:30pm, 6-9pm; Sa-Su-hol 8-11:30am, 1-4:30pm. 24-hr emergency room. Patient Advocate 206-5176. Also dance screenings, pediatrics, Cantonese, English, Mandarin, Russian, Spanish, & Vietnamese. Other languages available.

Tom Waddell Urgent Care Clinic. 50 Ivy St (bet. Van Ness & Polk). 355-7500. $0-full bill. (If you're uninsured, they will try to enroll you in MediCal; see above). Adults (18+): Drop-in M-Th 8am-6:30pm; F 8am-5pm. Sa 8:30am-5pm. TB testing M-F 8am, Sa 8:30-am. Homeless dental clinic MTh 7am (come early!!). Call for podiatry, English & Spanish.

Neighborhood Clinics
BAART Community Health. 433 TURK ST (bet. Larkin & Hyde). 928-7800. $0-full bill. M-F 7-10:45am, 12-3pm. 620 STEVENSON ST (at 7th). 863-3883. M-F 9am-2pm. Drop in or call for an appointment. Outreach & onsite counseling in English, Spanish, & Tagalog.

Curry Senior Center. 333 TURK (near Leavenworth). 885-2274. $0-full bill. For Tenderloin-SOMA residents 55+. Call for appt M-F 8am-5pm. Substance abuse counseling & case management. English & Spanish. For Cantonese, Laotian, Mandarin, Russian, Tagalog & Vietnamese, call for day & time.

Sister Mary Philippa Health Center. 2235 HAYES ST. (bet. Stanyan & Shrader). 750-3500. $0-full bill. Call for appt M-F 8:30am-4:30pm. Cardiology, rheumatology, orthopaedics, surgery, advice nurse, social services, nutrition, diabetes education & pharmacy available. Cambodian, Cantonese, English, Spanish, & Vietnamese. Other languages through telephone interpreter.

South of Market Health Center. 229 7TH ST. (bet. Howard & Folsom). 503-6000. $0-full bill. Call or drop in to make an appt M-Th 8am-5pm, Fsa 8am-3:30pm. Cantonese, English, Mandarin, Spanish, & Tagalog.

Outreach Clinics
A Woman's Place. 1049 HOWARD St (bet. 6th & 7th Sts). 487-2140. Free, will help you get on HealthySF. For women (including MTF transgender). Entrance is around the corner on Russ St. Substance abuse program, HIV program & case management available 8am-4pm. Nurse Practitioner M-F 1-5pm.

Martin de Porres. 225 POTRERO AVE (bet. 15th & 16th Sts). 552-0240. Free. Th 12-2pm nurse practitioner; 12:30-2pm, health education, referrals, over-the-counter medications. English & Spanish.

Mission Neighborhood Resource Ctr. 165 CAPP ST (bet. 16th & 17th). 869-7977. Free for homeless San Franciscans 18+. Drop-in: Nurse Practitioner or doctor M-F 8:15am & M-Th 1:45pm. HIV rapid test Tu 2-4pm; Homeopathy Tu 9am-12pm. Showers, lockers, laundry, case management & support groups available. English & Spanish.

San Francisco Day Labor Program. 3358 CESAR CHAVEZ (bet. Mission & S. Van Ness). 252-5375. Free. Drop-ins: Tu 9-11am, medical care. First 20 people are seen, preference given to day laborers. Job referrals M-F 7am-1pm, Sa 7am-noon. Orientation required for job referral: WSa 10:30am (Spanish), 11am (English). English classes available. English & Spanish.

Other Clinics
Glide Health Services. 330 ELLIS ST, 6TH FLOOR (bet. Taylor & Jones). 674-6140. $0-full bill. For San Francisco residents 18 or over. Call for appt M-F 8:30am-5pm. Drop-in: urgent care M-TWThF 8:30am-8:30pm; acupuncture M 9am-1pm, Tu 1-4pm, Th 1-5pm, F 1-4pm; Tb 1-4pm, F 1-4pm; confidential HIV rapid test if clinician assesses high risk M-Th 1:30-4pm, F 9-11:30am; TB test TWTh 9:30-11am & 1:30-3pm. Hepatitis & breast cancer screening, case management, diabetes, hypertension, smoking cessation & substance abuse services available.

Haight Ashbury Medical Clinic - HR360. 1735 MISSION STREET (at 13th St). 746-1940. $0-full bill. Call for an appt M-F 9am-5pm. Substance abuse treatment, acupuncture, drop-in dental screening 9am-4pm.

* Primary Care clinics provide full medical services including screening & referral.
† Urgent Care clinics provide limited medical services including screening & referral.
‡ Clinics that provide only mental health services, health education & substance abuse programs are not included on this chart.

In case of emergency, call 911.

resources.ocr_text:
SAN FRANCISCO SOCIETY FOR THE PREVENTION OF CRUELTY TO ANIMALS (SPCA)

PROGRAM DESCRIPTION: The SPCA maintains a state-of-the-art pet hospital which provides several veterinary services for free or at reduced rates. The Pets of Homeless Program provides free spay-neuter surgery for pets of homeless people. In addition, the Emergency Veterinary Care Fund provides urgent medical treatment for pets hit by cars, suffering seizures or heart attacks, or other medical crises. The SPCA impounds stray animals and missing animals that appear to either have been abandoned or to be stray. Animals receive medical care when they are impounded. If the SPCA impounds an individual's lost pet, they will not tell the individual over the phone if they have found them. The individual must come to the SPCA and claim their animal in person. If the individual acts in a disruptive manner towards the staff, their pet may not be returned. Their pet may also not be returned if the individual is believed to be homeless. The primary concern of the SPCA staff is the welfare of the animals.

COST: The pet hospital charges fees for veterinary care depending on service. Interest-free financing for emergency pet care is available for qualifying low-income owners of spayed or neutered animals. Owners of found animals are asked to pay a "pet bail" fee of $15 for each day the animal was kept at the SPCA, but they may be able to negotiate a work-trade agreement or reduced fee.

ELIGIBILITY: Pet owners wishing to receive financing for emergency pet care must be San Francisco residents.

LANGUAGES: English

HOURS: Hours vary by program and service, call for more information.

LOCATION: 2500 16th Street, San Francisco, CA 94110

WEBSITE: www.sfspca.org

Self Directed Walk In Program

WEDNESDAYS
Wellness Wednesday 2PM-4PM Every Wednesday 117 6th street @ Mission/Howard (door on the left)
A harm reduction & wellness lounge for gay, bi, & transgender/able men & their friends. Snacks, good music, good company. SF's only harm reduction drop in and syringe exchange by & for gay men manned by fabulous volunteers.

Stonewall Walk in Group every Wednesday at 6:00PM 1035 Market St. room 4A Join us in an open, non-judgmental space to talk & explore possibilities for yourself & changes you may want to make in your use. Facilitators Peter Carnini & Melissa Morelli

Stonewall Counseling Program Orientation Group Every Wednesday at 6PM. 1035 Market Street, room 3E
Attending a 3 orientation groups is your first step to becoming an enrolled Stonewall client. Learn what Stonewall is about, what group and individual counseling services are available to enroll clients, how counselors will work with you to support you in reaching your substance use goals, & get details about the many walk in services available immediately. Check it out. Facilitators Marvin Saavedra & Tiana Townsend

THURSDAYS
Private Needle Exchange, Vein Care, & Harm Reduction Counseling 1035 Market 4th fl. Room 11 Thursdays 4pm-6pm.
Have questions? Missing? Are other people doing your injections for you and you'd like to talk about it? Pick up supplies privately and talk vein care, how drugs are fitting into your world, or anything that is on your mind. Referrals & helpful info too! Come high, come low, come as you are. morris@staf.org (415) 487-8043 The safer injection slideshow, schedules + more on www.tpsf.com

Healing Arts Series Every Thursday 6PM 1035 Market street, room 3D 
Stonewall, PROP, & Speed Project clients are invited to this safe, supportive, non-judgmental space.
ACUPUNCTURE: 1st & 3rd Thursdays (limited to 10-15 people). A drop-in acupuncture treatment lounge.
BUDDHA'S BRAIN BOOKCLUB: 2nd & 4th Thursdays 6-6:15pm settle in/chill out 6:15-7:30 pm Book Club

Buddha's Brain: The Practical Neuroscience of Happiness, Love, and Wisdom Join Jeremy Prillwitz & Rick Andrews hosting a book study group exploring ways that stimulating & strengthening your brain can bring about more fulfilling relationships, a deeper spiritual life, & a greater sense of inner confidence & worth. We'll learn through reading, discussing interpretations & using simple mindfulness practices to activate the brain states of calm, joy & compassion instead of worry, sorrow & anger. This clear down-to-earth book is filled with practical tools & skills that you can use in daily life to tap the unused potential of your brain & rewire it over time for greater well-being & peace of mind. (Can be attended at any time.)

Castro Paso a Paso Grupo de Apoyo Every Thursday 6PM-7:30/Jueves 6:15-7:30PM 1035 Market, 4th fl. Room 4A Welcome to Castro Paso a Paso, a safe welcoming bilingual group for Latino gay, bi, & other men who have sex with men. We explore issues related to our substance use, sexuality & culture in a basic, harm reduction process. Facilitators Marvin Saavedra & Francisco Escobar

FRIDAYS  
TCB Friday (Taking Care of Business) Group Every Friday 2- 3:30PM 1035 Market street, room 3D
Come for some pre-weekend TLC at the TCB Friday walk in group for gay/bi men. Whether the coming weekend fills you with joy or the jitters plan for the weekend you want with your peers & the support of counselors Chris Powers & Chelsea Moore. Get nonjudgmental support to meet your substance use goals: from safer use, to planned use, to reduced use, to partial abstinence, to abstinence. Group begins with a short meditation & grounding exercise then the group chews on different topics each week.

Castro Harm Reduction Friday Night Every Friday 6-7:30PM 4200 18th St. #203
A fun, friendly, welcoming place for gay, bi, MSM, interested in exploring their relationship to drugs, sex, dating, & whatever you want to discuss. Come as you are, high or low or in between. Facilitators Melissa King & Terrance Harmon

Free confidential HIV & Hep C testing at Stonewall Tuesdays, Wednesdays, Thursdays 3pm-5:30pm / test takes 30 minutes

Walk in Individual Counseling Mon-Fri at 4PM
1035 Market 4th floor for gay/bi & trans men who have sex with men interested in substance use support/counseling at Stonewall.

STONEWALL/SFAF 1035 Market 4th floor 415 487 3100
www.stonewallsf.org www.tweaker.org www.tpsf.com

POSITIVE REINFORCEMENT OPPORTUNITY PROJECT
What is PROP? A 12 week program for gay, bisexual, & trans men who have sex with men & MTF transgender people who choose to stop using methamphetamine. PROP uses positive reinforcement & allows you to earn $$$ to support abstinence from speed. www.props4.org 
1035 Market street, 4th floor drop in Mon/Wed/Fri at 3PM
email or call andrews@sfaf.org Rick Andrews 487-3115

Compass Connecting Point is a unique program that gives any San Francisco family experiencing a housing crisis quick access to the services that they need most, including eviction prevention, emergency shelter, health care, child care and educational programs.

Services include:
• Intake interviews and placement into shelter
• Intensive counseling for families on the waiting list for shelter including assistance in job hunting and school enrollment, plus help accessing benefits, eviction prevention services, childcare, legal assistance, substance abuse treatment, mental health services, and 
• Interest free loans for move-in costs, deposits, back rent, debt payment, and outstanding bills through our Rental Assistance Project (RAP)
• Housing placement assistance, enabling many families to avoid shelter placement and move directly into housing
• Drop-in support services, including computer access, food, clothing, diapers and baby supplies, personal voicemail service, and transportation assistance
• Onsite healthcare through the Tom Waddell Health Center
• A toll-free hotline to provide crisis intervention and information about services
• Referrals to a wide network of Bay Area human services agencies

Drop-in hours are: Mondays 9AM-12PM, Wednesdays 10:30AM-12PM and Fridays 9AM-12PM
You must sign up for an intake before attending drop-in hours. To sign up for an intake, please call the hotline at 855-234-2667.

Compass Family Services also has several other programs, including an emergency shelter for families, a rental subsidy program for families, a two-year family transitional residential program, a childcare center, counseling, case management and parenting classes and groups in English and Spanish.

Hamilton Families
1631 Hayes Street, San Francisco, CA 94117
415-409-2100
https://hamiltonfamilies.org
Established in 1985, Hamilton Families is San Francisco's leading service provider to homeless families, with carefully designed programs to prevent homelessness, provide shelter and stability, return families to permanent housing and support the well-being of children.

The Hamilton Shelter Program in the Tenderloin provides safe shelter, three meals a day and critical social services to 50 families a night for up to six months. If your family needs emergency shelter, please call (415) 292-5228 at 11:00 am or 5:00 pm. 

Hamilton Transitional Housing houses and supports up to 25 families at high risk for chronic homelessness for 6 to 18 months. Families receive intensive social services to identify and address factors contributing to their homelessness. For more info, call (415) 409-2100.

Hamilton Housing Solutions prevents homelessness whenever possible and assists families who have become homeless with eviction prevention, housing search assistance, temporary financial assistance, and other support.

SEXUAL ASSAULT: SOME ISSUES

We all take for granted that feeling of anger, fear, and confusion that arises and continues after experiencing some form of physical, emotional or sexual violation. This is a natural and common reaction for those who are victimized, regardless of age, sex, or pre-existing mental-health issues.

This article, based on interviews with women who counsels lesbian/bisexual, has survived a form of male violence and on the surviving trauma, is an attempt to highlight the common responses and issues which many survivors share. The stigma still associated from the stereotyping of lesbian/bisexual women, especially in the lesbian/gay community, has in general, made it more difficult to report sexual assault.

PRACTICAL ISSUES

Lesbian survivors share all of the usual practical issues that other survivors face. Share experience (e.g., it helps were to report, how to determine if an incident was sexual assault, etc.). In addition, having to "come out" to a police officer or therapist, or social worker, can be an additional trauma on top of the sexual assault.

Pregnancy Pregnancy is an issue which concerns many survivors of sexual assault. Studies show that 5% of rapes of women result in pregnancy. Thus, it is something to be concerned about. In some religious or conservative communities, the issue of an unmarried woman becoming pregnant as a result of rape may be particularly difficult.

Risk of YTD and STDs For all forms of sexual assault, the risk of contracting YTDs and STDs is significantly higher. Again, this may be a particular concern for some survivors, given the stigma associated with these diseases. Information and support around these health issues are crucial.

9. A person who engages in "horseplay" or in "telling of sexjokes of innocent nature" is not considered sexual harassment.

10. A good way to determine if behavior is sexual harassment is to ask yourself "Would I want my spouse, child or other relative to experience this?"

How to Organize Students for Simple Action:
• Don't get bogged down with the seemingly numerous size of problems to take on. start small. Small groups with a clear focus can make big changes. Give credit to collective work at the same time.
• Be creative. brainstorming sessions with a small group of students on the issues you want to address. And we've all been through trauma in some way - One's project is another's beginner task.
• Believe in the people in your circle to problem solve and get involved. Once a project is begun, it is invovled. One's joy is another's momentum. Momentum will lead task. Use that.

One Step, Then: 
Before ever beginning an advocacy/organizing project, be sure to back down your goals - be realistic about what you can achieve. determine carefully what the real issue is so your advocacy matches, not sprawls. With any advocacy effort, be ready to adjust course over time - Flexibility is key.

"The System": 
One Step Closer - When you recognize the problem, next step is to explore what systems and institutions are involved and how they intersect to create the issue. This analysis is critical.  
Which keys open which locks? Learn the levers of power and how to push them. 

Meetings: To-Go - When your research is pointing to the project, begin planning a meeting or action. Organize the goals, target (who can address the issue), agenda, logistics. Invite and use the diverse talents of your constituents. Assign roles and responsibilities. Use this meeting to build energy, strategy, and next steps. Document everything.

Your Strengths: Are you Organizing a Project? - Too many issues. Prioritize and focus your strengths to work on the issue that most resonates with your own experience and skills. Don't try to address all the problems at once - Do what you can, and enlist others to work on other issues. The responsibility is shared.

If Only: Takes One. Though history general shows that large social change happens slowly and along with many efforts, it still takes one strong-willed individual who becomes a catalyst. That individual can be you.

Six Defensive Reactions
1. Surprise: We pretend to agree. We protect ourselves by going along with the situation even though we disagree or disapprove.

2. Superrational: We get logical, figure things out, and win with our minds rather than our hearts. Essentially, we avoid the emotional issue.

3. Withdrawal-Escape: We avoid talking or dealing with it, or change the subject. We leave emotionally and/or physically.

4. Righteous Indignation: W

Six Defensive Reactions
1. Surprise: We pretend to agree. We protect ourselves by going along with the situation even though we disagree or disapprove.

2. Superrational: We get logical, figure things out, and win with our minds rather than our hearts. Essentially, we avoid the emotional issue.

3. Withdrawal-Escape: We avoid talking or dealing with it, or change the subject. We leave emotionally and/or physically.

4. Righteous Indignation: We express moral outrage. We take the "high road" and condemn the other person or act, rather than deal with our own feelings.

5. Counter-Attack: We defend ourselves by attacking the other person. The attack may come with justification, sarcasm, or counter-criticism.

6. Compliance: We give in, agree, or try to please in order to avoid conflict. Sometimes we "act out" our reaction later on.

When we get defensive, we're getting into power struggles. Read this. Reach it to understand your own tendency to power struggle. To be successful in personal and professional relationships, we must learn ways to communicate that don't result in defensiveness and power struggles.

Reworked, Non-Defensive Communication Alternatives:
1. Reflection: "As I hear you, it seems that... Is that right?"
2. Feeling: "I feel... when..." 
3. Wants/Needs: "What I'd like is..."
4. Information: "Here's some information about..."

SOLE FACTS ABOUT YOUNG MOTHERS

Provided by: The Young Mothers' Program

- Often life circumstances and family background have limited their options. They're not always prepared for the challenges of young motherhood.

- As children, many had to deal with physical or sexual abuse, neglect, family violence, substance abuse, poverty, or other difficult circumstances. This can interfere with their capacity for healthy relationships and good parenting.

- 50% of teen mothers have experienced physical abuse. They may repeat the pattern if they don't get help.

- Teen mothers are less likely to finish high school. Without a diploma or job skills, their earning potential and future prospects are limited.

- Children of teen mothers are more likely to have health and behavioral problems, do poorly in school, and become teen parents themselves.

- Fortunately, many young mothers want to improve their lives and give their children a better future. They just need extra support.

MEET STRATEGIES FOR SUCCESS

(Column 1)
RESOURCES
- Transition to Parenthood Workshops
- Individual and Group Counseling
- Parenting Education
- Life Skills Training
- Educational and Career Planning
- Community Referrals 

CONTACTS
- Women's Resource Center
- Phone: 555-1234
- Email: info@wrc.org
- Website: www.wrc.org
- Address: 123 Main Street, Anytown, USA

ADDENDA & NOTES
- U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics. 1996. Current Population Survey. 
- Adler-Baeder, F. 1998. "Welfare Reform and Adolescent Mothers." NCFR Report. Winter.
- Thompson, M.S., & Peebles-Wilkins, W. 1992. "The Impact of Formal, Informal, and Societal Support Networks on the Psychological Well-Being of Black Adolescent Mothers." Social Work, 37(4).
- In a recent interview, a young mother identified as "Danielle" said, "I never learned how to take care of myself, let alone a baby. But I'm determined to do it this time and give my daughter a better life."

KINDERGARTEN REGISTRATION
SCHOOL YEAR 2016 - 2017

A child is eligible to attend kindergarten if he or she was born on or before September 1, 2011.

The South San Francisco Unified School District is urging parents who will have children in kindergarten next August to register them at this time in order to establish their children's priority for schools, programs, and classes with limited space and to help schools anticipate students' needs.

What Is Required to Register
• VERIFICATION OF RESIDENCE – a current utility statement (PG&E) issued to the student's parents/legal guardians.
• PROOF OF AGE – child's birth certificate
• IMMUNIZATION REQUIREMENTS FOR SCHOOL ENTRY
o 4 Polio (if only 3 doses given, 4th dose must be on or after 4th birthday)
o 5 DTP (if only 4 doses given, 4th dose must be on or after 4th birthday) 
o 2 MMR* (all doses must be on or after 1st birthday)
o 3 Hepatitis B vaccines
o 1 Varicella (chickenpox) Doctor's verification of history of disease is acceptable for Varicella vaccine.
o 1 TB Skin Test (PPD Mantoux) and dental examination are recommended but not required
• CHDP – Physical examination required for kindergarten entry, given on or after February 1, 2016.

Parents need not take their children to school for registration.

When to Register
Kindergarten registration for the 2016-2017 school year will start February 1, 2016 and end May 31, 2016. Schools are open for registration from 9:30 a.m. to 11:30 a.m. and 1:00 p.m. to 3:00 p.m. weekdays. All registrations after May 31, 2016 will be placed on a space available basis.

Where to Register
Parents are asked to register their child at the school, which serves their residential area. Please consult the following resources to determine school of attendance and to obtain additional information:
• www.ssfusd.org

Therefore, parents MUST register their child at their school of residence before requesting a transfer to a school of their choice. Staging media events
The most successful staging media events attract a wide range of people. This action of others helps, gives, and creates credibility.

Press conferences vs media events 
There is a difference. Press conferences are usually for more negative situations, while media events are for more positive situations.

More on media events:
- Media events usually have more positive. upbeat stories, announcements, recognitions, etc.
- Staging media events involve planning an event specifically to attract media coverage.
- media events usually have an A/V component, such as PowerPoint or video.
- media events frequently incorporate other elements to create a memorable experience, like music, speeches, demonstrations, etc.
- Proper planning is key for media events to be successful.

Qualities of successful media events:
- An interesting, newsworthy story
- Visuals that support and enhance the story
- Speakers who are engaging and articulate
- Planning for an audience and media attendance
- Promotional materials that are well-designed and informative

The press conference vs the media event:
Press conferences are generally more for negative situations and involve responding to media questions. Media events are more positive, with an emphasis on sharing information and visuals.

The key difference is that media events require more advance planning to create an engaging experience for the audience and media.

resources.ocr_text:
INTERNATIONAL REWORKSHOP

STRATEGIC PLANNING AT EXECUTIVE CITY WORKSHOP

RULES:
1. Assume that you have a certain quota/goal and want to get the most out of your people and organize them to best reach that goal and give maximum value. Consider their strengths, weaknesses, and interests first in establishing the quota/goal.
2. Assume that you have an organization and have to determine how to operate within regulations, utilize available resources, and optimize production. Consider the current landscape of regulations, resources, and production realities.
3. Assume that your goal is growth and goals that require your people to work extra or in new ways. Consider how to make this engaging and motivational for them.
4. Assume that they may appear very eager on the surface but internally anxious about the changes. Communicating to you in the best way to meet the goals may not always be their first priority.
5. Assume that people in the group are commenting in good faith, but have different perspectives and experiences to draw upon. Facilitating a constructive discussion that leads to a shared vision and shared goals may require significant skill.
6. Assume that targets/goals set up may evolve as the group provides more input and you gain a deeper understanding. Remaining open and flexible will be important.
7. Recognize that as your people experience the process, they may develop a more vested interest and greater engagement. Don't be surprised if some initial resistance leads to greater commitment over time.
8. Assume that issues which appear to be purely operational may have deeper roots related to culture, communication, or trust. Addressing these underlying factors may be key to lasting solutions.
9. Because some people in the group may have a tendency to get bogged down in details or become overly territorial, you may need to help them stay focused on the big picture and overall goals.

When you are the one who has to straighten the frame around your life, it's a different experience than when you are the one who helps others do this. As you've been straightening your frame, have you noticed...
That you no longer spend hours agonizing over the specific nuances of your daily life? Rather, your focus is on the bigger picture and what truly matters most.
That you've gained a healthier perspective on your relationships - choosing to invest in the ones that bring you life and letting go of the ones that drain you.
That you've rediscovered a passion for the things you used to enjoy but had let fall to the wayside, like a hobby or creative pursuit.
That your inner dialogue is more positive and life-giving, rather than negative and condemning.
That you feel a renewed sense of purpose and meaning, even in the midst of your current circumstances.
What you've gained is a frame that aligns with who you truly are - the person God created you to be. This frame allows you to see your life through His eyes, rather than the distorted lens of your circumstances, insecurities, or past experiences.
How you frame the story of your life will determine the trajectory of your future. When the frame is centered on God's truth and His plan for you, your life will take on new beauty, purpose, and freedom.
So keep straightening that frame, my friend. The view is about to get a whole lot clearer.

resources.ocr_text:
Human Trafficking Task Force e-Guide
Strengthening Collaborative Responses

Developed by the Office for Victims of Crime and the Bureau of Justice Assistance, this is an e-learning tool that offers human trafficking task forces and allied professionals practical information on the creation and day-to-day operations of task forces, as well as essential knowledge they need to effectively identify and assist victims and to investigate and prosecute human trafficking cases.

The e-Guide includes the following new sections & features:
• Guidance on how to work with underrepresented populations; strategies to strengthen multidisciplinary collaboration; examples of various task force models; discussion of investigative and prosecutorial strategies and more.

Your orientation 1-2 year fellowship 12 is your integration of a campus organization (as. A.S. Council, ICC, Big or Trekkers ) with the knowledge you have gained from the Band of Trekkers course. Your multiearlier the experience you gain the better equipped you will be to assist in the running of your student

You are now required to assist in your understanding of how an organization works. As the fellow, you are given the opportunity of applying what you have learned. Differences of opinion among the members may exist. You can help the group resolve conflicts by drawing upon the techniques of group dynamics.

Organizational Skills. As Com will be developed. How do individuals communication, decision making, conflict resolution, etc. (reliance of opinion).

What is the organization's goal? How do they differ versus your own. Explore these differences. What is the structure of the organization. How are decisions made.

Are the membership on basis specialized knowledge or aptitude vs group selection. 

Is the group rate on achieving it objectives, or just socializing and just for fun?

Meetings: What is their agenda? Are minutes recorded and distributed. How are items placed on the agenda. 

Funding: A good group has a source of funding, regular budget meetings and financial accountability. Where does funding come from, how is it controlled.

Community relation: Is this group connected to the campus community. Are they known, do people identify with them, are they isolated. Effect of relationships, how evaluated.

Goals: Are goals clearly articulated and shared, or vague and unknown. Do the members behavior support goal achievement.

Human interaction: show empathy, understanding. be fair, honest, allow disagreement, build trust. manage conflict.

Challenge: Provide data, gather missing information, meet resistance with ideas rather than force, look for positive solutions.

Evaluation: Reflect critically, identify successes and failures, propose changes. Create a plan of action. A good study will show your growth and provide concrete recommendations for the group.

resources.ocr_text:
SUICIDE INTERVENTION
"With suicide, the greatest risk is actually in the months following a crisis, not during the crisis itself. So for a suicidal person, the danger period is often the days and weeks after a suicidal episode, not the episode itself."

Callers have a ways been an area of concern. The outlook has generally been those who call for help, those who call for the "cry of loyos", are the ones who need it the most. Conversely, those who are really serious about ending it don't bother calling anyone.

This for this perception is false. Studies have shown the those who call suicide hotlines in crisis are often the most at risk. They are reaching out because they want to live, not die.

When the counselor reaches out in the beginning, it is critical to convey that they care and that the caller is not alone. Statements such as "I'm so glad you called" and "I'm here to help" go a long way. A connection, no matter how brief, can save a life.

Suicide is often an impulsive act. Many who attempt suicide do not necessarily want to die, but instead see it as the only way to end their pain. If someone can get through the crisis, the urge to die often subsides. So the counselor's role is to do whatever it takes to get the caller through that moment.

One of the most important things to stress is that the caller's safety is the top priority, not judgement. The counselor should make it clear that they are there to listen without judgement and to do whatever it takes to keep the caller safe.

It's also important to empower the caller. Phrases like "You're doing the right thing by calling" and "I know this is difficult, but you're being so brave" can go a long way. The counselor wants the caller to feel like they have the strength to get through this.

After the initial call, the most important step is to follow up. Studies show that regular check-ins in the days and weeks following a crisis can significantly reduce the risk of a future suicide attempt. So the counselor should schedule a time to call back and really make that connection.

Ultimately, the goal is to help the caller find reasons to live, not die. Discussing their support system, making plans, and talking through coping strategies can all be incredibly helpful. The key is to instill hope and show the caller that their life is worth living.

Summary
When use question arises, and conversation becomes personal: Listen, without judging, what concerns are being expressed. Hear empathy in their words, what are they feeling, is there an underlying need or want that is being communicated.

Try to understand first, rather than make assumptions. Think about what you have in common, find shared connection. Then ask yourself, how can I respond in a way that honors their experience and needs, without discounting mine.

Use gentle tones, avoid lecturing. Explore together how the situation might be viewed or addressed differently. Validate their feelings, let them know you respect their choices, even if you don't agree. 

Ultimately, the goal is mutual understanding and growth, so that all needs and perspectives can be heard, and a path forward can be found that works for everyone involved.

1. Ask:
Use questions to deepen your own understanding of what is going on, what the other person is experiencing. Avoid jump to conclusions or making assumptions.

2. Hear:
Share your perspective, but recognize there are often multiple ways of seeing the same situation. Be open to the other person's experience and different point of view.

3. See:
Describe what you see happening, without judgment. Recognize there may be patterns or issues at work that require a thoughtful, non-defensive approach.

4. Shift Limits:
Describe the problem in universal terms, not just about who is "right" or "wrong". See if there are any underlying needs or constraints that may be shaping the situation.

5. Set Limits:
Using "I" statements, tell the person how you feel. Respect their experience while being clear about your own boundaries and concerns. 

6. Challenge:
Tell the other person what you perceive, but challenge them in a way that encourages their reflection and growth, rather than shaming or blaming.

"Powerful, Non-Defensive Communication: By Sharon Ellison, M.S. ©1997, page 16"

Targeting Your Audience

1. Define Your Audience(s)
The target group for your public awareness effort is likely diverse. It may be your community, your existing clients, those in need of your services, the general public, the media, or policy-makers. The segments you wish to reach with your messages will inform how you communicate.

2. Tailor Your Messages to Your Audience
The language you use, the channels you choose, and the framing of your message will depend on your target audience(s). Consider how the messages will be perceived and what will motivate or resonate with each group.

EXAMPLE: Continuing the mental health campaign, messaging to service providers might focus on the clinical evidence and data. Messages to those impacted would be more personal, focusing on lived experience and community supports. Media messages would emphasize news-worthiness and policy impact.

3. The Future of Living Wage
Research relevant data and statistics. Develop concise, powerful key messages. Leverage personal stories to humanize the issue. Tailor content for different audiences - whether it's providers, participants, media, or policy-makers.

4. Framing & Messaging
Frame the issue in a way that resonates. Use clear, accessible language. Develop compelling narratives. Test messages with your target audience(s). Refine based on feedback.

5. Nuts & Bolts of Getting the Message Out
Identify the most effective communication channels for reaching your audiences. Develop a multi-faceted outreach strategy using a variety of tactics. Coordinate and integrate your efforts for maximum impact.

6. Campaign Strategies
Outline your overall campaign strategy and timeline. Assign responsibilities. Mobilize your team. Monitor, evaluate, and adapt your approach as needed.
