part developed into eclampsia, it could lead to seizures, organ failure, stroke and, in rare cases, death. No one knows for sure what causes it.

Dr. Maurice Druzin, an obstetrician at Lucile Packard Children's Hospital at Stanford, says it is likely triggered by flaws in how the placenta implanted into the wall of the uterus early in the pregnancy. If the placenta doesn't attach perfectly, toxic substances may be released into the mother's blood vessels that go to vital organs, he says.

"It's like if you have an orchestra of 100 musicians and you have one horn player who blows at the wrong time. The audience is going to know it doesn't sound good," says Druzin, who is also a professor of obstetrics and gynecology and maternal-fetal medicine at the Stanford School of Medicine. "When the placenta attaches, everything has to be perfectly in sync just like an orchestra."

So, the orchestra in my body wasn't in sync when my son was trying to develop. Experts say preeclampsia is more likely to happen in women with a history of diabetes, kidney disease, lupus, obesity and high blood pressure. None of these applied to me. However, hypertension does run in my family, and both of my sisters said they experienced some high blood pressure during their pregnancies. It is possible genetics played a role in my situation.

Signs and Symptoms
I had a suspicion something wasn't right, when at about four weeks before my due date, I was washing my hands in the bright light of a Target bathroom and noticed my fingers were really puffy. But I knew swelling can happen during pregnancy, so I didn't worry. I later found out that swelling in the face and hands is one of the symptoms of preeclampsia.

"A lot of the symptoms, like swelling and headaches, can happen anyway during pregnancy," says Dr. Jonathan Weiss, a perinatologist and high-risk pregnancy doctor at UCSF Benioff Children's Physicians. "But if the headaches don't go away with a couple of Tylenol, then you probably should call your doctor."

Signs and symptoms of preeclampsia include blood pressure greater than 140 over 90, swelling in the hands and face, abdominal pain, severe headaches, dizziness, vision changes like flashing lights and floaters, and vomiting and nausea.

In most cases, this condition appears after the 20-week mark, although it can occur earlier. 
"It's largely why women's prenatal visits are weekly toward the end of the pregnancy," Weiss says. "We want to make sure they are not developing preeclampsia."
The day after I received the news, I saw a specialist who concluded my son could be delivered without being premature since we were so close to his due date. I was immediately admitted to the hospital, put on a monitor to make sure the baby was doing well and given high blood pressure medication and a drug called Pitocin, which is used to induce labor.

The specialist asked me, "Are you ready to have this baby?" I immediately thought, no, absolutely not. We hadn't installed the car seat; the crib was still in a box; I didn't get a chance to wash the baby's clothes and I didn't have a suitcase packed for the hospital.

The Big Day
During the 24 hours plus that I was in labor, a cuff recorded my blood pressure every half hour. As my contractions became more painful, my blood pressure increased. It was not reassuring to see readings like 175 over 101 or 180 over 103. To make things worse, nurses came in every 20 minutes to say things like, "Wow, your blood pressure is really high! You need to relax." I had a condition that could kill me and I was having a baby and they wanted me to relax!

Yeah, OK. I told them to get the epidural going. Just when I thought it couldn't get any scarier, I got a call on my cell from my sister. My mom had just arrived at the hospital. She had heart condition and was dealing with numerous problems that year. Fortunately, her condition was stable.

Once the epidural kicked in, I started to relax and even got some rest. When I woke up the next morning, my cervix still wasn't dilated enough to have the baby. It was taking forever! One of the doctors sped up the process by breaking my water and after that, things started to move fast.

My son, Giulio, was born, and he was perfect. Because of the complications, I feared something was going to go wrong, but he was gorgeous. He had all his fingers and toes and weighed in at 7 pounds, 2 ounces.

Postpartum Scare
The doctors and nurses assured me that my postpartum experience would be challenging, but I was totally unprepared for how difficult it would be. I was in the hospital for a week, and the nurses checked my blood pressure around the clock, as it remained quite high.

Your experience can become the change:

THE COMMUNITY MENTAL HEALTH MOVEMENT

In the 1950s, a community-based movement emerged to transform mental health services in the United States. This community mental health movement arose in part as a reaction against the often-neglected conditions in large state-run psychiatric hospitals. The movement sought to develop a decentralized system of mental health services that would be more accessible and responsive to local communities.

Community mental health centers were established to provide a range of outpatient services, including crisis intervention, counseling, medication management, and referrals to other social services. The goal was to provide more humane, effective, and community-based care for individuals experiencing mental health challenges.

The community mental health movement also advocated for the deinstitutionalization of individuals with mental illness, working to transition them from large, isolated psychiatric hospitals to community-based settings. This shift was driven by a growing recognition that long-term institutionalization could be harmful and that many individuals could thrive with proper support in their local communities.

However, the transition to community-based care was not always smooth or well-resourced. Challenges included a lack of funding, a shortage of community-based services, and difficulties in coordinating care across different providers and systems.

Despite these challenges, the community mental health movement represented a significant shift in the way mental health services were conceptualized and delivered in the United States. It paved the way for a greater emphasis on human rights, autonomy, and community-based approaches to mental health treatment and support.

Philosophy by any other name remains an attempt to

The Basic Argument

Increases in human dignity are achieved not through blind
adherence to traditional authority and time-honored beliefs, but
by expanding one's capacity to think critically, to question, and to
reach one's own conclusions about the nature of the world and
one's place in it. True progress comes not from the passive
acceptance of doctrine, but from the active exercise of reason.

This is the essence of the Rationalist philosophy, as expounded by
the great thinkers of France. It is a vision that promises to liberate the
individual from the shackles of unquestioning faith and custom, to elevate
humanity through the powers of the mind. But it is also a philosophy

authority of church and tradition.

The Battered Women's Wage

- Mobilizing people to break the silence

- Encouraging self-help

National Domestic Violence Hotline:
1-800-799-7233 (SAFE)

Domestic violence is a national problem involving all races, ages, socioeconomic backgrounds, and educational levels. Common myths about domestic violence include:

It only happens to some groups - not me, my family, or friends.
It is a private, family matter, not a community problem.
Women enjoy the violence or can easily leave the relationship.
The violence only lasts for a short time and is not very serious.
Alcohol and drugs cause the violence.

The reality is:
Domestic violence affects people of all races, ages, socioeconomic backgrounds, education levels, and religious affiliations. Even if it hasn't happened to you or someone you know, it is still a community problem that affects everyone.
Violence in the home, even in small doses, is never okay and is a serious crime. Leaving an abusive relationship is extremely difficult and dangerous. Most women are killed by their abusers after they leave.
Alcohol and drugs do not cause domestic violence, but may make the violence worse. The batterer is always responsible for the abuse.

Some examples of domestic abuse include:
Physical abuse - hitting, slapping, kicking, choking, etc. 
Emotional abuse - name-calling, insults, undermining self-esteem, stalking, isolation from friends and family
Sexual abuse - forced sexual acts, withholding sex as punishment, denying reproductive rights

Domestic violence is a pattern of abusive behavior used to gain power and control over an intimate partner. It includes physical, sexual, emotional, economic or psychological actions or threats that influence another person. The violence escalates over time and often leads to more serious and frequent incidents. 

Speak up. You can help stop the violence. If you or someone you know is being abused, call the National Domestic Violence Hotline at 1-800-799-SAFE (7233). They can provide information, safety planning, and referrals to local resources.

Typical acts of [illegible] may include: Tripping and falling on an uneven floor or stairs, slipping and falling on a wet floor, being struck by a falling or moving object, being assaulted by another person, being involved in a motor vehicle accident, and suffering an allergic reaction to a substance.

If you have been injured due to another's negligence, you may be entitled to compensation for your injuries, medical expenses, lost wages, pain and suffering, and other damages.

Negligence is the failure to exercise reasonable care, which results in harm to another. In order to recover damages, you must show that the defendant owed you a duty of care, the defendant breached that duty, the breach was the proximate cause of your injuries, and you suffered damages as a result.

Some examples of negligence that may result in injury include:

Premises Liability:
If you are injured on someone else's property due to a dangerous condition on the premises, such as a wet floor, uneven surface, or inadequate lighting, the property owner may be liable for your injuries.

Motor Vehicle Accidents:
If you are involved in a car accident due to another driver's negligence, such as speeding, distracted driving, or driving under the influence, you may be able to recover damages from the at-fault driver.

Product Liability:
If you are injured by a defective product, the manufacturer, distributor, or seller of the product may be liable for your injuries.

Assault and Battery:
If you are assaulted or battered by another person, you may be able to recover damages from the perpetrator.

Slip and Fall Incidents:
If you slip and fall on a wet, slippery, or uneven surface, the property owner may be liable for your injuries.

Workers' Compensation:
If you are injured while performing your job duties, you may be entitled to workers' compensation benefits to cover your medical expenses and lost wages.

The Benefits of Hiring an Attorney:
Negotiating with insurance companies can be complex and challenging. An experienced personal injury attorney can help you navigate the legal process, gather evidence, and fight for the compensation you deserve.

Contacting the Attorneys at Parham & Associates:
If you have been injured due to another's negligence, contact the attorneys at Parham & Associates for a free consultation. We have over 50 years of combined experience and a track record of success in personal injury cases.

We serve clients throughout Virginia, and our attorneys are available to meet with you in our offices in Chesapeake, Hampton, Norfolk, or Virginia Beach. Call us today at (757) 547-5555 to schedule your free consultation.

resources.ocr_text:
THE CYCLES OF BATTERING

'The cycles of battering are a repetition of building a tension, an explosion building up a tension, an explosion building, a resolution, and then a tension building up again.'

Tension Building:
1. The woman can see tensions mounting. There is a change in the partner's behavior, attitude and conversation.
2. He is with holding affection, money, or basic needs.
3. Verbal abuse begins. He criticizes, curses, threatens to hit her.
4. She tries to calm him down, to avoid confrontation.

The Explosion:
5. An outburst occurs. He physically attacks her, destroys property, etc.
6. He may injure her and deny responsibility.
7. She may try to get away, to fight back, or to calm him down.

The Honeymoon:
8. He may be remorseful, and promise it will never happen again.
9. He is affectionate, kind, buying gifts, and acting loving.
10. He may blame the incident on work stress, alcohol, or other external factors.
11. She may believe he will change, and the cycle begins again.

In Stage 1, the man secapes that his actions were abusive. He blames her, the situation, or external factors. This starts the cycle over again.

The woman has grown to accept the violence as part of the relationship. She takes responsibility for his actions.
The violence is an attempt to regain power and control in the relationship.
The violence escalates in both frequency and severity over time.
The cycle continues with increasing danger to the woman.

Focus is diligence - grind to generate the motion.

7. THE FUTURE OF LIVING WAGE

RESOURCES

CONTACTS

ADDENDA & NOTES

Based on research groups in the UK from the Rowntree organization and 
the Resolution Foundation, the minimum income standard for a single 
person represents about 60% of the median household income. At the 
same time, the voluntary living wage is set at about 60% of the typical 
full-time wage. While these benchmarks provide a useful way to think 
about the living wage, they are not the same as the 'required income' for 
the minimum acceptable standard of living.
The government's official national living wage is currently set at 60% of 
the median hourly wage. This hourly figure of £8.91 for those aged 23 and 
over, represents around 52% of the median hourly wage. In contrast, a 
living wage based on the real cost of living would be higher - calculations 
by the Resolution Foundation and others suggest £10.85 per hour for the 
UK outside London, and £11.95 per hour within London.

There are a range of views on the future of the living wage:
• The national living wage is set to rise further in the coming years, but 
may still be below a real living wage based on minimum acceptable costs.
• Employers may choose to pay more than the statutory minimum, due 
to recruitment, retention and productivity benefits.
• Trade unions may campaign for higher living wages, and collective
agreements may set living wages above the statutory minimum.
• There are calls for the living wage to be set at 66% of median earnings,
which would be around £12 per hour.
• There are arguments that a higher living wage could reduce in-work 
poverty, boost productivity and economic growth.
• However, concerns remain about potential job losses if the living wage 
is set too high.

FIRM TURNAROUND & SALE
10. Turnaround and a Sale

• Liabilities can be reduced, perhaps through negotiation of existing 
debts, reaching agreements with creditors.
• Management teams can be strengthened, processes and systems
improved to increase profitability.
• New investors and capital can be attracted to the business.
• The business can be prepared for sale to a new owner who can invest
and develop it further.

This may enable the business to be kept going and employment 
safeguarded, rather than it going into receivership or administration.

resources.ocr_text:
The Big Scare
A Mom's Tale of Surviving Preeclampsia
By Teresa Mills-Faraudo

When I was thinking about having kids, friends with children reassured me that my pregnancy was a beautiful and natural experience, rarely with problems. Even my doctors rattled off facts and figures about how unlikely it is to have complications. No one talked to me about what could go wrong.

That's why I was so unprepared when things did go wrong.

Not long after becoming pregnant with my son, I discovered my husband and I were both carriers of cystic fibrosis, a life-threatening, genetic disease that causes persistent lung infections and eventually limits the ability to breathe. Because we were both carriers, there was a good chance our son could have the disease. After going through genetic testing and waiting weeks for the results, we finally found out my son didn't have it - he was only a carrier like us.

Phew! What a relief. I thought that was going to be the only big scare. Unfortunately, it wasn't.

For most of my pregnancy, prenatal visits were normal. I kept working. I even continued to jog and go to my samba dance classes after getting an OK from my doctor.

But about two weeks before my due date, I went for a routine prenatal visit and my blood pressure was really high. The doctor took it several times to make sure it didn't go down, and told me I needed to go on bed rest and see a specialist. I had preeclampsia, she said, and the only cure was to deliver the baby.

Before that moment, I hadn't even heard of preeclampsia. But I soon learned that 7 percent of pregnancies are affected by this condition, which is marked by high blood pressure and protein in the urine. This put me and my baby into panic mode: if the "pre" in preeclampsia turned into the real thing, it could be life-threatening.

I was told I needed to go on bed rest and to see a specialist. I had preeclampsia, she said, and the only cure was to deliver the baby.

resources.ocr_text: THE LIVING WAGE ESSAGE: THE OPTIONThe living wage is a reflection of fairness that the employer should pay a wage that allows an employee to live with dignity and meet basic needs. Wages should be sufficient to support a basic standard of living and enable a dignified life. A living wage is a wage rate at which a single adult working full-time can afford the minimum costs of living, including food, housing, transportation, healthcare, childcare, taxes and other essential needs. It represents the minimum income necessary for a worker to meet their basic needs.KEY ARGUMENTS:People who work full-time should not live in poverty. Fair compensation enables workers to afford a basic standard of living and participate more fully in their communities. Paying a living wage improves worker productivity and morale, reduces turnover, and ultimately benefits the employer through improved service and products. Paying a living wage demonstrates social responsibility and benefits the local community.ADDITIONAL TIPS:• People who work full-time should not have to rely on government assistance to meet their basic needs.• Paying a living wage demonstrates social responsibility and benefits the local community.• Living wage jobs increase the disposable income of workers, leading to increased spending at local businesses.• Higher wages reduce employee turnover and improve job performance, resulting in cost savings for employers.• Living wages promote family stability and child wellbeing by ensuring a basic standard of living.• Paying a living wage helps break the cycle of poverty and enables economic mobility.• Businesses that pay living wages see positive effects on recruitment, retention, morale and productivity.The great mystery of our time is how we convinced ourselves that we could enjoy the benefits of employment without accepting the social responsibility it entails. We have forgotten that the wage contract is first and foremost a social contract. The living wage movement is a moral awakening that asks us to remember and honor that contract.

resources.ocr_text:
The Living Wage Media Plan

The central theme of this living wage media plan is that despite being employed, many workers still do not earn enough to maintain a basic standard of living. For too long, the minimum wage has been set so low that it does not provide sufficient income to cover even basic necessities. We aim to raise awareness of this issue and promote policies that can help ensure all workers are able to earn a living wage.

Your About Campaign Planning Strategy
Conduct a plan to create and disseminate media that will educate the public on the need for a living wage. This may include press releases, op-eds, social media campaigns, and other communications to inform and engage the public. Consider the audience, message, and best channels to reach them effectively.

It's About Campaign Planning Strategy
Conduct a plan to work with policymakers, labor organizations, and community groups to advocate for living wage policies. This may involve testifying at hearings, meeting with legislators, mobilizing supporters, and collaborating on legislative initiatives. The goal is to build political will and enact changes that improve low-wage workers' economic security.

Planning Your MEDIA A CHECKLIST
1. Frame the issues: Identify key message themes that highlight the challenges low-wage workers face and the benefits of living wage policies.
2. Develop effective narratives: Create compelling stories that put a human face on the living wage issue and connect with people's values and experiences.
3. Target the right audiences: Determine which stakeholders (public, policymakers, media, etc.) to prioritize and tailor outreach accordingly.
4. Choose the best channels: Evaluate traditional and social media options to reach your target audiences most effectively.
5. Translate your message: Ensure your communications resonate across diverse communities by considering language, cultural, and accessibility needs.
6. Tap grassroots networks: Mobilize community organizations, faith leaders, and other trusted voices to help amplify your message.
7. Sustain the momentum: Plan for ongoing media engagement, with a mix of timely reactions and proactive campaigns over an extended period.
8. Measure impact: Track key metrics to evaluate the effectiveness of your media strategy and make adjustments as needed.

OPINION EDITORIAL
As the debate continues to rage over raising the minimum wage, it is important to step back and remember the purpose of the minimum wage - to provide a decent standard of living for America's working families. The current federal minimum wage of $5.15 per hour simply does not meet that goal. A family of three with one full-time minimum wage worker falls $3,540 below the poverty line.

The minimum wage has not been increased since 1997, and during that time its value has been eroded by inflation. A full-time minimum wage worker earns just $10,712 annually - an income that leaves a family of three thousands of dollars in poverty. This is unacceptable in the wealthiest nation on Earth.

The minimum wage must be raised to a level that allows full-time workers to earn a wage above the poverty line. Proposals to increase the minimum wage to $6.15 or $6.65 per hour would make a significant difference in the lives of millions of Americans struggling to make ends meet. These increases would lift the annual income of a full-time minimum wage worker to between $12,792 and $13,832 - incomes that would pull a family of three out of poverty.

Raising the minimum wage is not only the right thing to do, it also makes good economic sense. Increasing the minimum wage puts more money in the pockets of working families, who then spend that money in their local economies, creating jobs and economic growth. In fact, studies have shown that modest increases in the minimum wage have little or no negative effect on employment.

As the debate on the minimum wage continues, we must not forget the human faces behind the numbers - the single mothers struggling to feed their children, the elderly working to supplement their meager Social Security checks, the disabled individuals trying to make ends meet. These are the people who depend on the minimum wage to provide a decent standard of living, and they deserve our support.

It is time for Congress to raise the federal minimum wage to a level that reflects the true value of work and provides a path out of poverty for America's working families. Our nation's prosperity should be shared by all who contribute to it through their labor. Raising the minimum wage is an important step toward fulfilling that promise.

THE PRESS KIT

A good press kit can be an invaluable resource to reporters and high-profile journalists. It can give them a quick and reliable source of information about your organization, your key people, activities and accomplishments.

There are two kinds of press kits:

1. A starter press kit
contains the basic information about your organization: history, mission, key programs, biographies of key staff or board members, and any other important facts.

2. The more extensive press kits:
This can be a more in-depth multimedia presentation that includes video, audio, photographs and other visuals that give reporters a more complete picture of your organization.

THE RIGHT APPROACH:

• Your main press release should be clear, concise and compelling.
• You may want to include additional facts sheets or backgrounders on specific programs, services or initiatives.
• Consider including a selection of high-resolution photos that capture the essence of your organization. Make sure they are captioned and that you have permission to use them.
• You may also want to include business cards, newsletters, annual reports or other collateral materials that give reporters a more well-rounded sense of your work.
• The press kit should be easy to navigate and organized in a logical way. Use tabs, dividers or other design elements to make it user-friendly.
• Strive for a professional, polished look and feel. This is a reflection of your organization.

WHAT TO INCLUDE IN A PRESS KIT:

• Your main press release
• Fact sheets on your organization, programs, services
• Biographies of key staff/board members
• High-resolution photos (with captions and credits)
• Copies of recent media coverage
• Newsletters, annual reports, brochures
• Business cards for media contacts

THE DELIVERY:
• You may want to send your press kit electronically as a PDF or provide a link to download it from your website.
• Depending on the recipient, you may also want to consider a printed version that you can mail or hand-deliver.
• Make sure your press kit is easily accessible and up-to-date on your website.

Rising in the Deep South:
THE GOOD BOOK LONDON REVIEW WORKS A LIVING WAGE FOR TWO

Involve a literary legacy. By the Director-Transsub. Roman Anoreth:
Immerse yourself. Have and recommend all the things described in the ancient fervent Aryav tradition - a small, all-enveloping, immersive wonder-world. The environment is so captivating, so impossible to paraphrase or extract. Sundulph for the Paregorgic Ritual has changed none of this.

How We Got Started: A Begger
We began in 2010. The long story told. The Exceptionalist movement was already happening and we ached to contribute. Godlingwood, Trevain Granger, and myself - we were struck with the same idea independently. We knew a physical space was needed, a place of wonder and fellowship, in order to serve this movement. Vacant lots were disappearing fast in the neighbourhood. But a friend of a friend heard a whisper of a property sale, a former warehouse just down the road. We viewed it that day.

Know The Goal: Get A Grant
Reopisling the site was a community effort from the start. That was the plan: to build something together, run it cooperatively. Grants and funding proposals took years of patient work. Countless meetings, documents, negotiations. We had to convince every agency - no one quite understood what we were trying to create. Finally in 2015, we were awarded a significant grant. The Deep South Network for Social Change came through.

How We Organize: A Worker-Directed Co-Op 
The space itself took another two years to build out. We used the grant money judiciously, subcontracting skilled tradespeople but doing much of the work collectively. It was essential that this be a worker-directed co-op, not a top-down organization. All major decisions were made by consensus. We wanted the space to embody the values we hoped to share.

We look to the future and listen to the call of St. Vincent De Paul to "extend mercy towards others, so that there can be someone in need whom we meet without helping." St. Vincent De Paul Society's Wellness Center is dedicated to responding to the call of our community, embracing a holistic healing approach to the needs of our participants. Inspired by our core values of compassion, social justice and spirituality, we are committed to bringing wellness, recovery and clinical best practices to all who come through our doors. Using a harm reduction model, the Wellness Center strives to meet people where they are by focusing on lending continued support to those who are struggling with substance abuse issues and other debilitating diagnoses. Our daily program consists of stress reduction techniques, exercise, selections of personal and spiritual development as well as health topic sessions. Good nutritional guidelines play a pivotal role at the Wellness Center. We offer healthy free snacks and lunch based on a thoughtfully designed menu of fresh local foods with high/dense nutritional value.

All are welcome and encouraged to participate on the level that best fits their needs.

All Sessions are Free.
Drop-ins are Welcome.
Lunch is provided for those who participate in morning sessions.

THE STONEWALL PROJECT
Self-Directed Walk In Program Schedule October 2014-January 2015 Cycle

The Stonewall Project is a non-shaming & sex positive counseling program for gay, bi, & trans men looking to make changes to their alcohol, crystal meth, crack cocaine, powder cocaine, GHB, ketamine, &/or other drug use. We offer a broad range of services that recognize your strengths, integrate substance use & mental health counseling, mindfulness & wellness services. Stonewall is a treatment program committed to the harm-reduction philosophy. We invite you to bring all of who you are to services on your journey toward improved health, relationships, or functioning in the world. All goals are welcome, supported, & respected.

Self-Directed Program: Each week Stonewall offers a variety of walk in groups, book clubs, harm reduction education opportunities, syringe exchange services, individual counseling, & wellness services like meditation, massage & acupuncture. No paperwork, no intake, no waits. You decide what services are a good fit and how often.

Structured Enrolled Program: After attending three orientation groups & meeting with Stonewall's Intake Coordinator Kevin Mosley, you will be matched with a skilled therapist, social worker, or certified addiction counselor for six to eighteen months & attend two groups each week designed to support your goals. Additionally, Stonewall offers elective groups on healing trauma, stress, anger, communication, sex & sexuality, & mindfulness. Depending on your individual needs, we provide psychiatric assessments, anti-depressants/mood stabilizers or other psychiatric medications, & assistance linking to & obtaining services at other agencies. www.stonewallsf.org

Questions? Walk in Mon-Fri at 4PM 1035 Market, 4th floor or call (415) 487-3100 & speak with a counselor.

MONDAYS
Over the Influence Book Club Every Monday 12PM-1:30 1035 Market 2C strong coffee + snacks + nerds
A fabulous way to start the week. See what it's like to be part of a group culture where all goals from safer use, to abstinence are respected & supported. Give judgment & stigma around drug use & drug users a holiday to free up space for self love, optimism, & self care. Explore new ideas, share experiences, & check out this amazing book by the Harm Reduction Therapy Center. Join anytime on any chapter. Facilitators Terry Morris & Peter Carnini ALL WELCOME

Walk in Skills Building Group Every Monday 6-7:30PM 1035 Market room 3E
This interactive classroom will provide practical tools that can help in challenging situations & make more space for choice, new options for changing behaviors, & build skills to meet & maintain your substance use goals. Each week focuses on a different skill. You choose which weeks you attend and what topics are of interest: Self-Care, Motivation to Change - Decisional Balance, Triggers, Assessing High Risk Triggers, Stages of Change, Identifying Risky Behavioral Chains, Coping with High Risk Situations, Slips & Relapses, & Drug, Set & Setting. All goals around substance use are appropriate & welcome here; from safer use to abstinence. Facilitators Marvin Saavedra & Ken Campbell

TUESDAYS 
Crystal Clear: A Harm Reduction Group for African American Men Visioning Personalized Recovery
Every Tuesday at 12pm @ 1035 Market Street, Room 3E  Settle in, share a meal, & join the circle. If you would like to connect to & support other African American men as they grow their own & personal definitions & roadmaps to recovery... Join the Crystal Clear Recovery Group. Facilitators Terrance Harmon, Jamal Bey and Tiana Townsend

6th street Harm Reduction Drop-in Group for gay/bi men Tuesdays 2-3PM 117 6th st. @ Mission/Howard
Check in about what's up with your world & how drugs are fitting in your life. Come high-- come low--come sober: come as you are. NX Exchange always available. Doors 1:30 for strong coffee & snacks. Facilitators Terry Morris & Christopher Belmondo

Castro Alcohol Group Every Tuesday 6-7:30PM 4200 18th St. #203
Want to change your drinking habits? Find your way to safer drinking, controlled drinking, reduced drinking, or quitting at the Castro Alcohol Group. Facilitators Ken Campbell & Marvin Saavedra

"The history of a million failures becomes the charter of the success of one man." — Samuel Smiles

"They are political personalities of the past who may, or may not, have been connected with the struggle for national and social liberation, but who have all contributed in their own way to the making of the history of their country and have left an indelible mark in the minds of people."

Instalment. The challenge for the nation. Back on the home front. The liberation of our nation from the shackles of foreign domination had been a long and bitter struggle against the combined forces of British imperialism. The Indian people, men and women, had to wade through a sea of sacrifices, sufferings and heroic deeds to achieve this goal. Thousands gave up their lives in the cause of freedom. Many more were subjected to untold tortures and humiliations in British jails. But they never lost faith in the ultimate victory of their struggle. 

Time and again, the oppressor tried to crush this struggle by resort to sheer force. But the more they tried, the stronger grew the spirit of resistance among our people. At the same time, the Indian National Congress, under the able and inspired leadership of Mahatma Gandhi, had mobilized the entire country in a non-violent struggle against the British rule.

This was indeed a unique and unprecedented event in the history of mankind. For the first time in history, a nation was resisting a mighty foreign power, not with arms and violence, but with the force of moral and spiritual strength of its people. This was the miracle of Gandhism.

But the struggle was not without its sufferings and sacrifices. Thousands of our countrymen and women were arrested, beaten, jailed and even killed in the course of this struggle. The British Government tried to crush this movement by the most brutal methods. Ruthless repression, mass arrests, savage beatings, firing on unarmed crowds, these were the order of the day.

Yet, the indomitable spirit of our people remained unbroken. They faced these ordeals with a courage and determination that amazed the world. Undaunted by the severities of repression, they continued their march towards freedom. And in the end, the sheer moral force of their struggle compelled the mighty British Empire to loosen its stranglehold on our country.

The story of this epic struggle has become an enduring legacy for the people of India. It is a story of sacrifice, suffering and ultimate triumph of the human spirit over the forces of oppression. It is a story that will continue to inspire generations of Indians to come. For, in this struggle, the people of India had not only won their freedom, but had also reclaimed their lost dignity and self-respect.

The country, as it stands today, is the proud inheritor of this glorious legacy. It is our sacred duty to preserve and strengthen this legacy, to make it an integral part of the life and consciousness of our people. The institutions and values that grew out of this struggle must be zealously guarded and nurtured. The heroes and martyrs of this struggle must be remembered and honoured, not merely in words, but in deeds that uphold the ideals for which they fought and died.

This is the challenge before the nation today. To live up to the spirit and vision of our freedom struggle, to make the ideals of that struggle the guiding principles of our national life - this is the supreme test that history has placed before us. And we must not fail this test. For, in doing so, we shall be betraying not only the memory of our freedom fighters, but also the future of our great nation.

Tips for choosing healthy drinks for your child:
- Breast milk is best. Breastfeed your child for 6 months or longer.
- Give your child plain water with fluoride. Water from the tap (faucet) is safe and cheap.
- Give your child milk at scheduled meal and snack times.
- It is best not to put your child to bed with a bottle or sippy cup. If you do, the bottle or sippy cup should contain only water, nothing else.

Give your child cut-up or whole fruit instead of fruit juice.
If you give your child juice, wait until he is 6 months old. Offer your child no more than 4 to 6 ounces of 100-percent fruit juice each day. Serve juice in a cup.
If your child drinks from a sippy cup, it should contain only water or milk, nothing else. By age 12 to 14 months, most children can drink from a cup.

Do you know how much sugar is in each drink?
Teaspoons of sugar in each 4-ounce drink:
- Grape juice: 3 1/2
- Cola: 3 1/2
- Apple juice: 3
- Fruit drink: 3
- Chocolate milk: 2 1/2 
- Orange juice: 2
- Low-fat milk: 1 1/2
- Water: 0

The new health law puts affordable, quality health care
coverage within reach. These three tips can help you get

1 Affordable Health
Coverage is Available
Obamacare helps make quality, no-cost to low-cost
coverage available for millions of Californians. Covered
California, our state's health insurance marketplace, helps
you calculate if you qualify for Medi-Cal or a health plan
through private insurance. Financial assistance is
available for those who qualify. Visit www.CoveredCA.com
to learn more.

2 Health Care Coverage is Required
Starting January 1, 2014, most Californians will be
required to have health care coverage or pay a fee.

 If you already have health care coverage, you're set 
and do not need to do anything else.
 In 2014, not having insurance will cost you $95 or 1
percent of your annual income – whichever is greater.
In 2016, the fee will increase to $695 or 2.5 percent of
your annual income – again, whichever is greater.
 Not everyone will be required to have health care
coverage. Some exemptions exist. Find out more at
www.CoveredCA.com/individuals_and_families.html

3 Help is Available
Help with enrollment is available by phone, online or in
person. Enrollment into Medi-Cal is happening now, and
those who are eligible for private insurance through
Covered California can enroll between October 1, 2013
and March 31, 2014, with benefits beginning on
January 1, 2014. To learn more about your health care
coverage options and how to apply, visit
www.GetCoveredCA.com

SAMPLE
THE MESSAGES
G. CAMPAIGN STRATEGIES THE FUTURE OF LIVING WAGE RESOURCES CONTACTS
HOW DOES ECONOMIC SUSTAINABILITY WORK?
Economic sustainability seeks to identify resources and strategies that can generate living wages and create shared prosperity over the long term. It moves beyond traditional efforts to simply raise the minimum wage, and instead looks at systemic changes to make wages and productivity improvements more equitable.
POVERTY: A SYMPTOM OF ECONOMIC UNSUSTAINABILITY 
Poverty is a symptom of economic unsustainability. When wages fail to keep up with the cost of living, people struggle to afford the basics - housing, food, healthcare, and other necessities. This is not just a problem for low-wage workers, but also for many middle-class families.
THE POWER OF POLICY STRATEGIES
Policy strategies can help create the conditions for economic sustainability. These include measures to ensure that productivity gains are broadly shared, that workers have a stronger voice, and that the social safety net is robust enough to weather economic downturns.
ALTERNATIVE LIVING WAGE CALCULATION
A living wage is the minimum income necessary for a worker to meet their basic needs. The MIT Living Wage Calculator provides geographically specific living wage estimates that account for local costs of housing, food, healthcare, and other essentials. These estimates can inform policy and advocacy efforts.
PRODUCTIVE ALTERNATIVES TO THE 40-HOUR WORK WEEK
Many workers struggle to make ends meet even with full-time employment. Exploring alternatives to the traditional 40-hour work week, such as job sharing, flexible scheduling, and reduced hour models, could help improve work-life balance and economic security.
ECONOMY DRIVEN BY SHARED PROSPERITY
An economy driven by shared prosperity, where gains in productivity and technology are broadly distributed, is both more equitable and more sustainable in the long run. Policies that empower workers, strengthen social programs, and promote innovation can help create this vision.

Title: More tips for the pitch

When pitching a story:
- Be selective about who you pitch to. Do some research to find the right reporters, media contacts, and outlets for your story.
- Personalize your pitch. Mention why you think your story would be of interest to that particular outlet or reporter.
- Keep your pitch concise and to the point. Provide just the key details.
- Make sure your pitch contains a clear, compelling story idea.
- Time your pitch carefully. Consider when the reporter or outlet might be most receptive.
- Follow up, but don't be a pest. A single follow-up is usually sufficient.

When to call it quits:
- If you don't get a response after a few tries, it's probably time to move on.
- If a reporter expresses disinterest, believe them.
- If an outlet seems uninterested, shift your focus elsewhere.

Opportunities: Youth are vulnerable Workers

The youth labor force today is especially vulnerable. Many young workers are concentrated in jobs and industries that have been hit hardest by the COVID-19 pandemic. Young people often face lower wages, fewer benefits, and more precarious work. Strategies to improve job quality and access to living-wage jobs for young workers are important for supporting their economic security and well-being.

Threats: Age is a Wage Issue 

Younger workers often face wage discrimination and are more likely to be concentrated in lower-wage jobs, even when controlling for education and experience. Strategies to raise minimum wages, strengthen labor standards, and increase access to unions and collective bargaining can help ensure age does not determine a worker's pay.

Against the drifting snow,

The silent woods, the stillness all,

The trees, the rocks, the sky, the call
Of Nature's overthrow.

The desolation, the retreat,
The falling silence, the defeat—
The mountains in winter, white and still,
Brooding above the plain.

RULES AND REGULATIONS
FISHING & CAMPING
on LAND OWNED by
THE TOWN OF RENSSEERVILLE

It is mutually desirable that the natural beauty of these lands be preserved for the enjoyment of all who visit them. The following rules and regulations have been adopted to that end.

1. Fishing is permitted on waters owned and controlled by the Town. No fishing or camping is allowed on private lands except by permission of the owners.

2. Camp fires are permitted only in designated and properly equipped camping areas. All fires must be completely extinguished before leaving the camping area.

3. Camping is permitted only in designated camping areas. No tents, trailers or other camping equipment may be placed on these lands except in these areas.

4. Trash, litter and refuse must be placed in the containers provided or removed from the area.

5. Hunting and shooting are prohibited at all times.

6. The speed limit for all vehicles on town roads is 20 m.p.h.

7. Boating is prohibited on all town-owned waters.

8. No person shall use profane or abusive language or be guilty of any loud, boisterous or disorderly conduct.

9. No person shall deface, injure, cut, or destroy any tree, shrub, plant, building, sign or other property.

10. No person shall operate a motor vehicle in any area except on designated roads and parking areas.

11. The town reserves the right to refuse permission to camp to any person or persons and to request the removal of any campers who violate these rules.

VIOLATORS WILL BE PROSECUTED UNDER SECTION 1331 OF THE PENAL LAW OF THE STATE OF NEW YORK.

1. Create a strong media list. Use news, blogs, podcasts, and social media platforms to connect with your target audience.
2. Write a compelling narrative story. Connect the issues you're highlighting with the real-world impacts on the audience.
3. Work with TV news outlets early on to generate excitement and commitment. Secure strong champions for your cause.

TRAINING ON
Strengthening Military-Civilian Community Partnerships
To Respond to Sexual Assault

Community-based victim service providers who are not familiar with the military may find the system baffling and impenetrable. In a case where both community and military service providers respond to a victim of sexual assault, both need to know how to work together more effectively. With this training, participants can serve as knowledgeable resources for military installations throughout the United States.

Who is the training for?
The training is for civilian victim service providers and allied professionals who currently work with victims of sexual assault and who want to learn to improve services for victims who are members of the military.

What kind of training is it?
This is an interactive training that helps community victim service providers and allied professionals to establish partnerships with local military installations in order to effectively respond to the needs of sexual assault victims in the military. CEUs and a certificate of completion are available.

How do I get this training in my community?
Your organization can request this training from the Office for Victims of Crime Training and Technical Assistance Center (OVC TTAC). OVC TTAC will provide experienced instructors, an onsite coordinator, all training materials for the instructors, and a Participant Manual for each attendee at no cost to you or the participants. You will need to identify and secure a suitable training facility, supply audiovisual equipment, and invite your local service providers and allied professionals to attend. A minimum group of 30 people is required for the training. Visit https://www.ovcttac.gov/tr to obtain the application form. To learn more, send an e-mail to training@ovcttac.org.

For more information
Visit www.ovcttac.gov for more information about OVC TTAC and other trainings that are available in the OVC TTAC Training Catalog.

Strengthening Military-Civilian Community Partnerships To Respond to Sexual Assault training is the product of military-civilian partnerships among the following:
- U.S. Department of Defense, Sexual Assault Prevention and Response Office
- U.S. Army, Air Force, Navy, Marine Corps, and National Guard Sexual Assault and Response Office Program Managers 
- U.S. Department of Justice, Office for Victims of Crime
- U.S. Department of Justice, Office on Violence Against Women
- Pennsylvania Coalition Against Rape
- National Sexual Violence Resource Center
- A panel of national sexual assault subject matter experts

Transgender Health: Growing community leaders
617 transgender and gender-nonconforming people find safety and support in our transgender community drop-in center.

The program, the largest of its kind in the nation, links clients to a comprehensive array of transgender-competent, on-site medical, mental health, case management, and community support services regardless of HIV status.

Johanna, a client in our HIV care program for transgender women of color, participated in a three-day digital storytelling workshop where she learned how to create her own short film about her life, survival, transition, and HIV treatment. "Growing up I always felt different," she says. "I've known since the age of 5 that I wanted to be a girl." But she didn't start her transition until she was 45—twenty years after her HIV diagnosis. After years of battling addiction, homelessness, and poverty, she is now in treatment and her HIV viral load is undetectable. She's also working as a nurse in a health clinic and has started advocating for her community.
"At this point in my life, I'm comfortable with who I am," she says. "I'm a strong, Black woman. I'm the woman I always wanted to be."

See Johanna's story and many others at http://www.youtube.com/apiwellness

HIV CARE BY-THE-NUMBERS:
92% engaged in care
70% in treatment
66% virally suppressed

OUR CLIENTS         NATIONAL
engaged in care      40%
in treatment          37%
virally suppressed  30% 

HIV Care: Getting to Zero
464 people living with HIV access life-saving HIV treatment and care through our programs, including specialized services for transgender women of color, residents of the Tenderloin, and Asians and Pacific Islanders.

Our clients are considered the "hardest-to-reach"—they fight substance use, homelessness, poverty, and mental illness—and still they are making great strides in their treatment with the help of services tailored to their needs. Despite the barriers they face, they are outperforming the nation in managing the disease, making it less likely they will pass on the virus.

*Source: CDC National HIV Surveillance System and Medical Monitoring Project, 2011

HIV Prevention: Including gay youth and transgender women of color in PrEP
1,448
HIV tests provided to 
high-risk community
members

2,807
condoms
distributed

Now, young gay and bisexual men and transgender women of color will have access to innovative HIV prevention medication and support services. 
PrEP, or pre-exposure prophylaxis, is a pill that can protect people from HIV by taking a pill once a day.
Our Wellness Clinic is a PrEP provider and, with funding from Gilead, we are launching a comprehensive PrEP support program specifically for young gay and bisexual men (including transgender men) and transgender women of color. The program will include PrEP benefits navigation, case management, weekly support groups, a PrEP speakers bureau, and a social marketing campaign to educate the community about this new prevention option.

Capacity Building: Training the next generation of HIV providers
697 total clients
21 in-person trainings
9 California-specific
12 National

16 online trainings
5 webinars
2 four-week facilitated 
   e-courses, including
   9 live webinars

Almost 700 providers across the nation were trained to provide culturally-competent, high-impact HIV prevention services across the nation.

Our services include trainings, consultation, and general education to help individuals and organizations improve their ability to prevent HIV transmission in their communities and geographic areas. Our California Statewide Training & Education Program (C-STEP) sets the standard in HIV treatment and public benefits education and training for HIV and non-medical providers. Trainees can also access the most up-to-date information they need through our innovative online learning platform, offering both self-paced, facilitated, and peer-to-peer education.

resources.ocr_text:
TRENDS IN THE LIVING WAGE MOVEMENT:
Associated costs of living have increased by about 27% since 1968, while the minimum wage has decreased by 35% in its real value.

RESOURCES
- There is an increase in local living wage policies and ordinances. As of early 2000, over 100 living wage laws had been passed across the country.
- Living wage campaigns were focused on cities and counties to pass ordinances that set minimum wage levels pegged to the costs of basic needs.
- In Chicago, a city living wage ordinance requires city service contractors to pay a minimum wage that is indexed to inflation.
- In Chicago, the living wage law is $13.88 per hour with health benefits, or $15.43 per hour without health benefits.

CONTACTS
- Focuses on information, referrals, and advocacy to help individuals navigate social service systems, housing assistance, food assistance, childcare assistance, job search support, and other support services.

ADDENDA & NOTES
- The average living wage for a single adult in Oklahoma City is $11.18 per hour, based on analysis from the MIT Living Wage Calculator. For a family of 4 (2 adults, 2 children), the living wage is $23.34 per hour.
- The living wage can vary significantly across different states, cities, and even counties based on the local cost of living.
- Many workers earn wages that are not sufficient to meet their basic needs, even when working full-time. This has led to the growth of the living wage movement.
- The living wage is the hourly rate that an individual must earn to support themselves and their family, if applicable. It is a measure of the local cost of living, not the federal or state minimum wage.
- Proponents of the living wage argue it helps address income inequality and promotes self-sufficiency. Critics argue it can reduce job opportunities.
- Passage of living wage laws has been controversial, with debates over the appropriate level, coverage, and impact on the local economy and employment.

Two Typical Defensive Uses

As torture: typing to control which choices a person makes in a given situation means the user can, if they have power over them, essentially force them to believe or otherwise act against their will.

Example: If we can talk about our problems, then we might solve them, can. In this case, we are trying to convince the other that their problems, then we might solve them.

Example: If you don't get to your room clean, then you won't be allowed to go out. Here, we are using this power to influence the other's behavior.

Example: If you don't get your chores done, then you will not be allowed to watch TV. This is a common way for a parent to control a child.

Typing could also be used to identify patterns and/or predict how the other person may react to various scenarios - this could help someone gain an unfair advantage in negotiations or other interactions.

Here, we are using this period of time where the other person is confined or otherwise has reduced ability to control their own situation - to pressure them into doing what we want, even if it goes against their will.

This is an example of how typing can be used as a tool of coercion and control, rather than mutual understanding and problem-solving.

It's critical to ensure that typing is used ethically and not as a means to manipulate or dominate others. The responsible use of this technology should empower people, not take away their autonomy.

Here is the complete text extracted from the image:

Using Non-Discriminatory Communication Tools

A Few Basic Types of Questions

"You are"
"Your ideas"
"You and others"
"You as a"

That's it, folks.

What each of these sentences may have some truth in them is true:
"Women are..." We may say some things about women that are over-generalized.
"Asians are just so..." Black people, Latinos/Hispanics, Native Americans... There are problematic stereotypes.
"The handicapped, physically/mentally disabled, or elderly, for example, are usually..." Disability is often stigmatized.
"The gay/lesbian community is..." Sexual orientation is often misunderstood.

Many statements of generalizations are problematic. We may say "Women are intuitive" or "Students today just..."

We may say: "Doctors only care about money," or "Teenagers are rebellious and irresponsible."

The problem if they say: "Women are more caring and cooperative in the office." or "Older workers are more experienced and reliable." This may contain some truth, but can put people in boxes.

Whenever someone says: "These kids these days..." or "Lately, Hispanics have been..." this may tell us more about the speaker's attitudes and biases than about any group.

I believe it is much more effective if we ask: "What is your experience with women in the workplace?" or "How do you feel older workers contribute in the office?"

This shifts the discussion away from generalizations and stereotypes, and focuses more on the individual person's experience and perspectives.

The following types of questions would generally work better:
"Could you tell me more about your impression of older workers?"
"The research we've done suggests there are many ways people learn and communicate effectively. What has your experience been in this area?"

The goal here is to steer the conversation in a direction that draws out nuanced, person-centered perspectives rather than relying on broad generalizations. This approach is more likely to foster mutual understanding and productive dialogue.

VACCINES ADULTS NEED

Vaccines aren't just for kids! Adults need vaccines to protect against many serious diseases. This chart shows which vaccines are recommended for adults.

Take this guide to your healthcare provider and ask what vaccines you need. Remember, vaccines protect you and also keep you from spreading illness to others.

VACCINES FOR ADULTS	19-49 YEARS OLD	50-64 YEARS OLD	65 YEARS OLD & OLDER
Chickenpox (Varicella)	You need 2 doses of this vaccine if you've never had chickenpox.
Hepatitis A (Hep A)	To be protected against Hep A you need 2 doses of this vaccine, at least 6 months apart. It is especially recommended for travelers outside the U.S.
Hepatitis B (Hep B)	To be protected against Hep B, you need 3 doses of this vaccine, spread over a 6 month period.
Human Papilloma Virus (HPV)	This vaccine is currently available to people under age 27. It requires 3 doses.	Not recommended for this age group.
Influenza (Flu)	You need a dose every fall or winter.
Measles, Mumps, Rubella	You need 2 doses of this vaccine if you were born after 1956.	Not recommended for this age group.
Meningitis (Meningococcal)	If you are a young adult going to college and plan to live in a dormitory, you need this vaccine regardless of age. Some forms of meningitis are not vaccine preventable.
Pneumonia (Pneumococcal)	You need 1-2 doses if you smoke cigarettes or have certain medical conditions. Some forms of pneumonia are not vaccine preventable.	You need 1 dose at age 65 (or older) if you've never been vaccinated.
Shingles (Zoster)	Not recommended for this age group.	You need this vaccine if you are age 60 or older.
Tetanus, Diphtheria, Pertussis (Whooping Cough)	Everyone needs this vaccine. It only became available in 2005, so if you haven't had it since then, you should get a booster every 10 years.

If you are around pregnant women, infants or young children, be sure you get this vaccination.

If you travel outside the United States, you may need more vaccines. 
For information contact the Adult Immunization and Travel Clinic at (415) 554-2625.

VaccinesForAdults.org
Call 311 - San Francisco Department of Public Health

National Park Service

Golden Gate National Recreation Area

You Can Make A Difference

Volunteers at Golden Gate National Recreation Area, Muir Woods National Monument, and Fort Point National Historic Site learn new skills, teach others, and stay active and involved. They help to preserve these precious, diverse resources, of one of America's most popular National Parks for today's visitors and future generations.

Volunteers at the park play a vital role in many aspects of park operations. They bring wonderful enthusiasm, energy, knowledge, and a diverse perspective to everything.

Be A Park Hero!
 Collect data on birds of prey at the premier hawk watching site on the west coast.
 Develop and present programs for the general public and school groups.
 Remove non-native plants, grow native plants, and work in one of the park's nurseries.
 Restore and maintain structures like Battery Townsley.

Volunteer opportunities at Golden Gate National Recreation Area are as diverse as the natural and cultural resources of the park. History buffs, naturalists, artists, students, gardeners and many more people have found a place to share their skills at Golden Gate. Each volunteer's contribution makes a big difference!

Greet park visitors at a visitor center

Maintain the walking paths

What every manager should know:

By Maximizer, Inc.

The basis of this checklist is:
1) Basic business principles 
2) Psychological factors in the workplace
3) Your own experience and observation
4) Common sense

This isn't about making you work harder - it's about working smarter. The following items are designed to help you become a better manager. 
Go through the list and see how many of these simple things you're already doing. Then concentrate on the ones you've overlooked or need to improve.

1. Set clear, measurable goals for your department/team
2. Communicate these goals clearly and repeatedly 
3. Monitor progress and give frequent feedback 
4. Praise good work, don't just criticize poor work
5. Delegate authority and responsibility - don't try to do everything yourself 
6. Listen to your employees and encourage their ideas and input
7. Support your employees in their career development
8. Provide necessary training and resources 
9. Set a good example through your own actions and attitude
10. Address problems promptly and constructively
11. Be consistent and fair in your management style
12. Show appreciation for a job well done
13. Encourage teamwork and cooperation
14. Be accessible and approachable
15. Make decisions in a timely manner
16. Don't play favorites
17. Communicate openly and honestly
18. Admit your own mistakes
19. Back up your employees when appropriate
20. Reward long-term contribution, not just short-term results

There's a lot more, but this covers some of the basics that every manager should know. How do you measure up?

resources.ocr_text:
What is 2-1-1?

- 2-1-1 is an easy to remember telephone number that connects callers to information about critical health and human services available in their community.
- 2-1-1 reaches approximately 270 million people (90% of the total U.S. population) covering all 50 states (including 41 states with 90%+ coverage), the District of Columbia and Puerto Rico. Yet, millions of Americans still need to be connected.
- America needs 2-1-1 to be accessible nationwide. As the number of organizations providing specialized services is on the rise, people find it frustrating and confusing to access community services. 2-1-1 provides a one-stop service for vital information.
- While services that are offered through 2-1-1 vary from community to community, 2-1-1 provides callers with information about and referrals to human services for every day needs and in times of crisis. For example, 2-1-1 can offer access to the following types of services:

o Basic Human Needs Resource: food banks, clothing, shelters, rent assistance, utility assistance.
o Physical and Mental Health Resources: medical information lines, crisis intervention services, support groups, counseling, drug and alcohol intervention, rehabilitation, health insurance programs, Medicaid and Medicare, maternal health, children's health insurance programs.
o Employment Support: unemployment benefits, financial assistance, job training, transportation assistance, education programs.
o Support for Older Americans and Persons with Disabilities: home health care, adult day care, congregate meals, Meals on Wheels, respite care, transportation, and homemaker services.
o Support for Children, Youth and Families: Quality childcare, Success by 6, after school programs, Head Start, family resource centers, summer camps and recreation programs, mentoring, tutoring, protective services.
o Volunteer opportunities and donations.

WHAT IS LIVING WAGE

• The wage needed to meet a family's basic needs, including food, housing, utilities, transportation, healthcare, childcare, and other necessities, while also allowing for some savings.

• Considers the local cost of living, and is higher than the federal minimum wage.

THE FUTURE OF LIVING WAGE

• A living wage is a crucial part of addressing poverty and promoting economic security.

• As costs continue to rise, a living wage will become increasingly important to ensuring families can meet their basic needs.

• While some progress has been made, living wages remain out of reach for many workers.

RESOURCES

• Living Wage Calculator: livingwage.mit.edu
• Economic Policy Institute: epi.org
• Center for Economic and Policy Research: cepr.net
• National Employment Law Project: nelp.org
• Interfaith Worker Justice: iwj.org

CONTACTS

• Local Advocacy Organizations
• State or Local Government Offices
• Community Foundations

What is the problem?
For most people, gambling is an enjoyable activity, entertaining but the potential for loss can become excessive, emotional, and financial. Poorer gambling can develop into a gambling problem.

Symptoms of a Gambling Problem:
- Needing to gamble with increasing amounts of money to achieve the same excitement
- Becoming restless or irritable when trying to cut down or stop gambling
- Gambling as a way to escape problems or relieve anxiety or depression
- Trying to conceal the extent of involvement with gambling
- Returning another day to try to win back losses (chasing losses)
- Jeopardizing or losing a significant relationship, job, or school/career opportunity because of gambling
- Relying on others to provide money to relieve a desperate financial situation caused by gambling

If gambling is causing significant problems, you may need help:
Self-Help Books and Counseling
Telephone-Based Counseling
In-Person Counseling Services

Services Available:
Self-Help Workbooks
Telephone-Based Counseling
In-Person Counseling Services (such as individual, group, and family)
Referrals to Other Fee Services (such as Gamble Free Services)
Sometimes legal or financial assistance may also be needed.

For more information, call 1-888-960-7788 or visit www.ncpgambling.org.

When life hands you struggles, then it's the right time to seek the release. There are professionals and organizations ready to assist you with a variety of needs, free of charge or on a sliding scale based on your income.

My Stuff Got Stolen Out!

We're Here to Help, Not Judge

resources.ocr_text:
What's great about it
Most people would. They change the way they do business and even their lives. They want to be in control.
They say they want change, but really they only want to change so much. They say they want to be different, but they still 
want to be accepted and comfortable.
The gay community can be like that.They want to be just like everyone else, but often they want to make some special claims or benefits.
Gender rules may be relaxed, but there are still some gender norms and roles that are expected.
Interracial marriages are still some of the quickest to end in divorce.
Gays and lesbians want family rights, such as domestic partnership and adoption, but often the community has a hard time fully accepting kids in gay families.
Some people think being gay means having an exciting single lifestyle, but many gay people want to have kids and families, just like everyone else.
You can be pretty conservative in many aspects of your life, while still being "gay".
There's an emphasis about being "normal and successful", whatever that means.

Coming Out
It's a good idea to "come out" to family and friends. It can be very liberating, freeing you from having to hide a major part of your life.
But coming out is an ongoing process. You may have to come out again and again in different situations. 
Gay, lesbian and bisexual youth may need to come out to their parents, school and friends.
Will this feel better when their family and friends are accepting? Or will it feel daunting, like a trial run for future disclosures?
Will your life be changed by coming out? Or will people you thought would be supportive, become distant?

You tell 1 or 2 close friends, then the others. You tell your parents. You tell your coworkers. It's an ongoing process.
Your cell may still ring and it's your mom saying "Hey, I was talking to my friend and she didn't realize you're gay."
You can celebrate the victories, and brace yourself for the setbacks.
You will feel a new freedom, but also face new challenges. You tell a few more friends, and life goes on.

Sexuality: More than sex
Being LGBTQ+ is about more than just sex. It's about your whole identity and experience. Your relationships, your community, your life.
Some people mistakenly think LGBTQ+ people are only focused on sex. But being LGBTQ+ is a complete identity, not just a sex act.
Sexual orientation is only one part of a person's overall identity and experience. It doesn't define the whole person.
You have a life outside of your sexuality. You have hobbies, interests, a job, friends, and a community.
Your sexuality is just one aspect of who you are. It's an important part, but not the only part.

Your conventional medicines, treatments, and surgeries are just not working for you... What else is there? Perhaps you've already discovered how wholistic approaches, like acupuncture, massage, or yoga are making a difference. You are an active partner in your healthcare. This allows you to explore all possibilities - to make conscious choices about your treatment and to put your life and health back in your own hands.

PAYS FOR RISK TAKING: You're going to have to make some tough decisions, possibly take some risks to get the results you want. Your current prescribed drugs, which may be hazardous to your health in the long run, are not giving you the relief and results you desire. You've decided to look at alternative therapies that are safe and effective, that treat the whole person, not just the symptoms. This is a courageous step in your journey toward wellness.

A VISION FOR HEALTH: Your self-confidence grows as you become empowered to take charge of your own health care. You have learned how to be an active, informed consumer of healthcare services. You now know how to access the information and therapies that are most appropriate for your individual needs. You are discovering more about your own innate healing abilities, the body's natural tendency toward balance and homeostasis.

PAYOFFS FOR TAKING: You no longer accept your doctors' pronouncements as the final word. You take responsibility for researching and making decisions about your own care. You've educated yourself about a variety of safe, effective alternative therapies. You are willing to explore new approaches, even if they challenge the medical mainstream. This pays off in improved health and a greater sense of personal empowerment.

At the Crossroads reaches out to homeless youth and young adults at lives to build healthy and fulfilling lives.

WHY
We work with young people and organizations to make real changes that address the causes of homelessness.
Homelessness is a reality for thousands of our community's young people, who have few options or support when facing difficult circumstances.
Many of the young people we serve have experienced trauma, abuse, neglect, and dysfunctional families. 
We want to help them move past the struggles they've faced and into a future of stability and hope.

WHAT
We aim to break the cycle of homelessness by getting to the root causes and work closely with the young people we serve to address their individual needs.
We want to help young people leave homelessness behind and gain the skills and resources they need to thrive. Our services include:
- Housing - safe, stable homes
- Counseling - mental health and trauma-informed care
- Education - job training, life skills, college support
- Community - belonging, community engagement

HOW
At the Crossroads reaches thousands of young people each year through our partnerships with over 90 youth-serving organizations.
We walk the streets and visit homeless encampments to identify the most vulnerable youth and invite them to connect with our services.
We listen to the stories of young people and respond with practical, tailored assistance.
We don't just offer handouts; we work alongside young people to build stability and self-sufficiency for the long term.

What is WMIC?
WMIC is a new organization which focuses on promotion and marketing of Oriental medical professionals. We are trying to build a bridge between Chinese medicine and mainstream medical community.

The goals of WMIC are:
1. To promote and raise awareness of Oriental medicine in North America.
2. To create a professional network and support system for Oriental medical practitioners.
3. To bridge the gap between Oriental and conventional medicine and encourage collaboration.
4. To educate the public about the benefits and effectiveness of Oriental medicine.

Why join WMIC?
1. Increased public exposure and access to new patients.
2. Networking opportunities with other Oriental medical practitioners.
3. Referrals from WMIC's marketing and outreach efforts.
4. Continuing education and professional development resources.
5. Advocacy for Oriental medicine within the mainstream medical community.
6. Participation in WMIC's public education initiatives.

resources.ocr_text:
Ledning from Within
Poetic Poems
by Petter J. Palm

If a man has good thoughts, and expresses them clearly, the world will be the better for it.
But if a man has bad thoughts, I think it is far better that he should keep them to himself.
At least then they are only doing harm to himself, and will not be going about spreading poison.
To use words wrongly and to say what you do not mean is the worst thing a person can do.

There is no good talking about purity being more important than anything else, when you can't even control your thoughts. Talk is cheap. Only what we do is of any importance. What we say, the impressions we give, may sometimes be the opposite of what we are. We should be more careful about what we say and what we think, for our thoughts and our actions are the things that make us what we are.

We can never get ahead of the judgement of posterity, that's why we must be so careful of our thoughts and our deeds.

Nature deals gently with them who deal gently with her. You can't win her over by force; she'll only retaliate. But if you approach her softly, she'll be ready to share her secrets with you. The best thing is to meet her with reverence, and she'll respond in kind.

The great thing about art and poetry is that they have the power to move the soul. Words can sometimes penetrate deeper than actions. But words must ring true. Anything false or pretended will only breed contempt. The world has enough of that already.

People are quick to find fault, but slow to praise. That's why we must be very careful about our thoughts and our speech. It's so easy to destroy, but so hard to build up. We must think and act with the greatest care. That's the only way to make the world a better place.

Nelson Seal Prest J. Palm
Whitney 1916

resources.ocr_text: It has been found that the stream of consciousness is always onward, onward, onward. It has no halting-place, but is rushing, rushing, rushing, with a headlong speed. The attempt to grasp it, to arrest it, to detain it, even for a moment, is futile. It slips away, eludes us, runs through our fingers like a stream of water. Each attempt to arrest it but sweeps it the more rapidly onward. It seems to flow on with the rushing rapidity of a mighty river, with a force that is irresistible. This stream of consciousness has its sources far up in the unknown depths of the mind, and it is fed by countless springs and tributaries. It wells up from the hidden springs of sensation, of emotion, of impulse, of desire, of aversion, of love, of hate, and of a thousand other nameless urges and proclivities. These mingle and blend and intermingle, and the resulting stream is shot through with a thousand hues and a thousand varying currents, now swift, now slow, now deep, now shallow, now smooth, now turbulent, now dark, now clear. It is a veritable kaleidoscope of shifting impressions, ever changing, ever varying, never the same from one moment to the next. It is the very stuff of which our mental life is made. It is the warp and woof of the tapestry of consciousness. To attempt to arrest it, to seize it, to imprison it, is as futile as to attempt to arrest the rushing waters of Niagara and to hold them still. This is not to say that there is no order, no continuity, in the stream of consciousness. There is, indeed, a certain unity and coherence which binds the whole together and gives it a certain individuality. But this unity and coherence are not of our own making. They are not the result of our conscious effort to arrest and control the stream. They are, rather, the result of the subtle and elusive workings of the mind itself, of which we are but dimly aware. The more we strive to grasp and to control the stream, the more it slips away from us. The more we try to arrest it, the more rapid becomes its onward rush. This is the nature of the stream of consciousness.

We see: - Variety of the kinds of the ground, - Large grains - Large granules - Granules larger than 2/10 mm - Agrarial grains - Straw colour - Yellow - Marly-White

Cette image, prise en compte depuis le 19 aot 1996, permet de vérifier que ces matériaux sont constitués de quartz, de feldspaths et de micas. La couleur jaune ou blanc-jaunâtre des granules et des grains indique la présence de minéraux ferrugineux.

Vernon, Avril 22. - M. Danot informs us that the same result has been obtained in the analysis of the specimens received from "Womdien".

Cette étude montre que ces formations, de nature détritique, se composent essentiellement de minéraux primaires, tels que le quartz et les feldspaths. La présence de micas est également constatée. L'altération de ces minéraux a conduit à la formation de produits ferrugineux, responsables des colorations observées.
