6. CAMPAIGN STRATEGIES
THE FUTURE OF LIVING WAGE
RESOURCES
CONTACTS
5. NUTS & BOLTS OF GETTING 
THE MESSAGE OUT

Guaranteed minimum income
Should a living wage be:
- A household-based allowance?
- An individual-based allowance?
- Tied to the number of dependents?
- Tied to local cost of living?
- Adjusted for factors like age, marital status, disability?
Concern over the impact on incentives to work

The issues of implementation:
- The need for legislative change to implement living wage.
- The likely political hurdles - national, state, local.
- Challenges to enforce and monitor implementation, especially across diverse employment sectors.
- How to deal with businesses that seek to circumvent living wage laws.
- Concerns about the costs and funding of a living wage.

PROFILE ON WORKERS:
- Reliable worker household survey to gain reliable data on living costs and wages.
- Research and policy recommendations on how to structure living wage standards.
- Engage with unions and workers' associations to build support.
- Build coalitions with community, faith, and civil rights groups to create a diverse base of support.
- Train workers to be effective advocates in community outreach and media work.
- Develop replicable models of living wage campaigns and implementation.

- Research low-wage sectors, job types, demographics to identify priority areas.
- Pinpoint employers, industries, and locales with the greatest need and potential for living wage campaigns.
- Identify key policy opportunities - proposed legislation, ballot initiatives, contract negotiations.
- Analyze existing living wage laws and their impacts to build stronger policy models.
- Collect and disseminate worker testimonials to put a human face on the need.

- Develop and maintain a comprehensive database of living wage resources, models, and contacts.
- Build a network of legal, policy, and academic experts to provide research and strategic advice.
- Cultivate relationships with media outlets to ensure regular coverage.
- Coordinate with other living wage campaigns to share best practices and strategic insights.
- Provide training and technical assistance to local living wage efforts.

Young adult Allies can help
-Free assistance to get state-issued ID, birth certificates, Social Security cards, and more
-Guidance on requirements and process
-Help overcoming barriers like fees, transportation, documentation, etc.
-Referrals to other services as needed

The Gadlin's State Adventure
"If you've ever had a great idea and get excited about it, but then feel overwhelmed once you start the process, this resource is for you."
Shops at a rocky road gear up for an MW-wide change
Shopper's say "I can't wait! It'll make our shopping so much better!"
Store manager, Annie Williams, said "We've been planning this for a while now. It's going to be amazing and worth the wait!"
When excitement for the change is met with the reality, there may be challenges. But having support and resources along the way makes it easier.

Immigration with Laura
"I wish I knew there was this kind of help before I started trying to get my citizenship. I felt so alone and didn't know where to turn."
If you're going through the immigration process, whether for citizenship, a visa, or other status, there are organizations that can provide free or low-cost assistance. They can help with paperwork, understanding requirements, and navigating the system.

How do I apply?
Intake and application process varies by organization, but generally includes:
- Contact the organization to inquire about services
- Provide documentation as requested (ID, income info, etc.)
- Attend an intake appointment to assess your situation and eligibility
- If eligible, work with staff to complete application process

Larkin Street Youth Services
701 Sutter Street, Suite 2, San Francisco, CA 94109
1-800-669-6196
www.larkinstreetyouth.org
Larkin Street provides youth between the ages of 12 and 24 with the help they need to rebuild their lives. Each year, more than 4,000 youth walk through their doors seeking help. They give them a place where they can feel safe; rebuild their sense of self-respect, trust, and hope; learn school, life and job skills; and find the confidence to build a future. 
Larkin Street was founded in 1984 by a group of local business owners, church members, and neighbors who were concerned by the rising number of young people engaging in risky behaviors on the streets of San Francisco. With 25 comprehensive youth service programs located throughout San Francisco in over 15 sites, Larkin Street Youth Services is now an internationally recognized model successfully integrating housing, education, employment and health services to get homeless and at-risk kids off the streets. Services include a Drop-In Center, Referral Center, Medical Clinic, Substance Abuse, Mental Health and HIV Prevention Programs, Education and Employment Services, and Emergency, Transitional and Long-Term Housing.

Huckleberry Youth Programs
3310 Geary Boulevard, San Francisco, CA 94118
(415) 668-2622
www.huckleberryyouth.org
Huckleberry's mission is to educate, inspire, and support underserved youth to develop healthy life choices, to maximize their potential, and to realize their dreams. Since 1967, they have accomplished this by providing San Francisco and Marin youth and their families with a network of services and opportunities by caring peers and adults. They seek to empower young people to develop and maintain healthy relationships as well as promote their talents, leadership and health; to assist youth and their families in overcoming the obstacles they may encounter, which can include family concerns, drug and alcohol abuse, mental health challenges, teen pregnancy, sexually transmitted infections, violence, social and economic inequities, and physical and sexual abuse; and to assist clients in navigating complex social welfare, educational and juvenile justice systems.
Huckleberry also operates Huckleberry House, which offers continuous 24-hour crisis services and emergency shelter to high-need youth between the ages of 11 and 17. Located on Page Street (at Lyon) in San Francisco, Huckleberry House has the distinction of being the oldest program for runaway and homeless youth in the country. Program goals are to alleviate problems of runaway and homeless youth by providing 24-hour crisis intervention and resolution services, reunite the youth with their families, empower youth to identify healthy

This Women's Resource Center is one of the many services provided by the YWCA of White Plains & Central Westchester as part of its mission to help women and their families with counseling, support, advocacy and education. The Center's purpose is to serve as a resource and referral service for women seeking information on a variety of topics. The resource library contains materials on legal issues, health, sexuality, parenting, career development, relationships, spirituality, finances, self-esteem, and much more.

The Women's Resource Center is staffed by a coordinator and staffed by volunteers. Services are free and confidential. Hours are Monday through Friday 9 AM to 5 PM.

Funding for this project was provided in part through a grant from The Shelby Cullom Davis Foundation.

The Women's Resource Center is located in the YWCA of White Plains & Central Westchester at 515 North Street, White Plains, NY 10605. The telephone number is (914) 949-6227 ext 2155. The website is www.ywcawpc.org.

¿Usted es residente y necesita ayuda con un problema de facturación, servicio o seguridad con relación a un servicio público, y ya contactó a la compañía y habló con su representante?
¡La Oficina de Asuntos del Consumidor de la Comisión de Servicios Públicos de California (CPUC) está aquí para ayudarle! La Oficina de Asuntos del Consumidor asiste a los residentes que tienen preguntas sobre las tarifas o los servicios de electricidad, gas natural, teléfono o agua potable y alcantarillado, y ayuda a los residentes que no logran solucionar un problema con su compañía de servicios públicos.

Llame: 1-800-649-7570
Consulte: www.cpuc.ca.gov/PUC/CEC/e_complaint/
Escriba: CPUC Consumer Affairs Branch, 505 Van Ness Ave., San Francisco, CA 94102

¿Desea hacer un comentario sobre algún procedimiento o política de la CPUC?
Contacte a la Oficina del Consejero Público de la CPUC para dar sus opiniones o comentarios informales sobre los procedimientos de la CPUC y/o cuestiones relativas a las políticas. Los comentarios informales escritos que se envían por correo electrónico o a través del Servicio Postal de los EE. UU. son la forma más eficaz de expresar su reacción completa y precisa sobre un procedimiento de la CPUC y/o una cuestión relativa a una política. La Oficina del Consejero Público brinda información y consejos a los residentes y a grupos sobre cómo participar formalmente en un procedimiento de la CPUC y el modo de presentar una queja formal, así como los Medios Alternativos de Resolución de Conflictos.

Llame: 1-866-849-8390 o al 415-703-2074
Consulte: www.cpuc.ca.gov/PUC/aboutus/Divisions/CSID/Public+Advisor/
Correo electrónico: public.advisor@cpuc.ca.gov
Escriba: CPUC Public Advisor's Office, 505 Van Ness Ave., Room 2103, San Francisco, CA 94102

¿Tiene alguna queja sobre una compañía de mudanzas intraestatales, limusinas, autobuses de traslado al aeropuerto, o Compañía de Red de Transporte (INC o compañía de transporte compartido)?
Contacte a la Sección de Aplicación de Normas de Transporte para presentar una queja sobre transportistas de pasajeros —es decir, limusinas, compañías de transporte compartido— o transportistas intraestatales de enseres domésticos —es decir, compañías de mudanzas—.

Llame: Transportistas de pasajeros: 1-800-894-9444

Consulte: www.cpuc.ca.gov/PUC/aboutus/Divisions/CSID/Public+Advisor/
Correo electrónico: ciu_intake@cpuc.ca.gov
Escriba: CPUC Complaint Intake Unit – Transportation Enforcement Section, Safety and Enforcement Division, 505 Van Ness Ave., San Francisco, CA 94102
